title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
Two Tuesdays
Tuesday without AI:
Sarah, a program coordinator at a community nonprofit, arrives at 8:30 AM. She spends 45 minutes drafting a grant progress report, rewriting the executive summary three times. She spends 30 minutes composing emails to four partner organizations, each needing a slightly different tone. After lunch, she takes an hour to create slides for Thursday’s board meeting, struggling with formatting. She spends 40 minutes manually organizing meeting notes from last week into action items. At 4 PM she realizes she still hasn’t started the donor thank-you letters. She stays until 6:15.
Tuesday with AI:
Sarah arrives at 8:30 AM. She pastes her quarterly data into Claude and uses a BRIEFS-structured prompt to generate a draft progress report in 4 minutes. She edits for accuracy and voice — done in 20 minutes total. She drafts all four emails using a prompt template she built last month, adjusting each in 2 minutes — 15 minutes total. After lunch, she uploads her notes to ChatGPT and asks for a slide outline with speaker notes — she refines it into a polished deck in 30 minutes. She pastes last week’s meeting transcript into NotebookLM and extracts action items in 3 minutes. At 3 PM she generates personalized donor thank-you letters using a template prompt that pulls from her donor database. She leaves at 4:45 with everything done, including 30 minutes she spent learning a new AI tool she’d been curious about.
Same job. Same person. Same competence. The difference isn’t talent or work ethic — it’s workflow design. Sarah didn’t become smarter. She became AI-augmented.

Two Tuesdays — In YOUR Field

HealthcareEducationSmall BusinessGovernment


Without AI: A clinic manager spends 45 minutes writing follow-up care instructions for 8 discharged patients, each with different conditions. She spends 30 minutes on insurance pre-authorization paperwork. She manually reviews patient satisfaction surveys for monthly report.
With AI: She uses a BRIEFS-structured template to generate personalized care instructions in 2 minutes each (16 min total, then reviews for accuracy). Pre-auth paperwork is drafted by AI from structured inputs (10 min). Patient surveys are analyzed by AI with themes extracted (5 min). She leaves an hour early — and spends 20 minutes of that reading about a new clinical AI tool.


Without AI: A teacher spends 90 minutes creating a quiz for Chapter 7, writing 20 questions from scratch. She spends 40 minutes writing report card comments for 28 students. She spends 30 minutes formatting a lesson plan for an observation.
With AI: She prompts Claude with Chapter 7 learning objectives and gets 30 draft questions in 5 minutes, selects and refines 20 (25 min total). Report card comments are drafted from her grade book notes (15 min to generate + review). Lesson plan is reformatted with AI to match the observation template (10 min). Saved: 110 minutes.


Without AI: A bakery owner spends an hour writing this week’s social media posts (7 posts). She spends 45 minutes updating her website menu descriptions. She spends 30 minutes responding to customer review replies.
With AI: Social media posts drafted with a prompt template she built once (15 min to generate + customize). Menu descriptions updated from a master ingredients list (10 min). Review responses generated with appropriate tone for each (15 min). Saved: 95 minutes. She uses them to experiment with a new recipe.


Without AI: A county program coordinator spends 2 hours compiling data from 4 departments into a board report. She drafts 6 email summaries to different stakeholders. She writes a policy FAQ update.
With AI: Board report compiled using AI to merge and summarize data sources (45 min with verification). Email summaries generated from the same report, tone-adjusted per stakeholder (20 min). FAQ update drafted by AI referencing the latest policy documents (15 min). Saved: 100 minutes.





Sarah is fictional. The underlying numbers are real.
In 2023, researchers from Harvard Business School, Wharton, MIT, and Warwick partnered with Boston Consulting Group to run a preregistered randomized controlled trial on AI’s effect on knowledge work. They recruited 758 BCG consultants and randomly assigned them to complete 18 realistic consulting tasks either with or without GPT-4 access (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; peer-reviewed version, Dell’Acqua et al., 2025, Organization Science).
For tasks inside the capability frontier of the AI — drafting, ideating, structuring arguments, analyzing interview notes — the AI-assisted group completed 12.2% more tasks, completed them 25.1% faster, and produced work rated 40% higher in quality by independent graders. Consultants whose baseline performance was below the group average improved 43% — the authors called this the “performance equalizer” effect.
But the study also included one task that was designed to fall outside the AI’s capability frontier. On that task, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce the correct answer. The AI confidently produced plausible but wrong output, and consultants who deferred to it got worse results than they would have on their own.
The authors coined the term “jagged technological frontier” — AI capabilities are uneven and the edges aren’t obvious. Two tasks that look identical in difficulty can sit on opposite sides of what the AI actually does well.
Sarah’s Tuesday works because her tasks sit inside the frontier. The rest of this module teaches you how to tell the difference.






Common Misconceptions About AI Productivity




“AI saves time automatically” — It saves time when you INVEST time designing the right workflow. A bad prompt wastes more time than no prompt.
“AI writes better than me” — AI writes FASTER than you. Whether it writes better depends on the prompt, the task, and how much you edit. The Critic, not Ghostwriter approach preserves YOUR quality.
“Prompt libraries are cheating” — They’re efficiency. A surgeon doesn’t reinvent the checklist for each operation. You don’t reinvent the prompt for each email.
“Vibe coding = real software engineering” — It’s great for prototypes and personal tools. For anything involving security, reliability, or scale, you need a real developer.
“If I use AI for everything, I’ll forget how to do things myself” — This is the cognitive offloading trap from Module 1. Use AI to handle mechanical tasks. Keep the judgment and creativity muscles exercised.



This module gives you Sarah’s toolkit.

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
section: Before We Start: How to Evaluate an AI Tool
text:
Before We Start: How to Evaluate an AI Tool
New AI tools launch every week. Most aren’t worth your time. Before committing to any tool, run it through the 5-Question Test:






The 5-Question Test for AI Tools




Does it solve a problem I actually have? (Not a cool demo — a real friction point in my workflow)
Is it better than what I’m already doing? (Including the time to learn it)
Where does my data go? (Cloud? Local? Shared with third parties? Used for training?)
What does it cost — really? (Free tier limitations? Subscription creep? Hidden usage fees?)
Will it still exist in 6 months? (Is the company funded? Does it have real users? Or is it a demo?)

If any answer makes you uneasy, keep looking. The best AI tool is the one you’ll actually use consistently — not the one with the most features.

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
AI for Writing and Communication
Writing is the #1 use case for generative AI. But there’s a right way and a wrong way.

The Wrong Way: AI as Ghostwriter

“Write a report about our Q3 fundraising results.”

The AI produces a generic report with placeholder language. You spend 30 minutes editing it to sound like you, fixing inaccuracies, adding actual numbers. You would have been faster writing from scratch.


The Right Way: AI as Critic, Coach, and Collaborator
The Critic Approach — write YOUR draft first, then use AI to improve it:

“You are my critical peer reviewer. Do not rewrite my text. Diagnose and explain.
Evaluate my draft using this rubric: 1. Purpose and audience fit 2. Executive summary clarity (under 120 words?) 3. Argument structure and flow 4. Evidence quality and citation needs 5. Actionable recommendations 6. Professional tone and formatting
For each item, give: a 2-3 sentence diagnosis, one high-impact fix, and one example sentence starter I can use.
At the end, list 3 sources or data points I should locate to strengthen the argument. Do not fabricate citations.”

This prompt — adapted from a real university classroom exercise — keeps YOUR voice in the writing while using AI to identify weaknesses you’d miss. The AI reviews; you revise. The output is genuinely yours, genuinely improved.


The Coach Approach — AI helps you improve the PROCESS of writing:

“I need to write a professional email to a professor requesting a deadline extension. I tend to over-explain and sound apologetic. Coach me: what should I include, what should I leave out, and what tone should I aim for? Don’t write the email — help me write it better.”



Ready-to-Use Writing Prompts
Professional Email Coach: > “Rewrite this draft email for clarity and tone. Keep it under 120 words. Include 2 subject line options and a polite ask with a specific time window. [Paste email]”
Executive Summary Check: > “Evaluate my executive summary. Is it a standalone 120-word overview with purpose, scope, key findings, and recommendations? Give a pass/fail and a 5-bullet rewrite plan.”
Tone Adjustment: > “Rewrite this paragraph for [audience]. Current tone: [casual/formal/technical]. Desired tone: [casual/formal/technical]. Preserve all factual content.”






Guided Practice 6.1



Take something you’ve written recently — an email, a report section, a proposal paragraph. Paste it into an AI chatbot with the Critic prompt above. Compare the AI’s feedback to your own assessment. Did it catch something you missed? Did it miss something you knew was weak?


What most people discover

AI is excellent at catching structural issues (missing transitions, unclear topic sentences, inconsistent tone) and formatting problems. It’s weaker at judging whether your argument is convincing to your specific audience — that requires context the AI doesn’t have unless you provide it (BRIEFS!). The best workflow: AI catches the structural stuff so you can focus on the persuasive and strategic dimensions.









✅ Test Yourself: Writing with AI



Which approach produces better results — and why?

“Write a report about our Q3 results.”
Writing your own draft, then asking AI: “Review my draft using this rubric: [6 criteria]. Diagnose, don’t rewrite.”

(Answer: B — the Critic approach. You keep your voice, your knowledge, and your ownership. AI catches structural issues you’d miss. The output is genuinely yours, genuinely improved.)

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
AI for Organization and Planning

Meeting Notes → Action Items (in 60 seconds)
If your meetings generate notes or transcripts, AI can extract structure instantly:

“Here are notes from our team meeting. Extract: (1) decisions made, (2) action items with owner and deadline, (3) open questions that need follow-up, (4) topics deferred to next meeting. Format as a table.”



Project Planning

“I’m planning [event/project]. Timeline: [X weeks]. Team size: [N people]. Budget: [amount]. Generate a week-by-week project plan with milestones, task assignments, and a risk register with 5 likely risks and mitigation strategies.”



Study Planning (from BA 1028)

“I’m a first-year business major. I need to learn [topic], and my exam is in 10 days. Coach me with spaced practice. Build a 7-session plan with daily micro-tasks under 25 minutes, retrieval practice questions, and 3 mini-quizzes. At each step, ask me to produce an answer before revealing hints. Use a Socratic style.”



Budget Planning (from BA 1028)

“I have take-home income of $X per month and fixed costs of [list]. Build a student budget using a 50-30-20 baseline, a debt snowball if needed, and a 3-month emergency fund plan. Output a simple monthly table and a weekly checklist of actions. Ask me 5 follow-ups to personalize it.”

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
AI for Creative Work

The Brand Sprint: From Idea to Identity in 30 Minutes
This workflow, tested with university business students, takes a raw business idea and turns it into a brand brief with positioning, visual identity, and logo concepts — all AI-assisted.
The prompt (from BA 1028):

“Act as a brand strategist. Interview me with 8 questions to define the brand: target customer, value proposition, tone, 3 brand adjectives, competitor set, promise, and constraints (colors or symbols to avoid). Then propose: - A one-sentence positioning statement - A tagline with 3 variants - A mini brand kit: 3-color palette with hex codes, a heading font + body font, and a simple logo usage note - 3 logo concept directions written as prompts I can use in an image generation tool”

What this produced for students: A team creating a lemonade stand on campus got: positioning statement (“For students on the go, Roadrunner Lemonade serves fresh-squeezed, real-fruit lemonade that delivers a bright pick-me-up between classes”), three taglines (“Fresh squeeze, bright day” / “Sip sunny” / “Brighten your break”), a color palette (Sunshine Yellow #F6C700, Citrus Orange #FF8A00, Cool Blue #1F7A99), font pairing (Montserrat SemiBold + Lato Regular), and three image-generation prompts for different logo concepts.
30 minutes. From “we want a lemonade stand” to a complete brand identity. No design experience required.


Presentation Design

“I need to present [topic] to [audience] in [N] minutes. Create an outline with: slide titles, 2-3 bullet points per slide, speaker notes for each slide, and suggestions for one visual per slide. Aim for [N] slides maximum.”



Social Media Content

“I run a [type of business] targeting [audience]. Generate 5 social media post ideas for [platform]. Each should include: a hook (first line), body text under 100 words, 3 relevant hashtags, and a call to action. Tone: [professional/playful/informative].”



Brainstorming (from BA 1028)

“Act as a structured idea generator. Step 1: Ask me what context I’m brainstorming for (business, class project, event, or personal). Step 2: Generate 10 creative ideas across a variety of directions. Step 3: Group those ideas into 3 clusters or themes. Step 4: For each cluster, expand one idea into a 3-step action plan I could start on tomorrow. Always remind me that these are starting points and I should adapt or combine them.”

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
section: Vibe Coding: Building Tools Without Programming
text:
Vibe Coding: Building Tools Without Programming
One of the most surprising AI capabilities: you can build functional apps, dashboards, and tools by describing what you want in plain English. No programming experience required.

What You Can Build

A simple calculator or converter for your specific domain
An interactive quiz or assessment for your students/team
A budget tracker or project dashboard
A data visualization from a spreadsheet
A simple website or landing page
A form that collects and organizes responses



How It Works
Tools like Claude Artifacts, ChatGPT Canvas, Replit Agent, and v0 by Vercel let you describe what you want and the AI generates working code. You iterate by describing changes in natural language:

“Build me a simple web tool where I can paste a paragraph of text and it shows me: word count, sentence count, average sentence length, and reading level. Make it look clean with a blue and white color scheme.”

The AI produces a working tool. You test it. You say:

“Add a button that copies the results to my clipboard. Also add a section that suggests how to simplify sentences that are over 25 words.”

The AI updates the tool. No code written by you — just natural language descriptions of what you want.






Vibe Coding Limits



AI-generated code works great for simple, personal tools. It gets unreliable for complex applications, anything involving security (login systems, payment processing), or anything that needs to work perfectly every time (medical, legal, financial). Build toys and tools, not products. For anything serious, involve a real developer.

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
Building Your Prompt Library
The highest-leverage productivity habit isn’t learning new AI tools — it’s saving the prompts that work.

How to Build Your Library

Start with tasks you do weekly. Email drafts, meeting notes, report sections, data formatting.
Write and test prompts for each task. Use BRIEFS to structure them. Iterate until the output consistently meets your needs.
Save them somewhere accessible. A Google Doc, a Notion page, a text file on your desktop, a Notes app folder.
Include the template AND an example. Future-you will forget what each prompt does without an example output.
Update quarterly. AI tools change. Prompts that worked 6 months ago may need refinement.



Prompt Library Starter Kit







Task
Prompt Template




Weekly report
“Summarize the following accomplishments, challenges, and next steps into a [X]-word weekly update for [audience]. Tone: [professional/casual]. Format: bullet points under 3 headers.”


Email reply
“Draft a reply to this email. Context: [your situation]. Tone: [friendly/firm/neutral]. Length: under [N] words. Include: [specific ask or next step].”


Meeting prep
“Given this agenda and these background documents, prepare: 3 questions I should ask, 2 points I should raise, and 1 potential concern to address.”


Data summary
“Analyze this data and provide: key trends, notable outliers, and 3 actionable takeaways for [audience]. Include one recommended visualization.”


Content draft
“Write a [type] about [topic] for [audience]. Tone: [X]. Length: [N] words. Include: [key points]. Avoid: [what not to include].”

title: AI for Everyday Productivity
text:
Module 6 Summary






Key Takeaways




AI doesn’t save time automatically. It saves time when you invest time designing the right workflow. The 30 minutes you spend crafting a prompt library saves hours over a semester.
Critic, not Ghostwriter. Write your draft first, then use AI to review it. This keeps your voice, your ideas, and your ownership — while catching structural issues you’d miss.
Ready-to-use prompts exist for email coaching, executive summary checks, tone adjustment, meeting notes extraction, project planning, study planning, budgeting, brand sprints, presentations, and brainstorming.
The Brand Sprint workflow turns a raw business idea into a brand identity (positioning, tagline, colors, fonts, logo concepts) in 30 minutes. Tested with real university students.
Vibe coding lets you build simple tools by describing what you want in plain English. Great for personal tools, dangerous for anything that needs to be secure or reliable.
Build a prompt library. Save the prompts that work. Include templates AND examples. Update quarterly.
The 5-Question Test before adopting any new AI tool: Does it solve a real problem? Is it better than my current approach? Where does my data go? What does it really cost? Will it still exist in 6 months?





💭 Think About It


The productivity gains from AI are real — but they create a new question: what do you do with the time you save? Sarah left work at 4:45 instead of 6:15. She could use that 90 minutes to do more work (productivity trap), scroll social media (wasted potential), or learn something new, mentor a colleague, or think strategically about her organization’s future (growth). AI is a tool that gives you back time. What you do with that time is the real decision. The most AI-augmented professionals don’t just work faster — they think deeper because they’ve freed up the space to do so.

Time: 60 minutes | Tools needed: Any AI chatbot + your actual work materials

title: AI Agents and Automation
section: The Professor Who Deleted His Slides
text:
The Professor Who Deleted His Slides
In Fall 2025, a statistics professor at a mid-size public university tried an experiment that his colleagues thought was reckless. He taught two sections of the same course — MATH 3200, Probability and Statistics. Section A got the traditional experience: lecture slides, handwritten notes on the board, homework submitted through Canvas.
Section B got something radically different. No static slides. No lecture notes. Instead, every topic had its own custom AI tutor — a GPT built specifically for that chapter, loaded with the professor’s own notes, examples, and teaching philosophy. Every homework assignment had its own linked GPT for guided problem-solving. Students submitted both their written work AND the GPT conversation transcript showing their reasoning process.
The professor wasn’t being lazy. He was running a controlled experiment.
The results: On Exam 1, the AI section averaged 72.20 compared to the traditional section’s 68.20 — a 4-point advantage, with similar standard deviations (~21 in both groups). Students in the AI section reported that the most helpful features were R code assistance (9 mentions), alignment with class content (6), clear explanations (6), and step-by-step guidance (4).
That professor was Dr. Anjana Yatawara — the author of this course. And the custom GPTs he built for that experiment are the foundation of what you’ll learn in this module.
This isn’t theory. You’re learning from someone who built it, tested it, measured it, and has the data.






This Isn’t Just One Experiment



The ELEVATE result (AI section 72.20 vs traditional 68.20) isn’t alone. In Fall 2023, physics lecturer Gregory Kestin and colleagues at Harvard ran a preregistered randomized controlled trial (N=194 undergraduates) comparing an AI tutor built on GPT-4 against active-learning classroom sessions. Both topics, both directions, the AI tutor group showed more than twice the learning gains, spent less time on the lesson, and reported higher engagement and motivation (Kestin et al., 2025, Scientific Reports).
Critically, the AI tutor was not just ChatGPT — it was a carefully designed custom system with pedagogical principles embedded in the prompts and full answer keys grounding its responses. The design choices matter. A generic ChatGPT tutor does not produce these results. A constrained, knowledge-loaded, pedagogy-informed one does. That’s the architecture you’ll learn to build in this module.

title: AI Agents and Automation
section: Chatbots vs Agents: What’s the Difference?
text:
Chatbots vs Agents: What’s the Difference?
These terms get used interchangeably, but they’re different:








Feature
Chatbot
Agent




Behavior
Reactive — waits for your input, responds
Proactive — can plan, act, and follow up


Scope
Answers questions within a conversation
Can take actions: search the web, run code, send emails, manage files


Memory
Usually forgets between sessions
Can maintain context across sessions


Autonomy
Does what you ask, nothing more
Can break complex tasks into subtasks and execute them independently


Example
ChatGPT answering “What’s the weather?”
An agent that checks your calendar, sees you have an outdoor meeting, checks the forecast, and messages you to bring an umbrella



Custom GPTs sit in the middle. They’re more than a basic chatbot (they have persistent instructions and uploaded knowledge) but less than a full agent (they can’t take autonomous actions across systems). They’re the sweet spot for most people — powerful enough to be genuinely useful, simple enough to build without programming.






Common Misconceptions About AI Agents and Custom GPTs




“Custom GPTs are permanent” — They need maintenance. When your knowledge files change (updated syllabus, new policies), the GPT needs updating too. Budget time for upkeep.
“GPTs remember everything” — Custom GPTs have persistent INSTRUCTIONS but not persistent MEMORY of past conversations. Each user session starts fresh.
“More knowledge files = better” — Too many files can confuse the model. Upload only what’s directly relevant. A focused GPT with 3 files outperforms a bloated one with 30.
“Agents are always better than chatbots” — Agents introduce autonomy, which introduces risk. For most tasks, a well-designed custom GPT (no autonomy) is safer and more reliable than an agent (autonomous actions).
“Building a GPT requires coding” — Zero code required. The collection was built entirely through the GPT Builder interface with natural language instructions.




Custom GPTs for YOUR Field

HealthcareBusinessEducationGovernment



Patient FAQ GPT: Loaded with your clinic’s policies, hours, insurance info, and common questions. Reduces front desk call volume.
Discharge Instructions GPT: Generates personalized post-visit care instructions from structured inputs. Nurse reviews before giving to patient.
Continuing Education GPT: Loaded with latest clinical guidelines, quizzes staff on protocol updates.




Customer Service GPT: Trained on your product catalog, return policy, and FAQ. Handles first-line inquiries, escalates complex issues.
Onboarding GPT: New hire guide loaded with company handbook, benefits info, and role-specific training materials.
Sales Prep GPT: Loaded with competitor data and product specs. Sales reps ask questions before client meetings.




Course Tutor GPT: The ELEVATE model — loaded with textbook and answer keys, guided by the 7-step tutoring algorithm.
Syllabus GPT: Answers “when is the exam?” and “what’s the late policy?” so you don’t have to.
Assignment-Specific GPT: One per homework, loaded only with relevant chapter content. Prevents scope creep.




Policy FAQ GPT: Loaded with department regulations and procedures. Citizens and staff get instant answers to policy questions.
Grant Writing GPT: Loaded with RFP requirements and successful past proposals. Guides applicants through the process.
Compliance GPT: Tracks regulatory requirements and helps staff determine if their activities are compliant.

title: AI Agents and Automation
section: Building Custom GPTs: Step by Step
text:
Building Custom GPTs: Step by Step
A custom GPT is a personalized version of ChatGPT with three components:

Instructions — what it should do, how it should behave, what it should avoid
Knowledge — uploaded files it can reference (PDFs, docs, data)
Settings — whether it can search the web, generate images, run code


Step 1: Define the Purpose (5 minutes)
Before you build anything, answer these questions:

Who is this for? (Students? Customers? Your team? Yourself?)
What problem does it solve? (Tutoring? FAQ? Drafting? Analysis?)
What should it NEVER do? (Give final answers without explanation? Access data it shouldn’t? Pretend to be human?)



Step 2: Write the System Instructions (15-30 minutes)
The system instructions are the soul of your custom GPT. This is where the ELEVATE project’s 7-step tutoring algorithm lives:






The ELEVATE Tutoring GPT System Prompt (Yatawara, 2025)




“I want you to adopt the persona of a supportive tutor who encourages a step-by-step approach to solving statistics problems. When I provide a question, first restate it and confirm that you’ve understood. Then offer relevant resources (theorems, definitions, textbook sections, or sample exercises), and ask if I’m familiar with them. Prompt me to share my initial approach, validate correct reasoning, clarify misconceptions, and guide me toward the next step. If I struggle, ask whether I’d like a hint or an example. If I request the entire solution, gently encourage a step-by-step effort. Should I deviate from this incremental reasoning style or fail to provide a question, respond with a brief suggestion to reformat or clarify. Otherwise, keep your guiding statements to a few sentences and hints, not entire solutions. When all else fails, reveal only the first step and prompt me to proceed. After completion, summarize the key lessons and reinforce the textbook concepts before asking if I have further questions. Now please wait for me to ask the question.”

This prompt solves two problems simultaneously: instructional consistency (every student gets the same scaffolded experience) and knowledge grounding (the GPT references the uploaded textbook, not random internet content).




Step 3: Upload Knowledge Files (10 minutes)
Upload the documents your GPT should reference:

Course textbook or manual
Answer keys and worked examples
Policy documents and FAQs
Relevant data files or templates
Style guides or brand guidelines

The GPT will search these files when answering questions, grounding its responses in YOUR content rather than its general training data. This dramatically reduces hallucinations for domain-specific questions.


Step 4: Configure Settings (2 minutes)

Web search: Enable if the GPT needs current information. Disable if you want it to stay within your uploaded knowledge.
Image generation: Enable for creative tasks. Disable for academic/professional GPTs where images aren’t relevant.
Code interpreter: Enable if users will work with data, code, or calculations.



Step 5: Test and Iterate (20+ minutes)
This is where most people stop too early. Test your GPT with:

Happy path: The exact type of question it’s designed for. Does it respond well?
Edge cases: Unusual or ambiguous questions. Does it handle them gracefully?
Adversarial inputs: What happens if someone asks it to do something outside its scope? Does it stay on task?
Knowledge boundary: Ask something NOT in your uploaded files. Does it say “I don’t see this in my materials” or does it hallucinate?

Iterate on the system instructions until the GPT consistently behaves the way you want.


Step 6: Share and Deploy (2 minutes)

Private: Only you can use it
Shared link: Anyone with the link can use it (used for students in the ELEVATE project)
Published: Listed in the GPT store for anyone to discover

Trained on mosaic package and course-approved R functions only. Won’t suggest packages students haven’t learned.


DOE Assistant
Design of Experiments guidance
Loaded with experimental design materials. Helps students design their own studies.




The Review Protocol: How to Verify Student AI Use
When students submit work done with custom GPTs, the professor reviews:

The shared conversation link — students click “Share” in ChatGPT and submit the full transcript
The student’s own work — their final answer, calculations, or write-up alongside the transcript
Evidence of reasoning — did they revise or challenge the AI’s suggestions, or just copy?
SMARTS process — did they follow State → Map → Ask → Reason → Think → Summarize?

This transparency protocol solves the academic integrity problem without banning AI. The AI is a tool; the transcript is proof of how it was used.







✅ Test Yourself: Custom GPT Design



You want to build a GPT for new employee onboarding at your organization. Quick quiz:

What files would you upload? (Employee handbook, benefits guide, org chart, FAQ document, role-specific training materials)
What should it NEVER do? (Give legal advice, access employee records, make promises about benefits that aren’t in the documents)
Why would you disable web search? (To keep answers grounded in YOUR documents — you want it answering from company policy, not random internet content)

title: AI Agents and Automation
text:
Workflow Automation: Beyond Custom GPTs
Custom GPTs handle conversations. Automation tools handle workflows — connecting apps, triggering actions, and processing data without human intervention.

What Automation Looks Like

Without automation: You receive an email with a PDF invoice. You open it, manually enter the amounts into a spreadsheet, categorize the expense, and email the accounting team.
With automation: The email arrives. An automation tool detects the PDF attachment, extracts the amounts using AI, adds them to your spreadsheet, categorizes the expense based on the vendor name, and sends a summary to accounting. You do nothing.



No-Code Automation Tools









Tool
What It Does
Complexity
Cost




Zapier
Connects 6,000+ apps with if-then logic + AI
Low-medium
Free tier + paid


Make (Integromat)
Visual workflow builder, more complex logic
Medium
Free tier + paid


Microsoft Power Automate
Deep Microsoft 365 integration
Medium
Included with M365


n8n
Open-source, self-hosted, maximum control
Medium-high
Free (self-hosted)


Apple Shortcuts
On-device automation for Apple users
Low
Free





Common Automations Worth Building

Email → Summary → Task: When you receive an email longer than 200 words, AI summarizes it and creates a task in your to-do app
Meeting → Transcript → Action Items: After a Zoom meeting, AI transcribes it and extracts action items
Form → Data → Report: When someone submits a form, AI processes the data and generates a weekly summary report
New Article → Summary → Notification: When a key publication posts a new article, AI summarizes it and sends you a notification



The Autonomy Spectrum
Not every automation should run without oversight:








Autonomy Level
Example
When to Use




Fully automated
Spam filtering, data backup, format conversion
Low-stakes, reversible, well-understood tasks


Automated + notification
AI categorizes expenses and notifies you of the result
Medium-stakes, where you want visibility but not manual effort


Automated + approval
AI drafts a response and waits for you to approve before sending
High-stakes communication, financial transactions


Human-initiated
You trigger the automation manually when needed
Tasks that require judgment about WHEN to run









Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024): You Own What Your Agent Says



In November 2022, Jake Moffatt’s grandmother died. Needing to fly from Vancouver to Toronto for the funeral, Moffatt visited Air Canada’s website and asked its chatbot about bereavement fares. The chatbot said they could apply for the reduced fare retroactively, within 90 days of travel. That was wrong — Air Canada’s actual policy required applying before travel.
Moffatt booked a full-fare ticket, flew, and submitted the retroactive application. Air Canada denied it and argued in tribunal that the chatbot was “a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions.” The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected this argument: “It should be obvious to Air Canada that it is responsible for all the information on its website.” Air Canada was ordered to pay damages (Moffatt, 2024 BCCRT 149).
The lesson: If you deploy a customer-facing agent at your organization — whether it’s a Custom GPT, a Claude Project, or a Zapier automation — you own what it says. The guardrail principle isn’t optional. It’s legal liability.








The Guardrail Principle



An agent is only as good as the guardrails you give it. The skill isn’t building the agent — it’s knowing when to let it run and when to step in. Automate the boring. Supervise the important. If a mistake would be embarrassing, costly, or irreversible, add a human approval step.

section: When to Use What: A Decision Framework
text:
When to Use What: A Decision Framework
Do I need AI to have a CONVERSATION?
├── YES → Custom GPT (with instructions + knowledge)
│    └── Does it need to take ACTIONS (send emails, update databases)?
│         ├── YES → Full AI Agent (GPT Actions, Claude MCP, etc.)
│         └── NO → Custom GPT is sufficient
└── NO → Do I need to AUTOMATE a repeated workflow?
     ├── YES → Automation tool (Zapier, Make, Power Automate)
     │    └── Does it need AI to UNDERSTAND content (not just route it)?
     │         ├── YES → Automation + AI (Zapier AI, Make AI node)
     │         └── NO → Simple automation (no AI needed)
     └── NO → You probably just need a regular prompt (Modules 4-6)

Guided Practices






Guided Practice 8.1 — Design a Custom GPT



Pick ONE task from your real work or studies. Design (don’t build yet — just plan) a custom GPT for it:

Purpose: What does this GPT do? (one sentence)
System instructions: Write 5-7 rules it should follow. Include at least one constraint (what it should NOT do).
Knowledge files: What documents would you upload? (list 2-3)
Test prompts: Write 3 prompts a real user would send. For each, describe what a GOOD response looks like and what a BAD response looks like.
Autonomy level: Where does this sit on the spectrum — fully automated, automated with notification, automated with approval, or human-initiated? Why?



Example: Course FAQ GPT

Purpose: Answer student questions about MATH 2200 using only the syllabus and course materials.
Rules: (1) Only answer from uploaded files. (2) If the answer isn’t in the files, say so and direct to the professor. (3) Never give exam answers. (4) Be encouraging but honest. (5) Keep responses under 100 words.
Knowledge files: Syllabus, assignment descriptions, grading rubric.
Test prompts: “When is the midterm?” (should find exact date), “What’s the answer to homework 3?” (should refuse), “Can I use a calculator on exams?” (should check syllabus and answer).
Autonomy: Human-initiated. Low stakes — wrong FAQ answer is inconvenient, not harmful.









Guided Practice 8.2 — Automation Audit



List 5 repetitive tasks you do every week. For each:

How long does it take?
Could any part be automated? (Which tool — Zapier, AI, spreadsheet formula, or none?)
What’s the risk if the automation makes an error?
Verdict: automate, partially automate, or keep manual?

Total up the time you’d save. Is the setup effort worth it?

title: AI Agents and Automation
text:
Module 8 Summary






Key Takeaways




Chatbots react. Agents act. Custom GPTs sit in the middle — persistent instructions and knowledge, but no autonomous actions.
Building a custom GPT takes 30-60 minutes: define purpose → write system instructions → upload knowledge → configure settings → test extensively → share.
The ELEVATE tutoring prompt solves instructional consistency AND knowledge grounding simultaneously. The 7-step algorithm guides without giving away answers.
The transcript review protocol — shared conversation links + student’s own work — solves academic integrity without banning AI.
The MATH 3200 experiment showed the AI section (72.20) outperformed the traditional section (68.20). This isn’t theory — it’s measured.
Automation tools (Zapier, Make, Power Automate) handle workflows, not conversations. Use them for connecting apps and processing data.
The autonomy spectrum: fully automated → automated + notification → automated + approval → human-initiated. Match the autonomy level to the stakes.
Automate the boring. Supervise the important. If a mistake would be embarrassing, costly, or irreversible, add a human checkpoint.





💭 Think About It


The professor who deleted his slides wasn’t being reckless. He was asking a question that most institutions are afraid to ask: what if the AI version is actually better? His data says the AI section outperformed the traditional one. His students said the custom GPTs were helpful. His transcripts showed students reasoning through problems instead of copying answers. The experiment didn’t prove AI is always better. It proved that well-designed AI integration, with the right guardrails and the right pedagogy, can outperform the status quo. The key phrase is “well-designed.” A bad custom GPT is worse than no GPT at all. The design is everything.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Note



This document is the research-backed rationale for the Module 4 practice ladder in AI from the Ground Up. It is written for three audiences: (1) instructors adopting the curriculum, (2) reviewers evaluating the course for tenure or grant purposes, and (3) myself, as a reference when revising future iterations.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Summary
Module 4 of AI from the Ground Up teaches the BRIEFS and SMARTS frameworks — the keystone communication skills of the course. The module’s first draft contained strong conceptual content but thin practice architecture: a single three-prompt rewriting exercise and a before/after lab. Field use and review revealed the same failure mode documented in the literature: learners could recognize the patterns but not reliably produce them under their own steam.
The revised module replaces the single guided practice with a 10-exercise stepwise practice ladder (Exercises 4.A through 4.J), designed so each exercise reduces the scaffolding by one step. This follows the well-validated faded worked example pattern from cognitive load theory, with direct empirical support from recent studies on prompt engineering pedagogy specifically.
The ladder’s design is defensible on six lines of evidence, summarized below.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
The Problem the Ladder Solves
Zhang et al. (2025) studied translation students learning to use ChatGPT for professional translation tasks. These students possessed strong disciplinary knowledge — they knew genre conventions, target audience considerations, and translation theory. Nevertheless, without structured scaffolding, they wrote prompts that were “short, informal, and often lacking in contextual detail.” Theoretical knowledge did not transfer to prompting skill.
This is the specific failure the Module 4 ladder addresses. Reading about BRIEFS takes ten minutes. Becoming fluent in BRIEFS requires scaffolded, deliberate practice.
The same pattern appears across the prompt engineering pedagogy literature:

Qian (2025), in a systematic review of prompt engineering in education, identified the gap between “technique-based” and “process-based” approaches and the need for structured instructional scaffolds to bridge them.
The IJETHE systematic review (Kim & Frick, 2025) found that frameworks are most effective when treated as “scaffolds to help educators articulate their educational goals” rather than as rigid formulas to be memorized.
A PRISMA review of 30 K-12 STEM studies (arXiv 2410.11123) found that while simple and zero-shot prompting dominate classroom practice, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting produce measurably better outcomes — a gap between what students default to and what works.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
section: The Pedagogical Pattern: Backward-Faded Worked Examples
text:
The Pedagogical Pattern: Backward-Faded Worked Examples
The ladder implements the faded worked example pattern first formalized by Renkl and Atkinson (2003) in Educational Psychologist. The pattern:

Begin with a fully worked example (recognition-level practice — Exercise 4.A).
Successively fade solution steps (Exercises 4.B, 4.C — partial production).
End with independent problem solving (Exercises 4.D, 4.H, 4.I — full production).
Add collaborative review at the end to consolidate (Exercise 4.J).

The underlying rationale is cognitive load theoretic. Novice learners have limited working memory capacity; unguided problem-solving from the outset overloads them. Worked examples reduce extraneous cognitive load, allowing learners to build schemas. As expertise grows, examples become redundant (the expertise reversal effect), so scaffolding is gradually removed.
Empirical support for this pattern in education generally:

Renkl and Atkinson (2003): successive fading produces better learning than example-problem pairs alone.
Renkl, Atkinson, and Große (2004): position of faded steps does not matter; what matters is that fading triggers self-explanation activities.
Sweller, Ayres, and Kalyuga (2011): comprehensive cognitive load theory synthesis.
Chen, Kalyuga, and Sweller (2015, 2016): worked example effect confirmed at micro level (each solution step).
Miller-Cotto (2026, British Journal of Educational Psychology): working memory moderates the fading effect, but the fading benefit holds broadly across 6th-grade geometry students.

Empirical support specifically for STEM scaffolding:

Belland, Walker, Kim, and Lefler (2017) meta-analyzed 144 experimental studies with 333 outcome measures on computer-based scaffolding in STEM education. Their random-effects meta-analysis found a consistently positive effect (ḡ = 0.46) on cognitive outcomes across contexts of use, scaffolding characteristics, and levels of assessment.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Exercise-by-Exercise Rationale

Exercise 4.A — Recognize Before You Produce
Design: Six weak prompts; learner identifies which BRIEFS element is most-missing.
Rationale: Recognition precedes production. VanLehn’s (1996) staged model of cognitive skill acquisition identifies an early phase where learners build declarative knowledge before procedural skill. Recognition-level exercises serve this phase without imposing production load.
Specific prediction: Across the six prompts, ~60% of cases should diagnose as missing Intent, matching the Whisperers Study finding (Yatawara, 2026) that intent is the #1 signal. This creates a direct empirical tie-in to the module’s framing.


Exercise 4.B — Single-Element Insertion
Design: Learners add each of the six BRIEFS elements to a bare prompt one at a time, in isolation.
Rationale: Element isolation is standard in deliberate practice (Ericsson, 1993). Drilling scales in isolation before playing a song is the canonical analogy. The exercise deliberately resists combination — combining elements is Exercise 4.D’s job.
Self-explanation prompt (“Which element was hardest?”): This is the load-bearing pedagogy piece. Self-explanation prompts increase germane cognitive load — the productive load associated with schema construction. Renkl (1997) and subsequent replications show that prompting self-explanation during example study roughly doubles learning gains.


Exercise 4.C — Completion Drill
Design: Three BRIEFS skeletons with 2–3 elements filled in; learner adds the rest.
Rationale: Completion problems occupy the middle rung of the faded-worked-example sequence (Renkl, Atkinson, and Große, 2004). The given elements anchor the learner and reduce element-interactivity load while still requiring production.
Design choice: Each skeleton deliberately leaves a different mix of elements empty. Skeleton 2 and 3 both leave Stakes empty, because Stakes is the element students most often under-specify. This is a targeted intervention, not random.


Exercise 4.D — Full BRIEFS Production
Design: Three bare prompts (“Help me with my resume,” etc.) rewritten using full BRIEFS; then three from the learner’s own life.
Rationale: This is the production capstone for the BRIEFS-specific skill. It replaces the original course’s single Guided Practice 4.1.
Variation 4.D.2 (your own three) is the handoff point where the course becomes personal. The three prompts produced here are reused in Exercise 4.J (peer critique) and Lab 4 (Before/After experiment). This creates spaced retrieval across the module — students revisit their own work under different demands.


Exercise 4.E — Calibration Handshake Drill
Design: Three scenarios, each requiring the learner to write all three phases of the handshake (own message → model’s probable restatement → confirm-or-correct).
Rationale: The calibration handshake was the most striking finding of the Whisperers Study (Yatawara, 2026) — all 26 models across 5 providers independently converged on the same three-phase protocol. The drill exists because Phase 3 is the phase users skip, and the habit must be built deliberately.
Phase 2 (“what will the model say back?”) is the exercise’s pedagogical payload. Writing Phase 2 requires perspective-taking — imagining the model’s interpretation of your message. This is the same skill that undergirds the study’s meta-finding: models fail when they model the user poorly. Practicing the reverse — modeling the model — sharpens first-message precision.


Exercise 4.F — Technique Selection
Design: Five tasks; learner matches each to one of five core techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, role-based, structured output) and writes the actual prompt.
Rationale: Technique choice is a distinct skill from BRIEFS. BRIEFS designs the content of the first message; technique choice designs its form. The arXiv 2410.11123 PRISMA review found that K-12 STEM prompt engineering defaults to zero-shot, missing the accuracy gains available from few-shot and chain-of-thought. The exercise explicitly targets this gap.


Exercise 4.G — SMARTS Multi-Turn Walkthrough
Design: Learner writes all six SMARTS turns on a real complex task, then compresses to a 3-turn variant.
Rationale: SMARTS is a process-based framework (Qian, 2025’s terminology) and cannot be practiced in isolation the way BRIEFS elements can. The full 6-turn walkthrough is the only way to feel the interaction shape. The compression variation (6 → 3 turns) introduces the principle of “use the framework at the level the task warrants” — a lesson against over-engineering.


Exercise 4.H — Anti-Pattern Gallery
Design: Seven broken prompts (Wall of Context, Frankenstein, Yes-Man Bait, Phantom Context, Role Dump, Format/Content Mismatch, Leading Question); learner diagnoses and proposes a one-move repair.
Rationale: Diagnostic skill is a higher-level cognitive target than production skill (Bloom’s taxonomy: “evaluate” > “create” at the surface, though they interact). The exercise is also the most explicitly engaging — diagnosing broken artifacts is famously rewarding in code review, medical education, and proofreading contexts.
Coverage choice: The seven anti-patterns were chosen for distinct failure modes. Leading Question (#7) is included specifically because sophisticated-looking hallucinated confirmation is one of the most dangerous outputs of poor prompting — and one learners rarely recognize as a problem until shown.


Exercise 4.I — Transfer and Red-Team
Design: Part 1: re-target a BRIEFS prompt across three radically different domains (agriculture, medicine, software, education). Part 2: find a case where BRIEFS is the wrong tool.
Rationale: Transfer is the real test of skill acquisition (Barnett and Ceci, 2002). The cross-domain rewriting forces the learner to distinguish structure (the BRIEFS skeleton, preserved) from content (domain-specific details, changed). This is the near-transfer vs far-transfer distinction; the exercise explicitly trains far transfer by crossing domain boundaries.
The red-team portion is the single most important exercise in the module. Naming when not to use a framework is a stronger signal of mastery than using it appropriately. A learner who can articulate three cases where BRIEFS fails (creative exploration, single-fact lookup, emotional processing) has internalized the framework’s boundary conditions — which are more important than the framework itself.


Exercise 4.J — Rubric-Based Peer Critique
Design: Paired learners exchange one of their Exercise 4.D.2 prompts and score using a 5-dimension rubric. A structured critique script (say what’s working → identify weakest dimension → propose one targeted revision) constrains the feedback form.
Rationale: Peer review is validated for prompt engineering specifically:

Turan et al. (2024) in Education Sciences documented that “I Learn with Prompt Engineering” assignments requiring peer-review with pre-defined rubrics produced better downstream prompting than solo practice. The rubric is non-optional — peer review without a rubric degrades into vague impressions.
In software engineering education (Ho et al., 2024; the Socratique “Mr. Pepper” study), structured peer code review is the canonical skill-building mechanism, and the evidence base is a natural fit for prompt engineering given the artifact-review similarity.
Classical peer-review findings (Topping, 1998) hold that the reviewer learns more than the reviewee, because scoring a rubric forces tacit standards to become explicit.

The critique script is adapted from SE code review practice (Bacchelli and Bird, 2013; Rigby and Bird, 2017). It solves two peer-review failure modes: over-gentle feedback that loses signal, and over-harsh feedback that damages motivation. The “one targeted revision” constraint channels cognitive effort toward actionability.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Self-Explanation Prompts
Every exercise includes a self-explanation prompt — a short written reflection question designed to trigger schema-building processes during example study.
The self-explanation literature is one of the most robust findings in educational psychology:

Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, and Glaser (1989): self-explaining worked examples distinguishes high-learners from low-learners.
Renkl (1997): self-explanation activities mediate the worked-example effect.
VanLehn and Jones (1993); VanLehn, Jones, and Chi (1992): computational models of self-explanation converge on the same prediction — explanation generates schema.
Renkl and Atkinson (2003): self-explanation prompts, embedded in faded worked examples, produce larger gains than worked examples alone.

The specific self-explanation prompts in the ladder are written to target personal blind spots (“Which element was hardest for you?”) rather than generic principles (“What did you learn?”). Blind-spot targeting is the difference between self-explanation that builds schema and self-explanation that rehearses surface features.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Measurement and Validation
The ladder is designed to be measured. Three measurement opportunities are built in:

Lab 4 (Before/After Experiment) — direct measurement of prompt quality improvement on learner-selected tasks. The lab collects 10 prompts and 10 responses per student with three-dimension scoring (Relevance, Accuracy, Usefulness). This is the closest available approximation to a randomized within-subject comparison.
Self-Assessment Part B (pre/post) — self-reported competency on 10 items aligned to the ladder exercises. Administered before Module 1 and after Module 14.
Module 4 Quiz — 18-item knowledge check with a 14/18 (78%) badge threshold. Two items directly test knowledge from the ladder exercises (Exercise 4.A’s diagnostic pattern; Exercise 4.H’s anti-pattern recognition).

For formal efficacy testing, the natural design is a between-sections quasi-experiment: one section receives the full ladder, a second receives only the original Guided Practice 4.1, and Lab 4 serves as the common outcome measure. This design is viable in any regular offering of the course and would produce a publishable effect size estimate in 1–2 semesters.

title: Module 4 Practice Ladder: Pedagogical Rationale
text:
Limitations and Open Questions
1. Dose effect unclear. I do not yet know whether the full 10-exercise ladder is necessary, or whether a subset (e.g., 4.A, 4.D, 4.H, 4.J) captures most of the gain. The between-sections design above would also estimate a dose-response curve if variants of the ladder were compared.
2. Expertise reversal not formally handled. For advanced learners, worked examples lose their effectiveness (Kalyuga, Chandler, and Sweller, 1998). The facilitator guide addresses this informally (pair advanced learners with novices in 4.J; fast-forward through 4.A–4.C), but no adaptive mechanism is built into the ladder itself.
3. Transfer horizon unmeasured. Lab 4 measures near-term prompt quality. Whether ladder-trained learners produce better prompts 6 months later, in novel domains, is unknown. Measuring this would require a longitudinal follow-up, which the course currently cannot support.
4. Cultural and linguistic generalization. All examples use English-language prompts aimed at US higher-education contexts. Whether the ladder generalizes to students working in other languages or cultural contexts is unknown.
These limitations are research opportunities, not reasons to delay adoption.

title: About This Course
text:
Dr. Anjana Yatawara is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Mathematics . His research spans financial econometrics, statistics education, environmental justice, and applied data science.
Dr. Yatawara’s AI research includes the LLM Whisperers Study (surveying 29 AI models across five competing companies to understand what models need from users), the ELEVATE Project (three-wave assessment of AI-integrated instruction across four undergraduate courses), and a published experiment demonstrating that campus-hosted small language models with RAG can match GPT-4 for domain-specific educational tasks at 92% lower cost.
The frameworks in this course — BRIEFS and SMARTS — emerged directly from that research. They’re not teaching opinions. They’re derived from what AI models themselves, across providers, independently said they need.

title: About This Course
text:
Why This Course Exists
Most AI courses teach you which buttons to click. This one teaches you how to think.
The Central Valley is home to agricultural workers, healthcare professionals, teachers, county employees, small business owners, first-generation college students, and tradespeople who all face the same question: How does AI change my work, and what do I need to know?
Existing AI courses are either too technical (assume programming) or too shallow (how to write a ChatGPT prompt). This course sits in the middle: deep understanding without requiring code, practical skills grounded in research, and real examples from the fields where our students and community members actually work.

How to Use This Course
Sequential learner? Start at Module 1 and work through to Module 14. Each builds on the previous.
Already know some AI? Take the Self-Assessment and skip to the modules where your scores are lowest.
Instructor using this in a course? See the Facilitator Guide for pacing, assessment suggestions, and adaptation tips.

title: About This Course
text:
Course Design Philosophy
This course follows five principles:

Examples before theory. You see real prompts, real cases, real data before learning the framework that explains them.
Central Valley relevance. Examples feature teachers, nurses, farmers, county employees, and small business owners — not just Silicon Valley engineers.
Research-grounded. Every framework traces back to published research — the Whisperers study, the ELEVATE project, the SLM-RAG experiment, or cited external sources.
Hands-on from day one. Every module includes guided practices and a lab. You learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Honest about limitations. AI is powerful. It also hallucinates, reinforces bias, and raises hard ethical questions. This course doesn’t shy from any of it.

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
section: The Pope in a Puffer Jacket
text:
The Pope in a Puffer Jacket
In March 2023, an image went viral showing Pope Francis wearing a stylish white Balenciaga puffer jacket. It was shared millions of times. News outlets scrambled to confirm or deny it. For a few hours, a significant portion of the internet believed the Pope had suddenly become a fashion icon.
The image was entirely AI-generated. A Reddit user named Pablo Xavier had created it using Midjourney in about 30 seconds. When asked how he made it, he said he was “just messing around.”
The Pope image marked a turning point: the moment the general public realized that AI could create images indistinguishable from photographs. Not blurry, not obviously fake, not “AI-looking.” Photorealistic images that fooled millions of people, created in seconds by someone with zero design training.
This module covers the entire multimodal landscape — images, video, audio, and more. The capabilities are extraordinary. So are the responsibilities.

Multimodal AI in YOUR Field

HealthcareBusinessEducationAgriculture



AI-generated anatomical diagrams for patient education
Medical imaging AI that highlights areas of concern on X-rays and CT scans
Text-to-speech for accessibility in patient communications
Video walkthroughs of post-surgical care instructions




Product photography generated from text descriptions (no photoshoot needed)
Brand identity packages: logos, color palettes, marketing visuals
Video ads and social media content at scale
Presentation visuals generated from slide content




Illustrations for course materials generated from learning objectives
Audio summaries of readings for students with visual impairments
Educational animations explaining complex processes
Multilingual content creation for diverse classrooms




Drone imagery + AI for crop disease identification
Infographics generated from yield data for stakeholder reports
Training videos for equipment operation and safety procedures
Visual documentation of field conditions for compliance










Common Misconceptions About Multimodal AI




“AI images are always detectable” — Detection is getting harder. The Pope jacket fooled millions. AI detection tools have significant false positive and false negative rates.
“AI art isn’t creative” — The AI isn’t creative. The PERSON directing it can be. Creativity lives in the vision and judgment, not the execution tool.
“Video AI is ready for production” — It’s ready for short clips, b-roll, and concepts. Full production-quality video still needs human direction and editing.
“AI-generated voice is always fake-sounding” — Modern text-to-speech is nearly indistinguishable from human voice. Voice cloning from a few seconds of audio is real and raises serious ethical concerns.
“If I generated it, I own it” — Copyright for AI-generated content is unsettled law. Adobe Firefly offers the clearest commercial licensing. For other tools, check the terms.

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
text:
How AI Image Generation Works

The Short Version
Image generation models (DALL·E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Ideogram, Flux) use a technique called diffusion. Here’s the intuition:

Start with pure noise — random colored pixels, like TV static
Gradually remove the noise — step by step, guided by your text prompt
Each step makes the image slightly more coherent — shapes emerge, colors form, details sharpen
After hundreds of steps — a fully formed image appears

It’s like a sculptor starting with a rough block of marble and chipping away until a figure emerges — except the sculptor is guided by your words.
The model learned what images look like by training on billions of image-text pairs from the internet. It knows that “sunset over mountains” typically involves orange/pink skies, silhouetted peaks, and warm light — because it’s seen millions of examples. When you prompt it, it’s not searching a database. It’s generating a new image that matches the patterns associated with your words.


Image Generation Tools

Writing Prompts for Images
Image prompting is different from text prompting. The key variables:
Subject: What’s in the image (“a golden retriever puppy sitting in autumn leaves”) Style: The artistic approach (“watercolor painting,” “photorealistic,” “flat vector illustration,” “anime style”) Composition: How it’s framed (“close-up portrait,” “wide landscape,” “bird’s eye view”) Lighting: The mood (“soft golden hour light,” “dramatic studio lighting,” “neon cyberpunk glow”) Details: Specific elements (“wearing a red collar,” “with a mountain background,” “in the style of Wes Anderson films”)
Example — from vague to specific:

❌ Vague: “a dog”
✅ Better: “a golden retriever puppy sitting in a pile of autumn leaves, soft afternoon sunlight filtering through trees, shallow depth of field, warm color palette, photorealistic style”







Guided Practice 7.1



Using any image generation tool you have access to (DALL·E through ChatGPT, Ideogram, or Bing Image Creator — all have free options), generate images for:

A professional headshot-style portrait of a fictional character for a business website
An infographic-style illustration explaining how photosynthesis works
A logo concept for “Roadrunner Lemonade” (the brand from Module 6)

For each, write at least two prompt versions — one simple, one detailed. Compare the results.


What to notice

The detailed prompts produce dramatically more usable results. Also notice what the AI struggles with: text in images (often garbled), hands (sometimes wrong number of fingers), and consistent character design across multiple images. These are known limitations of current models that are improving rapidly.

Realistic Use Cases Today

What Video AI Can’t Do Yet

Consistent characters across scenes (the person looks different in each clip)
Complex physics (water, hair, and fabric often look wrong)
Long-form narrative (anything over 30-60 seconds breaks coherence)
Reliable text or UI elements in video







✅ Test Yourself: Multimodal Basics




How do diffusion models generate images? (Start with noise, gradually remove it guided by the text prompt)
Name one thing AI image generators still struggle with. (Hands/fingers, text in images, consistency across multiple images)
What’s the current practical limit of AI video? (Short clips 5-60 seconds; consistent characters and complex physics are still weak)

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
text:
AI Audio and Music

Text-to-Speech
Modern AI can generate speech that is nearly indistinguishable from human voices:

Natural narration for presentations, videos, and podcasts
Voice cloning — replicating a specific person’s voice from a few seconds of audio sample
Multilingual dubbing — translating AND speaking in another language while matching the original speaker’s voice



Music Generation
Tools like Suno and Udio generate original music from text descriptions:

“Upbeat acoustic folk song with guitar and harmonica, about a road trip through California, male vocals, tempo 120 BPM”

The output is a complete song — vocals, instruments, production — generated in about 30 seconds. Quality ranges from “surprisingly good” to “obviously AI” depending on the genre and complexity.


NotebookLM Audio Overviews
As covered in Module 5, NotebookLM can generate podcast-style audio discussions of your uploaded documents. Two AI voices have a natural-sounding conversation about your material — useful for reviewing content while commuting or exercising.

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
text:
Combining Modalities: The Creative Pipeline
The real power of multimodal AI emerges when you chain tools together:

Example Pipeline: Course Marketing Video
1. TEXT → Write a script using ChatGPT/Claude
2. TEXT → IMAGE → Generate visuals for each scene with DALL·E/Midjourney
3. TEXT → AUDIO → Generate narration with text-to-speech
4. IMAGE + AUDIO → VIDEO → Combine in a video editor (or use Runway)
5. REVIEW → Human review for quality, accuracy, and appropriateness


Example Pipeline: Brand Identity Package
1. TEXT → Brand Sprint prompt (from Module 6) → positioning, tagline, colors
2. TEXT → IMAGE → Logo concepts using image generation
3. TEXT → DOCUMENT → Brand guidelines document using AI writing
4. TEXT → IMAGE → Social media templates using brand colors/fonts
5. REVIEW → Human refinement and final selection
The person with this workflow isn’t a designer, videographer, copywriter, or musician. They’re a director — someone who knows what they want and can guide AI tools to produce it. The bottleneck is no longer skill. It’s taste, judgment, and intent.

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
text:
Recognizing AI-Generated Content
As AI-generated content becomes more sophisticated, recognizing it becomes an essential literacy skill:

Visual Tells (as of 2026)

Hands and fingers — still occasionally wrong (extra fingers, merged digits)
Text in images — often garbled or misspelled
Background inconsistencies — objects that blend or defy physics
Texture repetition — identical patterns in hair, fabric, or foliage
“Too perfect” quality — an uncanny smoothness that photos don’t have
Symmetry that’s too exact — real faces and objects are slightly asymmetrical



Detection Tools
Tools like Content Credentials (Adobe), AI-or-not, and Hive Moderation attempt to detect AI-generated images and text. They’re useful but imperfect — false positives (marking human content as AI) and false negatives (missing AI content) are common. Don’t rely on any single detector.


The Deepfake Concern
AI-generated video and audio of real people (deepfakes) pose serious risks:

Political manipulation — fake videos of candidates saying things they never said
Financial fraud — fake CEO video calls authorizing wire transfers (this has actually happened)
Personal harassment — fake explicit content of real people
Erosion of trust — when anything could be fake, nothing feels trustworthy







The Ethics of Multimodal AI



Creating AI-generated images, video, or audio of real people without their consent is unethical and often illegal. Creating misleading content designed to deceive is always wrong, regardless of the technology used. The Pope puffer jacket was humorous. A deepfake of a political candidate is dangerous. The technology is the same — the intent and impact are what matter.

title: Multimodal AI — Creating Beyond Text
text:
Module 7 Summary






Key Takeaways




Image generation uses diffusion — starting from noise and gradually shaping it guided by your prompt. Detailed prompts with subject, style, composition, and lighting produce far better results.
Video generation is advancing rapidly but still limited to short clips. Best for b-roll, concepts, and social media — not long-form narrative.
Audio AI can generate near-human speech, clone voices, and create original music. Powerful for content creation, risky for deception.
The creative pipeline chains modalities: text → image → audio → video. The bottleneck is no longer skill — it’s taste, judgment, and intent.
AI-generated content can often be recognized by visual tells (hands, text, texture), but detection is imperfect and getting harder.
Deepfakes pose real risks: political, financial, and personal. Creating deceptive content of real people is unethical and often illegal. (See Module 10 — Ethics for a deeper analysis of AI ethics and fairness.)
Your creative judgment — knowing what’s good, appropriate, and honest — is now the most valuable skill in the room.





💭 Think About It


Multimodal AI means anyone can create professional-quality content — images, video, music, entire brand identities — with zero traditional training. This is democratizing in the best sense: a small business owner in any city can create marketing materials that rival a New York agency’s output. But it also means the barrier between real and fake has collapsed. A world where anyone can generate a photorealistic image of anything means verification isn’t just an AI skill — it’s a survival skill. Every image, every video, every audio clip you encounter now requires the question: Is this real?

Lab 7: The Brand Sprint (Full Version)
Time: 60 minutes | Tools needed: Any AI chatbot + any image generation tool (free options: DALL·E via ChatGPT, Bing Image Creator, Ideogram)
Purpose: Design a complete brand identity from scratch using AI — the full BA 1028 workflow.
Part A — The Brief (15 min) 1. Choose a real or hypothetical project: a campus club, a side business, a nonprofit event, or a personal brand. 2. Use the Brand Sprint prompt from Module 6. Let the AI interview you with 8 questions about your brand. 3. Review the AI’s brand output: positioning statement, tagline variants, color palette, font pairing, and logo concept prompts.
Part B — Visual Identity (20 min) 4. Take the 3 logo concept prompts the AI generated and run them through an image generation tool. 5. Generate at least 2 variants of each concept (6+ images total). 6. Select your favorite 2-3 outputs.

Part D — Reflection (10 min) 9. Write 3-4 sentences: How long would this have taken without AI? What required YOUR judgment that AI couldn’t handle? What would a professional designer do differently?

section: Module 4 Deep-Dive: Running the Practice Ladder
text:
Module 4 Deep-Dive: Running the Practice Ladder
M4 is the keystone. Every subsequent module assumes fluency in BRIEFS and SMARTS. The 10-exercise practice ladder is designed to build that fluency systematically, using the faded-worked-example pattern validated in cognitive load research (Renkl & Atkinson, 2003; meta-analysis g = 0.46, Belland et al., 2017).

The ladder at a glance










#
Exercise
Scaffolding
Skill
Time




4.A
Recognize Before You Produce
Fully worked
Diagnose missing BRIEFS element
8 min


4.B
Single-Element Insertion
High scaffold
Produce each BRIEFS element in isolation
12 min


4.C
Completion Drill
Partial scaffold
Fill missing elements in a skeleton
10 min


4.D
Full BRIEFS Production
Low scaffold

15 min


4.E

High scaffold

10 min


4.F

Mixed

12 min


4.G

20 min


4.H

Low scaffold

15 min


4.I
Transfer & Red-Team
Independent
Re-target across domains; break BRIEFS
15 min


4.J
Rubric-Based Peer Critique
Independent + collaborative
Score a partner’s prompt using the 5-dim rubric
20 min



Total ladder time: ~2 hours. Add Lab 4 (45 min) for ~3 hours total practice. For a two-week treatment, split the ladder across sessions.


Recommended Session Structure (Two 75-min Sessions)
Session 1 — BRIEFS Mastery (75 min) - Lecture/discussion: Whisperers Study + BRIEFS framework (25 min) - Exercise 4.A — Recognize (8 min individual, 5 min pair-share) - Exercise 4.B — Insertion (12 min individual) - Exercise 4.C — Completion (10 min individual, 5 min debrief) - Exercise 4.D — Production (15 min individual) - Closing check: call on 2-3 students to read their 4.D.2 prompts aloud; class diagnoses score (5 min)
Session 2 — SMARTS + Mastery (75 min) - Exercise 4.E — Handshake (10 min) - Lecture/discussion: Core + Advanced techniques (15 min) - Exercise 4.F — Technique Selection (12 min) - Lecture/discussion: SMARTS framework (10 min) - Exercise 4.G — SMARTS Walkthrough (20 min, assigned if time-short) - Exercise 4.H — Anti-Pattern Gallery (8 min)
Session 3 (optional, 45 min) — Transfer and Peer Review - Exercise 4.I — Transfer & Red-Team (15 min) - Exercise 4.J — Peer Critique (20 min pair work + 10 min whole-class debrief)
Then: Lab 4 assigned as homework.


Expected Difficulty Curve
Students should find: - 4.A easy → 4.B harder than expected. The transition from recognition to production is the steepest jump. Expect slow work on 4.B. Do not rush it. - 4.C surprisingly comfortable. The given elements anchor students; they report “oh I can do this” here. Good place to build confidence. - 4.D feels familiar if 4.B-4.C went well. If students struggle on 4.D, it’s because they skipped the deliberate practice in 4.B. Send them back. - 4.E feels unnatural. Writing Phase 2 (“what will the model say back?”) is a novel exercise in perspective-taking. Normalize the discomfort. - 4.F easy for technically-oriented students, hard for the rest. Pair strong-technical with less-technical students here. - 4.G longest exercise, most complaints. Some students will want to skip SMARTS steps. Don’t let them. The walkthrough is the only way to feel the difference between “ask the AI a question” and “think WITH the AI.” - 4.H genuinely fun. Diagnosing broken prompts is the rare pedagogy exercise students actually enjoy. Use this energy. - 4.I stretches everyone. The red-team portion (find where BRIEFS fails) is the most important 5 minutes of the module. - 4.J transformational for many. Reviewing someone else’s prompt is often when students finally see their own patterns. Expect several “oh” moments.


Common Pitfalls and How to Handle Them
1. Students rush 4.B. They want to skip to writing full prompts. Forbid combining elements until they’ve done each on its own line. The isolation is the point.
2. Students resist 4.E’s Phase 2. “How am I supposed to predict what the model will say?” Tell them: you’re not predicting — you’re calibrating your expectations so Phase 3 has something to check against. If your prediction is wildly off, your Phase 1 was weak.
3. Students skip the self-explanation prompts. These are the payload. Require at least one written self-explanation per session (submitted as a discussion post) or the exercise value drops by roughly half. This is backed by Renkl 1997 and multiple replications.
4. Pairings in 4.J go sideways. Some pairs will critique too gently (“your prompt is great!”) or too harshly. Give them the critique script before they start. Model one critique out loud for the whole class first.
5. The strong students finish early. Expertise reversal is real — cognitive load research shows that as learners become more expert, worked examples start hurting them. For your stronger students, fast-forward through 4.A-4.C and have them focus on 4.H and 4.I (the diagnostic and transfer exercises). Or: pair them with weaker students for 4.J, where the act of reviewing sharpens the stronger student’s own standards.
6. The weak students stall on 4.D. If a student can’t write three full BRIEFS prompts after 4.A-4.C, send them back to 4.B. They need more deliberate practice on isolated elements. Do not let them limp through 4.D producing low-quality work — that will cement bad habits.
7. Students ask “can’t I just read about BRIEFS and skip the exercises?” Answer with the evidence: Zhang et al. (2025) studied translation students with strong theoretical knowledge and found they still wrote short, informal prompts unless given structured scaffolding. Knowledge doesn’t transfer to skill without practice. This is the same reason reading about squats doesn’t make you able to squat.


Grading the Ladder
Recommend completion grading, not quality grading, for the ladder itself. Students need to feel safe experimenting. Grade strict on Lab 4 (which comes after the ladder and is the quality checkpoint).
If you must grade quality on the ladder, grade only Exercise 4.D.2 and Exercise 4.I (the independent production exercises) using the 5-dimension rubric from Card 5 in the Framework Cards appendix.

Assessment Strategy

Formative (During the Course)

Module quizzes (built-in JavaScript games) — self-paced, not graded
Micro-checks (Test Yourself boxes) — embedded comprehension checks
Think About It reflections — submit as discussion posts or journal entries
Lab deliverables — the primary formative assessment
M4 ladder exercises — completion-graded, not quality-graded (see above)
Self-explanation prompts — brief written reflections after each major exercise; these drive learning



Summative (End of Course)

Post-course Self-Assessment — compare to pre-course baseline
Capstone Project (Module 14) — the culminating assessment
Portfolio — optional: collect all lab deliverables into a portfolio



Suggested Grading Breakdown (Credit-Bearing)








Component

40%

Quiz Policies

Quizzes are learning tools, not gatekeepers. Unlimited retries, best score counts.
Each module quiz has 10-18 questions randomized from a pool. Students see different questions on each attempt.
Badge threshold: 80% (e.g., 14/18 for M4). Students who earn the badge have demonstrated competency.
For grading: award full credit for earning the badge (any number of attempts). Partial credit for 60-79%.



Lab Submission Expectations

Labs are the primary evidence of learning. Each lab produces a tangible deliverable.
Grade on: completeness (did they do all parts?), quality (is the work thoughtful?), and reflection (do they show learning?).
Do NOT grade on whether the AI output was “correct” — grade on whether the student evaluated, iterated, and reflected on it.
Late policy: recommended 1-week grace period. Labs build on each other, so falling behind compounds.



Capstone Rubric Reference
The capstone rubric (Module 14, Step 5) evaluates five dimensions:

25%
