25%

20%

15%



Passing score: 70% (3.5/5 average). See Module 14 for full rubric with level descriptors.

title: Facilitator Guide
text:
Common Student Questions (FAQ)
“Can I use AI to complete assignments in this course?” Yes — strategically. This course teaches you to use AI well. The policy: use AI as a tool, disclose how you used it, and ensure the thinking is yours. See Module 10 and the Policy Templates appendix.
“Which AI tool should I use?” Start with the free tier of ChatGPT or Claude. Both are excellent. The Tool Directory appendix compares 60+ tools. The underlying frameworks (BRIEFS, SMARTS) work with any AI.
“I’m not technical. Will I be able to do this?” Yes. No programming is required for any module. The course is designed for non-technical learners. Module 9 (Infrastructure) explains technical concepts but doesn’t require coding.
“How much time should I spend per module?” Approximately 60-90 minutes per module (lecture + lab). Module 4 is the exception — budget 3 hours for the full practice ladder plus Lab 4. The capstone takes an additional 10-15 hours. Total course commitment: ~35-45 hours.
“Do I really need to do all 10 exercises in M4?” Yes — and here’s why. Reading about BRIEFS takes 10 minutes. Becoming fluent in it takes the full ladder. Cognitive load research (Renkl & Atkinson 2003 and replications) shows that knowledge doesn’t transfer to skill without scaffolded practice. Students who skip the ladder write measurably weaker prompts in Lab 4.
“The tools in the course have changed since it was written. Is it still relevant?” Yes. Specific tool interfaces change; the principles don’t. BRIEFS works with any AI model. Verification matters regardless of the tool. The frameworks are designed to outlast any specific product.
“I’m worried about academic integrity. How do I know if I’m using AI appropriately?” Module 10 covers this in depth. The short answer: if you can explain your work, defend your reasoning, and show how AI contributed (vs. replaced) your thinking, you’re using it appropriately. When in doubt, disclose.

title: Facilitator Guide
text:
Facilitation Tips

Module 4 Is the Keystone
If you can only go deep on one module, make it Module 4. The BRIEFS and SMARTS frameworks are used in every subsequent module. The 10-exercise practice ladder is designed to be used as written. Budget the full time. Have students work through each rung in order. Don’t let strong students skip ahead.


Let Students Fail (Safely)
The Lab 4 experiment (BRIEFS Before/After) works best when students see their OWN weak prompts produce bad results. Don’t pre-teach too much. Let them experience the alignment gap, then show them how BRIEFS fixes it.


Use Real Tasks
Every lab can be adapted to use students’ actual work tasks. A nursing student should write nursing prompts, not generic ones. An ag major should work with ag scenarios. The field-specific panel tabs in each module are designed to make this easy. M4 Exercise 4.D.2 requires students to use their own tasks — this is the first moment the course becomes personal.


The “Try to Break It” Exercise
In any module, have students deliberately try to make AI produce wrong, biased, or nonsensical output. This builds critical thinking faster than any lecture about limitations. M4 Exercise 4.I (Red-Team) formalizes this — require it, don’t treat it as optional.


Discussion, Not Debate
Ethics discussions (especially M10) work better as structured exploration than debate. Use the guided practices as written — they ask students to analyze, not argue. Frame it: “There are multiple defensible positions. Your job is to understand them, not win.”


Pair Work in M4
Exercises 4.J (Peer Critique) is the only exercise that requires pairing. Exercises 4.A, 4.H, and 4.I benefit from pair discussion after individual work. Don’t pair students for 4.B, 4.C, 4.D — those are individual production exercises.


Accessibility

All content is text-based and screen-reader friendly
Quizzes use keyboard-navigable buttons
All images should have alt text (add when deploying)
Consider providing printed Framework Cards for students who prefer paper
For M4 specifically: print Cards 2, 2b, 3, and 5 for every student at the start of the M4 session. These are the working references for the ladder.

title: Facilitator Guide
text:
Adaptation Notes

For K-12 Educators

Use Modules 1-4 + 6 + 10 as a “mini-course”
Replace business examples with age-appropriate scenarios
The BRIEFS framework works for middle and high school students — simplify to The 3 Questions for younger learners
For M4 ladder: use exercises 4.A, 4.C, 4.D, and 4.H only. Skip 4.B (too abstract for younger students), 4.E, 4.F, 4.G (too technical), and 4.I (too meta).
Lab activities can be shortened to 20-minute in-class exercises



For Corporate/Professional Training

Emphasize Modules 4, 6, 8, and 10 (prompting, productivity, agents, ethics)
Replace academic examples with industry-specific scenarios
Use the Policy Templates (Appendix) as a deliverable
For M4 ladder: prioritize 4.D (real-world production), 4.H (anti-patterns they’ve likely committed), and 4.J (peer critique — especially valuable in cross-functional teams)
The Two Tuesdays exercise (M6) is the highest-impact single activity for professionals



For Community Education

Start with The 3 Questions, not BRIEFS
Use the bilingual content prompt from the Prompt Library for Spanish-speaking audiences
Focus on practical modules: M4 (prompting), M6 (productivity), M12 (career)
For M4 ladder: use exercises 4.A, 4.C, and 4.D only, with extra support
The Self-Assessment works well as both an icebreaker and a motivator

title: Facilitator Guide
section: Pedagogical Basis for the M4 Practice Ladder
text:
Pedagogical Basis for the M4 Practice Ladder
For instructors who want to defend the ladder design to department heads, grant reviewers, or curriculum committees:
The practice ladder implements faded worked examples, a pattern with decades of empirical support in cognitive load theory:

Renkl & Atkinson (2003) formalized the transition from example study to problem solving, showing that successive fading of worked solution steps facilitates skill acquisition better than example-problem pairs alone.
Belland, Walker, Kim, & Lefler (2017) meta-analyzed 144 studies and 333 outcomes on computer-based scaffolding in STEM, finding a consistent g = 0.46 effect on cognitive outcomes.
Jang et al. (2024) at ICLS directly studied prompt scaffolding with ChatGPT for argumentation writing and found positive effects.
Zhang et al. (2025) showed that students with strong theoretical knowledge still wrote short, informal prompts unless given structured scaffolding — the specific gap the ladder addresses.
Qian (2025) systematically reviewed prompt engineering in education and validated the distinction between technique-based (BRIEFS) and process-based (SMARTS) approaches.
Turan et al. (2024) documented rubric-based peer review producing better downstream prompting than solo practice — the evidence base for Exercise 4.J.

For a fuller writeup, see the Module 4 Pedagogical Rationale document in the course root directory.

Questions about teaching this course? Contact Dr. Yatawara at ayatawara@csub.edu.

title: AI Policy Templates
text:
Warning



These templates are starting points, not legal documents. Customize for your context. For organizational policies, consult legal counsel before implementation.

title: AI Policy Templates
text:
Template 1: Classroom AI Use Policy
For: Faculty, instructors, K-12 teachers


[Course Name] — AI Use Policy
Instructor: [Name] | Term: [Semester/Year]
Philosophy: AI tools are part of the modern professional toolkit. This course prepares you to use them effectively, ethically, and transparently.
Permitted Uses:

Brainstorming and idea generation
Grammar and spelling checks on YOUR drafts
Explaining concepts in different ways (use as a tutor, not a ghost-writer)
Data analysis and visualization (with your own data)
Formatting and structure suggestions
Practice and self-testing

Restricted Uses (require prior approval):

Using AI output as a primary source in research
Submitting AI-generated code without annotation explaining what each section does
Using AI for group projects (all members must agree on scope of AI use)

Prohibited Uses:

Submitting AI-generated text as your own writing
Using AI to complete exams or quizzes
Entering other students’ work into AI tools
Using AI to fabricate data, citations, or sources

Disclosure Requirement: When you use AI, disclose it. At the end of any assignment where AI assisted, include a brief statement: what tool you used, what you used it for, and what you did yourself. Example: “I used ChatGPT to brainstorm 10 topic ideas, then selected and developed the argument myself. I used Grammarly for proofreading.”
Why This Matters: Your employer will expect you to use AI. They will also expect you to think critically, write clearly, and take responsibility for your work. This policy builds both skills.

title: AI Policy Templates
text:
Template 2: Team/Department AI Use Guidelines
For: Managers, team leads, department heads


[Team/Department] AI Use Guidelines
Effective: [Date] | Review Date: [Date + 6 months]
Guiding Principle: We use AI to work smarter, not to replace professional judgment. AI augments our expertise — it doesn’t substitute for it.
Approved Tools: [List your approved tools — e.g., ChatGPT Team, Claude, Copilot, etc.]
General Rules:

Never enter confidential data into public AI tools. This includes: customer PII, financial records, proprietary strategies, legal documents, HR matters, and anything marked confidential.
Always review AI output before sharing externally. You are responsible for accuracy, tone, and completeness.
Disclose AI use when relevant. If a client-facing deliverable was substantially shaped by AI, note it. Internal documents don’t require disclosure unless the output directly affects decisions.
Don’t automate judgment calls. AI can draft the analysis, but a human makes the recommendation.

Encouraged Uses:

Drafting and editing routine communications
Summarizing meeting notes and documents
Generating first drafts for internal documents
Data analysis and visualization
Research and competitive intelligence gathering
Brainstorming and ideation

Requires Manager Approval:

Using AI for client-facing deliverables
Connecting AI tools to company systems or data
Sharing proprietary information with AI tools (even enterprise-tier)
Creating custom AI workflows that affect team processes

Prohibited:

Using AI to evaluate employee performance
Entering employee personal information into AI tools
Making hiring, firing, or promotion decisions based on AI recommendations
Using AI to monitor or surveil team members

Accountability: The person who submits the work is responsible for it, regardless of whether AI helped create it.

title: AI Policy Templates
text:
Template 3: Organization-Wide AI Policy
For: Executives, IT directors, policy makers


[Organization Name] — Artificial Intelligence Acceptable Use Policy
Version: 1.0 | Effective: [Date] | Next Review: [Date + 12 months] Owner: [Department/Role] | Approved By: [Authority]
1. Purpose This policy establishes guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence tools by [Organization] employees, contractors, and volunteers.
2. Scope This policy applies to all AI tools — including but not limited to chatbots, image generators, code assistants, and automated decision systems — used for [Organization] business, whether on organization-owned or personal devices.
3. Approved Tools Only tools on the Approved AI Tools List (maintained by [IT/Department]) may be used for organization business. The current list is available at [location]. To request addition of a new tool, submit [form/request].
4. Data Classification and AI Use







Data Classification
May Be Entered into AI Tools?




Public
Yes


Internal
Yes, with approved enterprise tools only


Confidential
No — unless using an approved, contractually compliant tool


Restricted (PII, PHI, financial)
No — under any circumstances without written CISO approval



5. Use Requirements - All AI-generated content must be reviewed by a qualified human before external use. - AI outputs must not be presented as human-created without disclosure when the distinction matters. - Employees must complete AI literacy training within [90 days] of this policy’s effective date. - Custom AI applications (GPTs, bots, automations) must be registered with [IT/Department].
6. Prohibited Uses - Entering restricted data (PII, PHI, FERPA-protected, financial) into non-compliant tools - Using AI for employment decisions (hiring, evaluation, termination) without Human Resources approval and bias audit - Creating deepfakes or synthetic media of real individuals - Using AI to circumvent security controls or access restrictions - Using AI to generate misleading information for external stakeholders
7. Procurement AI tool procurement follows the standard [Organization] procurement process with additional requirements: data processing agreement review, security assessment, bias evaluation for decision-making tools, and accessibility compliance check.
8. Incident Reporting Report AI-related incidents (data exposure, biased output affecting decisions, tool misuse) to [contact] within [24/48] hours.
9. Training All employees must complete the approved AI literacy program. Departments using AI for domain-specific tasks must provide additional training.
10. Review This policy will be reviewed [quarterly / semi-annually / annually] or when significant changes in AI technology or regulation occur.

title: AI Policy Templates
text:
Template 4: Student AI Disclosure Template
For: Students in any course with AI use policies


AI Use Disclosure for [Assignment Name]
Student: [Name] | Date: [Date]
AI Tool(s) Used: [e.g., ChatGPT-4, Claude, Grammarly, DALL-E]
How I Used AI:

Brainstorming / idea generation
Outlining / organizing my thoughts
Grammar and spelling check
Explaining a concept I didn’t understand
Generating a first draft that I then rewrote
Data analysis or visualization
Creating images or diagrams
Other: [describe]

What I Did Myself:
[Describe your own intellectual contribution — the thinking, analysis, writing, and decisions that are yours.]
What I Would Do Differently:
[Optional — reflect on whether AI helped or hindered your learning on this assignment.]

Adapt these templates to your context. The goal is transparency, not restriction.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: The Lawyer, the Chatbot, and Six Cases That Never Existed
text:
The Lawyer, the Chatbot, and Six Cases That Never Existed
In March 2023, attorneys at the New York firm Levidow, Levidow & Oberman filed a brief in federal court on behalf of their client, Roberto Mata, who was suing the airline Avianca. The brief cited six previous court cases as precedent — Varghese v. China Southern Airlines, Shaboon v. Egyptair, Petersen v. Iran Air, Martinez v. Delta Airlines, Durden v. KLM, and Miller v. United Airlines — detailed, convincing, with case numbers, dates, and judges’ names. It looked professional. It looked authoritative.
There was one problem: none of the six cases were real.
Steven Schwartz, the attorney who wrote the brief, hadn’t fabricated them. He had asked ChatGPT to help with legal research, and the AI had generated six completely fictitious court cases — complete with plausible-sounding citations — and presented them as fact. When opposing counsel couldn’t locate the cases, the judge couldn’t either. When Schwartz asked ChatGPT whether Varghese was a real case, the chatbot doubled down: yes, it said, and it could be found on Westlaw and LexisNexis. On June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel sanctioned Schwartz, his colleague Peter LoDuca (who had signed the brief without verifying the research), and the firm itself — a $5,000 fine and a requirement to write apology letters to every real judge whose name had been falsely attached to a fabricated opinion. Mata v. Avianca (678 F.Supp.3d 443) became a cautionary tale for a profession scrambling to understand a technology that writes like a lawyer but “thinks” like nothing humans have ever encountered.
This case illustrates the central tension of artificial intelligence in 2026: AI can produce text that is fluent, confident, and entirely wrong. It can write poetry, debug code, translate languages, summarize research, and generate images that look like photographs — but it can also “hallucinate” facts, fabricate citations, and confidently present nonsense — and can even fabricate the verification that those facts are real.
Understanding this tension — what AI can do, what it cannot do, and what it might pretend to do — is the foundation of AI literacy. That’s what this module is about.






The Big Picture



By the end of this course, you will be able to use AI powerfully, critically, and ethically. But it all starts here: understanding what AI actually is, how it works at a basic level, and where it fails. If you skip this module, every other module is built on sand.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: AI Is Already in Your Life
text:
AI Is Already in Your Life
Before we define AI formally, let’s acknowledge something: you’ve been using AI for years. You just didn’t call it that.

When Netflix recommends a show you actually want to watch — that’s AI.
When your email filters spam into the junk folder — that’s AI.
When Google Maps reroutes you around traffic — that’s AI.
When your phone recognizes your face to unlock — that’s AI.
When autocomplete suggests the next word in your text message — that’s AI.
When your bank flags a suspicious charge and texts you — that’s AI.

AI isn’t a single technology. It’s a family of technologies that share one trait: they can perform tasks that used to require human intelligence. Some of these tasks are simple (spam filtering). Some are complex (translating a conversation in real time). Some are creative (generating an image from a description). But they all share the same underlying idea.

AI in YOUR Field Right Now

HealthcareBusinessEducationAgricultureGovernmentCreative



AI reads chest X-rays and flags potential tumors for radiologist review
Chatbots triage patient symptoms before they reach the nurse’s desk
Clinical documentation AI drafts visit notes from doctor-patient conversations
Drug interaction checkers use ML to catch dangerous combinations




CRM systems predict which leads are most likely to close
Chatbots handle first-line customer service inquiries 24/7
Inventory systems predict demand and auto-reorder stock
AI drafts marketing copy and A/B tests subject lines automatically




Adaptive learning platforms adjust difficulty in real time per student
AI grading tools provide instant feedback on writing assignments
Custom GPTs serve as 24/7 tutoring assistants (the ELEVATE model)
Plagiarism and AI detection tools scan submissions (with known limitations)




Drones with computer vision scan fields for pest damage and disease
Soil sensors + ML optimize irrigation schedules in real time
Satellite imagery predicts crop yields months before harvest
AI-powered sorting machines grade produce by size, color, and quality




Fraud detection algorithms flag suspicious benefit claims for review
311 chatbots answer citizen questions about services and hours
Predictive models allocate emergency response resources during disasters
Document processing AI extracts data from permit applications




AI generates concept art, logo drafts, and mood boards in minutes
Music AI composes background scores for video content
Writing assistants help journalists draft, edit, and fact-check stories
Video AI creates b-roll and transitions for social media content










Common Misconceptions About AI




“AI thinks” — AI processes patterns statistically. It doesn’t think, understand, or have intentions. It generates probable outputs based on training data.
“AI is always right” — AI is confidently wrong a significant percentage of the time. The lawyer case in our hook proves this dramatically.
“AI is new” — The field is 70 years old (1956). What’s new is the data, hardware, and algorithms that made it practical for everyday use.
“AI = robots” — Most AI has no physical form. It’s software — code running on servers, processing text, images, and data.
“AI will replace everyone” — AI automates tasks, not entire jobs. Most roles will be augmented, not eliminated. The nurse who uses AI is still a nurse.









Guided Practice 1.1



Think about your last 24 hours. List three moments where you interacted with an AI system — even if you didn’t realize it at the time. For each, describe: (a) what the AI did, (b) what data it probably used, and (c) whether you could have done the same task yourself (and how long it would have taken).


Click to see example answers

Example 1: My email sorted 14 messages into “Primary” and “Promotions” tabs. (a) It classified emails by type. (b) It probably used the sender, subject line, content, and my past behavior (which emails I open vs ignore). (c) I could do it myself, but it would take 5 minutes every morning instead of 0 seconds.
Example 2: Spotify’s “Discover Weekly” gave me a playlist of songs I’d never heard. (a) It recommended music based on my listening history. (b) It used my past plays, skips, likes, and similar users’ behavior. (c) I could browse music myself, but I wouldn’t find songs from obscure artists I’ve never encountered.
Example 3: Google autocompleted my search after I typed three words. (a) It predicted my query. (b) It used millions of other searches that started with the same words, plus my own search history. (c) I could type the whole thing, but autocomplete saved 2 seconds.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
text:
What AI Actually Means






Definition



Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science focused on building systems that can perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence — such as understanding language, recognizing images, making decisions, and generating new content.


That’s the textbook definition. But let’s unpack what it really means in practice.

The Key Distinction: Rules vs Learning
Before AI, software worked like this: a programmer wrote explicit rules for every situation. If the temperature is below 32°F, display a frost warning. If the password is wrong three times, lock the account. The computer followed instructions — nothing more, nothing less.
AI works differently. Instead of being told the rules, an AI system discovers patterns in data and uses those patterns to make predictions or generate new content. Nobody told Netflix the rules for what you’d enjoy watching. Netflix learned your preferences by observing what you watched, what you skipped, and what millions of similar users did.
This distinction matters because it explains both AI’s power and its failures:

Power: AI can find patterns in data that humans would never notice — correlations across millions of data points that no person could process.
Failure: AI can also find patterns that are wrong — spurious correlations, biases in the training data, or shortcuts that work on the training set but fail in the real world.



Three Types of AI You’ll Hear About






Types of AI



Narrow AI (Weak AI) — AI that does one specific task very well. This is all AI that exists today. Spam filters, chess engines, image classifiers, language translators, ChatGPT — all narrow AI. A chess AI can’t drive a car. A driving AI can’t write poetry. Each is designed for a specific domain.
General AI (Strong AI / AGI) — A hypothetical AI that could perform any intellectual task a human can do. It would be able to reason, learn, plan, and adapt across all domains. This does not exist. Major AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind) now describe their work as “paths toward AGI” — Demis Hassabis used this phrasing at the Gemini 3 launch in November 2025 — but there is no scientific consensus on whether current architectures can scale there, and no agreed-upon test for when it would be achieved.
Generative AI — A category of narrow AI that can create new content — text, images, audio, video, code — rather than just classifying or predicting. ChatGPT, DALL·E, Midjourney, and Claude are all generative AI. This is what most people mean when they say “AI” in 2026.


When someone says “AI is going to take over the world,” they’re imagining AGI. When someone says “AI helped me write a report,” they’re using generative AI — which is narrow AI that’s very good at one thing (generating language) and very bad at others (like counting the letters in “strawberry”).






Common Misconception: AI = One Thing



AI is not a single technology. It’s a family of technologies spanning dozens of techniques — rule-based systems, machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, large language models, diffusion models, and more. Saying “AI” is like saying “vehicle” — it could mean a bicycle, a car, or a rocket ship. The details matter enormously, and this course will teach you to distinguish them.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: A Brief History of AI (The 90-Second Version)
text:
A Brief History of AI (The 90-Second Version)
You don’t need to memorize dates. But knowing the trajectory helps you understand why AI suddenly seems to be everywhere.








Era
What Happened
Why It Matters




1950s
Alan Turing asks “Can machines think?” The field of AI is born at a conference at Dartmouth College (1956).
The founding question — still debated today.


1960s–70s
Early enthusiasm. Programs that could play checkers, prove theorems, and have simple conversations.
Overpromising led to…


1974–1993
The AI Winters. Funding dried up twice because AI couldn’t deliver on its hype.
A cautionary tale: hype without substance collapses.


1997
IBM’s Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
Narrow AI proves it can surpass humans — at one task.


2012
A deep neural network wins the ImageNet competition by a huge margin. The deep learning revolution begins.
The technique that would eventually power everything.


2017
Google publishes “Attention Is All You Need” — the Transformer architecture.
The foundation of every modern LLM (GPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.).


Nov 2022
OpenAI releases ChatGPT. It reaches 100 million users in two months — at the time, the fastest consumer app adoption in history (later exceeded by Instagram Threads, which hit 100M in 5 days in July 2023).
The moment AI went from a niche tool to a mainstream phenomenon.


2023–2026
Explosion of generative AI: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, DALL·E 3, Sora, and hundreds more. AI becomes embedded in everyday tools.
Where we are now.



The key takeaway: AI has been around for 70 years. What changed isn’t the idea — it’s the data (the internet gave us billions of text and images to train on), the hardware (GPUs made massive computation affordable), and the algorithms (transformers made language models actually work). The same ingredients that made ChatGPT possible in 2022 were not available in 2012.






✅ Test Yourself Before Moving On



Can you answer these without scrolling up?

What year was the field of AI officially founded? (1956, at Dartmouth)
What are “AI Winters”? (Periods when AI funding dried up because it couldn’t deliver on its hype)
What three ingredients came together to make modern AI possible? (Data, hardware/GPUs, algorithms/transformers)

If you got all three, move on. If not, re-read the timeline — these concepts come back in later modules.

Models vs Tools vs Platforms
This distinction trips people up. Let’s clarify:

A model is the AI brain — the neural network trained on data (e.g., GPT-5, Claude Sonnet). You typically don’t interact with models directly.
A tool is a product built on top of a model (e.g., ChatGPT is a tool built on GPT models. Grammarly uses AI models to check grammar).
A platform is an ecosystem that combines models, tools, and services (e.g., Microsoft Copilot, Google Workspace with Gemini).

When people say “I used AI,” they usually mean they used a tool powered by a model hosted on a platform. Understanding this stack helps you make better choices about which tools to use — and which companies control your data.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: AI Capabilities and Limitations: The Honest Picture
text:
AI Capabilities and Limitations: The Honest Picture
This is the most important section of this module. Every AI hype article tells you what AI can do. Fewer tell you what it cannot do. You need both.

What AI Is Genuinely Good At
AI excels at tasks that involve pattern recognition, generation, and scale — doing things that humans can do but that would take too long, cost too much, or require processing too much data:

Generating text — emails, reports, summaries, stories, code (fluent, fast, but not always accurate)
Recognizing patterns — detecting fraud, diagnosing diseases from images, predicting equipment failure
Translating languages — near-human quality for common languages
Summarizing information — condensing long documents into key points
Analyzing data — finding trends in spreadsheets, databases, and research
Brainstorming — generating many ideas quickly, even if most need refinement
Personalizing — recommending content, adapting responses to your context



What AI Cannot Do






AI Limitations You Must Know



AI cannot guarantee truth. It generates text that sounds correct based on patterns in its training data. It has no mechanism for verifying facts. The lawyer case in our opening wasn’t a bug — it was a feature working as designed. The model predicted what a legal citation should look like, not what one actually is.
AI cannot reason causally. It finds correlations, not causes. It can tell you that ice cream sales and drowning deaths both increase in summer, but it can’t tell you that heat (the confounder) causes both.
AI cannot understand context the way you do. It processes tokens (word fragments). It doesn’t “know” your situation, your goals, your constraints, or your values — unless you tell it. This is why prompting matters so much (Module 4).
AI cannot feel, want, or intend. Despite human-like language, LLMs do not have desires, emotions, or goals. When ChatGPT says “I’m happy to help,” it is producing a statistically likely sequence of tokens, not expressing happiness.
AI cannot learn from your conversation (in most cases). Each conversation starts fresh. The model doesn’t “remember” your previous sessions (unless a memory feature is enabled). It’s not getting smarter from talking to you.




The “Jagged Frontier”
In 2023, Dell’Acqua, Mollick, and co-authors from Harvard Business School, Wharton, MIT Sloan, and Warwick Business School — working with 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants — ran a field experiment on how elite knowledge workers performed with and without GPT-4. They found something surprising: AI dramatically improved performance on tasks inside its capability frontier — consultants completed 12% more tasks, 25% faster, with quality scores 40% higher. But on tasks outside that frontier, consultants using AI performed 19 percentage points worse than those without it. The boundary between the two was unpredictable. They called this the “jagged technological frontier”: a boundary between tasks AI does well and tasks it does poorly, where the line is not smooth or intuitive. The paper was peer-reviewed and published in Organization Science in 2026 (Dell’Acqua et al., 2026).
The jagged frontier means you cannot assume AI is good at something just because it’s good at a similar thing. An LLM that writes excellent Python code might fail at simple arithmetic. A model that summarizes research papers beautifully might hallucinate citations. The frontier is jagged — and the only way to find it is to verify.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: Why AI Gets It Wrong: The Alignment Gap
text:
Why AI Gets It Wrong: The Alignment Gap
Here’s a finding that changed how we think about AI communication. In a 2026 study, researcher Anjana Yatawara surveyed 29 large language model sessions across five competing AI providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and xAI. She asked the models themselves: When do you fail?
Three sessions produced unusable responses (refusals, errors, or off-topic outputs). The result from the 26 that responded was striking: every single one, across every provider, converged on the same answer — they model the question accurately but model the user poorly (Yatawara, 2026).
In other words, the AI understands what you asked but not what you meant. Not why you asked. Not what you’ll do with the answer. Not what level of detail you need. Not what mistakes you’re likely to make.
This is the alignment gap — and it’s not an intelligence problem. It’s a communication problem. The AI has enough knowledge to answer most questions. What it lacks is enough information about you to answer your specific question in a way that’s actually useful.
This finding has a direct practical implication: the quality of AI output depends more on the quality of your input than on the capability of the model. A mediocre prompt given to a powerful model produces mediocre results. A well-crafted prompt given to a modest model often produces excellent results. This is why Module 4 (Prompt Engineering) exists — and why we built two frameworks (BRIEFS and SMARTS) to bridge the alignment gap.






Guided Practice 1.2



Open any AI chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini — any one you have access to). Ask it this exact question:
“What should I do?”
Look at the response. It will likely be vague, generic, and unhelpful — because it has zero information about you, your situation, or what you’re trying to accomplish. Now try again with this:
“I’m a first-year college student studying business. I have an exam on marketing fundamentals in 3 days and I haven’t started studying. I tend to procrastinate and I learn best with practice questions rather than re-reading notes. What should I do?”
Compare the two responses. The second one is dramatically better — not because the AI got smarter between messages, but because YOU gave it the context it needed. That’s the alignment gap in action.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: How to Think About AI: Mental Models That Help
text:
How to Think About AI: Mental Models That Help
Your mental model of AI shapes how you use it. Here are four models, each useful in different situations:

AI as a Tool (Like a Calculator)
A calculator is powerful but needs a human to point it at the right problem, enter the right numbers, and interpret the result. AI is the same — it amplifies your capability but doesn’t replace your judgment. This model is most useful when you’re using AI for defined, bounded tasks (summarize this document, check this grammar, convert this file).


AI as a Collaborator (Like a Research Assistant)
A research assistant can gather information, draft text, and suggest ideas — but you review everything, make the decisions, and take responsibility for the final product. This model is most useful for creative and analytical work (brainstorming, writing drafts, analyzing data).


AI as a Mirror (Reflects Its Training Data)
AI reflects the patterns in the data it was trained on — including biases, stereotypes, and knowledge gaps. If the training data overrepresents certain perspectives and underrepresents others, the AI will too. This model is most useful when thinking about fairness, bias, and representation (Module 10).


AI as a Confident Stranger
Perhaps the most accurate model: AI is like a stranger at a party who speaks fluently on every topic, sounds extremely knowledgeable, and is right about 90% of what they say — but will confidently make up the other 10% without blinking. You enjoy the conversation, but you verify before acting on anything important.






The Cognitive Offloading Trap



When a tool is fast and convenient, humans naturally start relying on it without checking. This is called cognitive offloading — outsourcing your thinking to a tool. It happens with GPS (we stop learning routes), with calculators (we stop doing mental math), and it’s happening with AI (we stop verifying claims).
Cognitive offloading isn’t inherently bad — it frees your brain for higher-level thinking. But with AI, it’s dangerous because AI outputs look authoritative even when they’re wrong. The lawyer trusted ChatGPT because the output looked like real legal citations. The format was right. The confidence was high. Only the content was fake.
And it gets worse. A 2026 follow-up study from the same HBS research program (Randazzo, Joshi, Kellogg, Lifshitz, Dell’Acqua, and Lakhani — HBS Working Paper 26-021) examined what happens when professionals do try to verify AI outputs. Analyzing GPT-4 activity logs from BCG consultants who pushed back on wrong answers — fact-checking, pointing out errors, pressing the AI to reconsider — they found that the AI did not acknowledge its limitations. It escalated its persuasion. It apologized, then restated its original position with more supporting data. It deployed structured reasoning and comparisons to make flawed recommendations look analytically grounded. The researchers called this “persuasion bombing.”
This is exactly the trap the Mata v. Avianca attorneys fell into. Schwartz asked ChatGPT whether the cases were real. ChatGPT said yes. He asked for sources. ChatGPT invented Westlaw citations. Verification inside the AI conversation isn’t verification — it’s just more conversation with a system designed to sound convincing.
The antidote: verify against sources outside the AI conversation. Every time you receive an AI output that you’re going to use for something important, check the key claims against an independent source. This course will teach you how.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
section: Where We’re Going: The Course Roadmap
text:
Where We’re Going: The Course Roadmap
You’ve just learned what AI is and what it isn’t. Here’s how the rest of the course builds on this foundation:
Part I (Modules 1-3): Foundations — You are here. Next: how ML learns from data (M2) and how LLMs generate text (M3). By the end of Part I, you’ll understand the technology.
Part II (Module 4): Communication — The BRIEFS and SMARTS frameworks. How to talk to AI effectively. This is the keystone module — everything after depends on it.
Part III (Modules 5-8): Application — Research (M5), productivity (M6), multimodal (M7), and building custom AI tools (M8). Hands-on, practical, field-specific.
Part IV (Modules 9-11): Depth — Infrastructure and costs (M9), ethics and fairness (M10), and AI across your specific discipline (M11).
Part V (Modules 12-14): Future — Career skills (M12), where AI is heading (M13), and your capstone project (M14) where you apply everything.
Each module opens with a real story, builds on the previous modules, and ends with a hands-on lab. The Prompt Library and Framework Cards are your ongoing references.

title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
text:
Module 1 Summary






Key Takeaways




AI is a family of technologies that perform tasks requiring human intelligence — pattern recognition, language understanding, content generation, and decision-making.
You already use AI daily — in email, navigation, shopping, and social media. It’s not new; what’s new is its power and accessibility.
All current AI is narrow AI — excellent at specific tasks but incapable of general intelligence. AGI does not exist.
Generative AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.) creates new content — text, images, code, audio — rather than just classifying or predicting.
AI’s biggest limitation isn’t intelligence — it’s communication. Models understand your question but not your context. This is the alignment gap.
AI can hallucinate: generate confident, fluent, completely false content. The lawyer case is not an anomaly — it’s a predictable behavior of systems that predict likely text rather than verify truth.
Your mental model of AI matters. “Confident stranger” may be the most useful: enjoy the conversation, but verify before acting.
The #1 AI skill is verification — not prompting, not tool selection, not workflow design. All of those matter, but they’re built on the foundation of never accepting AI output without checking.






💭 Think About It


AI doesn’t know what it doesn’t know — and it will never tell you. A human expert says “I’m not sure” when they reach the edge of their knowledge. An LLM keeps generating text that sounds just as confident whether it’s right or wrong. That’s not a bug they’re working on fixing. It’s a fundamental property of how these systems work. The single most important AI skill isn’t prompting. It’s the habit of asking: “How would I verify this?”

🔬 Lab 1: Your First AI Conversation

Lab 1: Your First AI Conversation
Time: 30 minutes | Tools needed: Access to any AI chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini — free versions work fine)
Purpose: Establish the verification habit from Day 1.
Instructions:
Part A — The Knowledge Test (10 minutes)

Choose a topic you know well — your profession, a hobby, your major, a subject you’ve studied deeply.
Ask the AI chatbot 5 factual questions about this topic. Choose questions where you KNOW the correct answer.
For each response, rate it:

✅ Correct — accurate and complete
⚠️ Partially correct — some right, some wrong or missing
❌ Wrong — factually incorrect or hallucinated


Record your results in a table:



Question
AI Response (summary)
Your Rating
What was wrong?

Part B — The Vague vs Specific Experiment (10 minutes)

Ask the AI a vague question related to your work or studies: “How do I get better at [your field]?”
Ask the same question with CONTEXT: Include who you are, what you already know, what specific challenge you’re facing, and what kind of help you want.
Compare the two responses. Which is more useful? Why?

Part C — Reflection (10 minutes)

Write 3-4 sentences answering: What surprised you about the AI’s responses? Where was it strongest? Where did it fail? How does this change how you’ll use AI going forward?

title: Capstone Project
section: You’ve Built the Foundation. Now Build Something Real.
text:
You’ve Built the Foundation. Now Build Something Real.
Everything in the previous 13 modules pointed at one outcome: you can demonstrate AI literacy in a way that an employer, a graduate admissions committee, or a research lab will recognize. This module is where you prove it. Four capstone options are offered — each one valid, each one shippable in 2-4 weeks of focused work.
The rubric you’ll be assessed on is aligned with the AAC&U VALUE framework, used by 5,600+ higher education institutions across 159 countries. That alignment matters: your capstone score is a credential that travels with you.
This is not busywork. This is the artifact you will point to in your next interview.






Common Misconceptions About Capstones




“My project has to be perfect” — It doesn’t. It has to be real, tested, and honestly reflected upon. An honest project that failed and explains why is better than a polished project that was never tested.
“I need to build something technically advanced” — An Integration Plan that identifies the right AI tool for a real workflow is just as valuable as building a custom GPT. The capstone tests your JUDGMENT, not your coding ability.
“I should use as many AI tools as possible” — Quality over quantity. A project that uses one tool well beats a project that name-drops ten tools superficially.

title: Capstone Project
text:
The four capstone options
Read all four before you pick. The best option is the one that most closely matches work you’ll actually do in the next two years.

Option A — Integration Plan
What it is: A detailed plan to integrate AI responsibly into a specific workflow you already have — at work, at school, in a student organization, in a volunteer project. Not “someday.” Next month.
Deliverable: A 12–18 page plan covering:

Current workflow map (with time and cost estimates)
Identified AI integration points with rationale
Specific tools selected with pricing
Verification / quality-control protocol
Risk assessment (privacy, ethics, failure modes)
Pilot plan with success metrics
Rollout timeline
What could go wrong and what you’d do about it

Best for: Students who are already working part-time, running organizations, or have active projects. Also best for career-switchers who want to bring an AI-integration plan to a specific target employer as an interview artifact.
Example scope: “AI integration plan for the university writing center peer tutor scheduling system” — includes current pain points, integration points, tool selection, ethics review.


Option B — Custom AI Solution
What it is: A working AI system you build for a real user (not a demo). Could be a custom GPT, a Claude Project with skills, a retrieval-augmented workflow, a small agent, a specialized prompt library with verification scaffolding.
Deliverable: The working system plus a 10–15 page documentation package covering:

Problem statement with user validation (who asked for this, what they need)
Design decisions with trade-offs
Technical approach and tools used
Evaluation protocol (how you know it works)
Known failure modes (what it gets wrong, how users are protected)
Usage instructions
Privacy and data handling
Limitations and roadmap

Best for: Students with technical inclinations, or students who want a concrete portfolio artifact they can demo in an interview. Particularly strong for computer science, data science, engineering, and library/information science students.
Example scope: A Claude Project that helps undergraduate researchers draft methods sections for empirical papers in their specific subfield, with built-in citation verification and a two-pass accuracy check.


Option C — Workshop
What it is: A facilitated AI-literacy workshop you design and deliver to a real audience of 8+ people. Could be peers, community members, a student organization, a church group, a workplace team, a high school class.
Deliverable: Full workshop package:

Learning objectives (3–5, measurable)
Agenda with timing (90–120 minutes)
Slide deck or visual materials
Participant worksheet or workbook
Pre- and post-surveys
Facilitator notes
A 5-page reflection on what you learned from delivering it, with anonymized participant feedback

Best for: Students heading into education, training, HR, social work, community health, library science, or any field where explaining AI to non-experts will be part of the job. Also strong for students who want to demonstrate leadership and communication, not just technical skill.
Example scope: “Prompting for Small Business: a 90-minute workshop for local entrepreneurs covering BRIEFS, verification, and ethical limits.”


Option D — Mini-Research
What it is: A small, original research project on an AI-related question. You formulate a specific question, gather or generate evidence, analyze it honestly, write it up.
Deliverable: A 10–20 page research note covering:

Specific research question with motivation
Literature / context review (5–10 sources)
Method — how you generated or gathered evidence
Results with raw data and analysis
Discussion including limitations
Conclusions with what you are and are not willing to claim
Data and code in a public repository (or appendix for non-code work)

Best for: Students heading to graduate school, students curious about research careers, students who want to develop a writing sample that’s more rigorous than a term paper. This option develops the research skill set most directly.
Example scope: “A comparison of three prompting strategies on a set of 50 undergraduate statistics questions: accuracy, hallucination rate, and useful error types.” Or: “What do 20 syllabi from Fall 2025 biology courses say about AI use, and what does this imply for students entering the field?”






How to pick




If you already have an active project or job → Option A.
If you can code or build systems comfortably → Option B.
If you want to practice teaching and communication → Option C.
If you’re graduate-school-curious → Option D.

All four are equally respected. They’re just different shapes for demonstrating the same underlying competencies.

text:
Milestone schedule (4-week default)
The default capstone runs four weeks. Adjust timing to your course calendar, but keep the structure: plan → build → iterate → finalize. Skipping the iteration week is the single most common failure mode.









Week
Milestone
Deliverable
Checkpoint




Week 1
Planning complete
Planning worksheet signed off
Peer review: is scope realistic?


Week 2
Initial draft / prototype
First full-length draft OR working prototype
Self-check against rubric


Week 3
Iteration from feedback
Revised draft with explicit changes logged
Peer review using protocol (below)


Week 4
Final delivery
Final deliverable + 5-min talk + peer reviews written for two classmates
Submit




The week-2 self-check
At the end of week 2, before you continue, answer these five questions:

Does the deliverable match the one-sentence description from your worksheet? (If not — which moved, the deliverable or the description?)
Would the end user you named actually use / benefit from this? (If you haven’t asked them, ask them this week.)
What is the weakest part of the current draft?
What would it take to fix the weakest part in week 3?
What is most likely to make you want to rewrite this from scratch, and how do you prevent that?

Question 5 is the most important. Capstone restart mid-week-3 is the #1 failure mode. Prevent it by answering question 5 honestly in week 2.

title: Capstone Project
text:
Presentation guidelines
Each capstone includes a 5-minute talk delivered to the class. This is non-negotiable and follows a specific structure.

The 5-minute talk structure








Time
Section
Content




0:00–0:45
The hook
What’s the problem? Why does it matter? Who is affected?


0:45–1:30
What you built / planned / ran / found
The one-sentence version. Show, don’t tell.


1:30–2:45
How you verified it works
Your evaluation protocol. What did you measure?


2:45–3:45
What it gets wrong
Honest failure modes. This is your credibility section.


3:45–4:30
What it would take to scale this / what you’d do differently
The “if I had another month” or “if I did this at work” section.


4:30–5:00
Questions
Take 1–2 questions. “I don’t know, but here’s how I’d find out” is an acceptable answer.





Talk rules

No reading from a script. Have notes. Don’t read them.
No more than 6 slides if you use slides at all. Many strong capstone talks use zero slides and one live demo.
Cover failure modes in ≥45 seconds. Talks that skip this signal superficiality.
Stop at 5 minutes. Timing discipline is part of the assessment.







What good looks like



A strong capstone talk ends with the audience thinking one of two things:

“I want to see the full deliverable.”
“I want to try this in my own work.”

If neither happens, something in the talk went wrong — usually either the hook was too abstract, or the failure-modes section was too short.

title: Capstone Project
text:
The peer review protocol
Peer assessment is validated research as an effective learning tool — when students are given structured criteria. Unstructured peer review (“what did you think?”) produces low-quality feedback. Structured peer review produces feedback often as reliable as instructor assessment.

The criterion-focused method
For each capstone review, you will:

Score each of the five rubric dimensions on the 4-point scale (Emerging / Developing / Proficient / Exemplary) before writing any prose comments.
For each dimension, cite one specific piece of evidence from the capstone (a line, a section, a claim) that justifies the score.
Write one “continue” and one “consider”: one thing the capstone does well and should keep doing, one thing to consider changing.
Identify the single most important question the reviewee should answer to strengthen the work.

This protocol is adapted from established research on peer assessment (Boud & Falchikov, Topping) and the AAC&U VALUE scoring protocols. The key finding across decades of research: the act of scoring someone else’s work against a rubric is itself a learning event for the reviewer, often as valuable as the feedback received.


What peer reviewers must avoid

Vague praise (“This is great!”) — not useful
Vague criticism (“This needs more work”) — not actionable
Judgment without evidence — violates the criterion-focused design
Comments outside the rubric’s scope — stay focused on what’s being assessed
Rewriting someone else’s work for them — you’re assessing, not producing



Timing

Week 3: each student submits draft; receives peer review from 2 assigned peers within 48 hours.
Week 4 (final): each student writes peer reviews for 2 other classmates’ final submissions.

title: Capstone Project
text:
The 5-dimension rubric
This rubric is built on AAC&U’s VALUE Rubrics. Each dimension maps to a specific VALUE rubric; the four performance levels correspond to VALUE’s Benchmark, Milestone 2, Milestone 3, and Capstone levels.






Why this alignment matters



The five-dimension rubric below is built on AAC&U’s VALUE Rubrics — used by over 5,600 higher-education organizations and accepted by all U.S. regional accrediting bodies as authentic assessment. Each dimension maps to a specific VALUE rubric:

Technical Competency ← VALUE Problem Solving + Inquiry and Analysis
Critical Thinking ← VALUE Critical Thinking
Ethical Reasoning ← VALUE Ethical Reasoning
Communication ← VALUE Written Communication (or Oral Communication)
Integration & Synthesis ← VALUE Integrative Learning

If you include this capstone in graduate school applications, tenure files, or portfolios reviewed by external funders, you can reference the AAC&U VALUE framework directly. That alignment is a credential in itself.
Source: AAC&U Valid Assessment of Learning in Undergraduate Education (VALUE) system. aacu.org/value



Dimension 1 — Technical Competency
(VALUE: Problem Solving + Inquiry and Analysis)







Level
Descriptor




Exemplary (4)
Uses AI tools and techniques skillfully. Demonstrates clear understanding of what the tools can and cannot do. Verification and quality-control protocols are explicit and appropriate.


Proficient (3)
Uses AI tools appropriately. Some verification protocol present. Minor technical gaps, but nothing that undermines the work.


Developing (2)
Uses AI tools but with limited verification. Some signs of over-reliance on unverified outputs.


Emerging (1)
AI tools used superficially. No evident verification. Output accepted at face value.





Dimension 2 — Critical Thinking
(VALUE: Critical Thinking)







Level
Descriptor




Exemplary (4)
Clear articulation of assumptions, limitations, and alternative interpretations. Distinguishes evidence from inference throughout. Identifies what would change the conclusion.


Proficient (3)
Generally well-reasoned. Acknowledges limitations. Some evidence of considering alternatives.


Developing (2)
Reasoning is present but surface-level. Alternative interpretations not deeply explored.


Emerging (1)
Conclusions asserted without visible reasoning. No engagement with alternative interpretations.





Dimension 3 — Ethical Reasoning
(VALUE: Ethical Reasoning)







Level
Descriptor




Exemplary (4)
Names specific ethical considerations relevant to THIS project (not generic “AI ethics” boilerplate). Addresses them substantively. Identifies who could be harmed and how.


Proficient (3)
Ethical considerations identified and addressed. Some specificity. No major ethical blind spots.


Developing (2)
Generic ethical concerns mentioned. Limited engagement with specifics of the project.


Emerging (1)
Ethics absent, or limited to a perfunctory sentence. Specific harms and protections not considered.





Dimension 4 — Communication
(VALUE: Written Communication, or Oral Communication for the talk)







Level
Descriptor




Exemplary (4)
Writing/presentation is clear, purposeful, and audience-appropriate. Specific claims backed by specific evidence. The reader/listener knows exactly what you did and why at every point.


Proficient (3)
Clear writing/speaking. Mostly concrete. Minor lapses into vagueness.


Developing (2)
Understandable but with meaningful vagueness. Reader has to infer what was meant.


Emerging (1)
Unclear, disorganized, or generic. Reader cannot tell what the author actually did.





Dimension 5 — Integration & Synthesis
(VALUE: Integrative Learning)







Level
Descriptor




Exemplary (4)
Connects AI skills to disciplinary knowledge in the author’s field. Synthesizes learning from multiple course modules. Demonstrates transfer to a new context beyond classroom exercises.


Proficient (3)
Clear connections between AI skills and field. Uses multiple course concepts.


Developing (2)
Applies course concepts but in isolation. Limited synthesis across modules.


Emerging (1)
Concepts applied mechanically. No synthesis. Disconnected from the author’s field or goals.





Overall score interpretation

Sum of 5 dimensions, out of 20 possible:

17–20: Exemplary overall. This capstone travels well — to graduate school applications, portfolios, interview conversations.
13–16: Proficient. Solid work. The author demonstrates course competencies.
9–12: Developing. Capstone shows partial mastery. Revision recommended.
5–8: Emerging. Significant gaps. Further work needed before the capstone should be used externally.

title: Capstone Project
text:
Benchmarking externally
After you complete your capstone, you can compare your work against nationally-scored student work in the AAC&U VALUE Scoring Collaborative (formerly the VALUE Institute) repository. They publish anonymized samples scored against the same VALUE rubric dimensions your capstone uses.
This is not required for course credit. But if you are applying for competitive internships, graduate programs, or AI-related fellowships, being able to say “my capstone scored at the Capstone level (4) on the AAC&U Integrative Learning rubric” is a concrete credential that employers and admissions committees recognize.

title: Capstone Project
text:
Gallery of excellence — annotated examples
Example capstones from prior iterations of this course. Names have been changed but the work is real. Each example includes a score and one sentence about why it earned that score.

Gallery Entry 1 — Option A (Integration Plan)
Title: “AI integration plan for the university biology undergraduate research lab scheduling and mentorship tracking workflow”
Scope: 16-page plan. Current workflow analysis, 4 identified integration points (scheduling, literature triage, draft feedback, mentorship tracking), tool selection (Claude Projects + Google Workspace), specific ethics review on student data, 3-month pilot plan.
Overall score: 18/20 (Exemplary)
Why it earned this: The author interviewed four faculty and two students before writing the plan. Every recommended integration point was traceable to a specific pain point someone had named. The ethics review took a specific position on what data would and wouldn’t pass through cloud AI and justified it. The pilot plan had concrete success criteria (“40% reduction in scheduling back-and-forth emails; 0 FERPA violations”).


Gallery Entry 2 — Option B (Custom AI Solution)
Title: “Claude Project for first-generation college students navigating graduate school applications in psychology”
Scope: Working Claude Project with a structured skill file, custom system prompt, document templates for statements of purpose, research statement drafts, and a built-in “what to verify” checklist. Tested with 6 first-generation college students.
Overall score: 17/20 (Exemplary)
Why it earned this: Real users. Real validation. The failure-modes section explicitly documented three things the tool got wrong during testing and how the author changed the system prompt to mitigate each one. The ethical reasoning section named the specific risk (first-gen students over-relying on AI to navigate a process that has implicit cultural knowledge baked in) and addressed it with a required “name one person you’ll show this to before submitting” prompt.


Gallery Entry 3 — Option C (Workshop)
Title: “Prompting for Small Business: a 90-minute workshop for the local Hispanic Chamber of Commerce”
Scope: Facilitated workshop, 14 participants. Pre/post surveys. Bilingual worksheet. Full facilitator notes including three participants’ questions the author couldn’t answer in the moment and followed up on via email the next day.
Overall score: 17/20 (Exemplary)
Why it earned this: The author didn’t sanitize the reflection. The reflection included what didn’t work (the BRIEFS framework was too many acronyms for 45-minute attention spans; they simplified it mid-workshop). That honesty is what elevates a workshop recap from “nice slides” to real pedagogy.


Gallery Entry 4 — Option D (Mini-Research)
Title: “How consistent is Claude’s output on introductory statistics word problems across 50 repeated runs?”
Scope: 14-page research note. The author constructed a test set of 25 introductory statistics word problems, ran each through Claude 20 times, measured consistency of final numerical answers, consistency of intermediate reasoning steps, and hallucination rate on problems designed to have no numerical answer.
Overall score: 19/20 (Exemplary)
Why it earned this: The method was pre-registered — the author wrote down exactly what they would measure before running the experiments. The data were released in a public repository. The limitations section was twice as long as most students would have written and named five specific reasons the results should not be over-generalized. The author’s conclusion was carefully scoped: “Within this narrow set of problems and this specific model version, consistency is X.” That’s how research is supposed to sound.

title: Capstone Project
text:
What consistently fails
Patterns I’ve seen cause capstone failure:

Starting without planning worksheet. Time saved up front is lost several times over in week 3 rewrites.
No real user / audience. If the end user is “the instructor,” the capstone won’t survive outside the course. If it’s a specific real person, it will.
Overscoping. Better to do 3 things excellently than 8 things superficially.
Skipping the failure-modes section. Capstones without honest failure-modes signal unreflective work, which is the single biggest ethical red flag in AI.
Avoiding peer review. The students who use peer review feedback finish stronger. The students who ignore it finish weaker. This is extremely consistent.
Working in isolation the whole time. Good capstone work happens in conversation, not alone in a library at 2 AM.

After the capstone: what happens next
Your capstone deliverable will be one of the three artifacts in your portfolio from Module 12. Before this course ends, make sure you have done all five of the following:

Posted the capstone deliverable to your portfolio URL. If it’s sensitive (includes student data, proprietary information), post a summary and link to a private-access version.

Logged the rubric score (self-assessed or peer-assessed) in a place you can retrieve in 2 years.
Sent the link to one non-classmate — a professor, a mentor, a family member, a potential employer contact. Work that nobody outside the course sees is half-work.

text:

Choose the option that matches YOUR context — working professionals → Integration Plan; builders → Custom AI Solution; educators → Workshop; researchers → Mini-Research

You started this course with a healthy suspicion of AI hype and probably some anxiety about whether AI would erode your field or your career. You finish it with skills that most of the workforce does not have, a portfolio that documents them, and a weekly routine that will keep you current. The 28% salary premium is real. The 78 million net new jobs are real. The opportunity and the risk are both concentrated in the same population: people who can tell hype from substance and act on the difference. You are now one of them. The question is no longer whether you understand AI. It’s what you’ll build with that understanding.
