And in Fall 2025, the controlled experiment in MATH 3200 (Module 8) showed the AI section (mean 72.20) outperforming the traditional section (mean 68.20) on Exam 1, with comparable standard deviations (~21 in both groups).
These aren’t hypothetical projections. They are measured outcomes, replicated twice — once at Harvard with a major external team, once at a mid-size public university in a local context. AI is transforming disciplines right now.






Common Misconceptions About AI in Your Field




“AI will replace professionals in my field.” AI replaces tasks, not jobs. The nurse, teacher, farmer, and lawyer who use AI effectively become more valuable, not obsolete.
“AI works the same in every field.” Privacy constraints (HIPAA, FERPA, attorney-client privilege), accuracy requirements, and ethical stakes vary enormously. A chatbot for a bakery’s FAQ has different requirements than one for a hospital’s triage.
“My field is too specialized for AI.” RAG (Module 9) grounds any AI in your domain’s documents. Custom GPTs (Module 8) build domain-specific assistants. General AI + your knowledge = specialized AI.
“The AI applications in my field are too new to trust.” Some are mature — medical imaging AI has dozens of FDA clearances dating back years. Some are experimental. The SMARTS framework and verification habit (Module 1) help you tell them apart.
“I should wait until AI is more mature.” By the time AI is “mature” in your field, your colleagues who started in 2024 will have three years of practical experience. Start with low-stakes applications and build.

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
AI in Education
The landscape. AI is reshaping every layer of education — K-12 through graduate school, from tutoring to administration.
Current applications.

Personalized tutoring — custom GPTs that adapt to each student’s level and pace (Kestin’s PS2 Pal at Harvard; the ELEVATE GPTs)
Automated feedback — instant feedback on writing drafts, code submissions, and problem sets
Course design — AI-assisted syllabi, learning objectives, rubrics, and assessment banks
Administrative efficiency — syllabus FAQ bots, scheduling assistants, enrollment support
Accessibility — real-time captioning, text-to-speech, content translation, reading-level adaptation
Student support — early-warning systems that flag at-risk students based on engagement patterns (with the ethical caveats from Module 10)

Case Study: The ELEVATE Custom GPT Ecosystem. Dr. Yatawara built and deployed 10+ custom GPTs across multiple courses:








GPT
Course
Purpose




Chapter 1–4 Tutors
MATH 3200
Topic-specific guided learning, each loaded only with that chapter


Exam Review Bot
MATH 4200
Generates practice problems and walks through solutions step by step


R Tutor
MATH 2200
Coding help using only course-approved R packages


Syllabus GPT
MATH 3200
Answers policy questions, eliminates repetitive emails


DOE Assistant
MATH 2200
Guides students through experimental design



Key insight. The GPTs succeeded because they were constrained — each was loaded with only the relevant course content and instructed to guide, not hand out answers (the 7-step tutoring algorithm from Module 8). This is exactly the same constraint that made Kestin’s PS2 Pal work and the same one Bastani et al. identified as the difference between AI that protects learning and AI that actively undermines it. The MATH 3200 controlled experiment (Module 8) showed the AI section outperforming traditional (mean 72.20 vs. 68.20) on Exam 1 — consistent with the Kestin and protected-Bastani pattern.
Ethical considerations. Academic integrity policies, equitable access to AI tools, student data privacy (FERPA), and the risk of over-reliance on AI feedback. Detector-based integrity enforcement is especially fraught — see Module 10’s discussion of the 61.3% TOEFL false-positive rate. And now, Bastani et al.’s finding that unguarded AI access during practice can actively harm learning is the strongest empirical case yet for transparency requirements over AI use in coursework. An instructor isn’t just enforcing honesty — they’re protecting students from process substitution.






Guided Practice 11.1 (Education)



If you’re an educator: choose one assignment from a course you teach. Design a custom GPT for that specific assignment using Module 8’s principles. Write: (a) the system instructions, (b) what files you’d upload, (c) what the GPT should never do.
If you’re not: think of a course you’ve taken. What would have helped most — a tutoring GPT, an exam-review GPT, or a study-skills GPT? Write the system instructions for one.


Key design principles to remember


Constrain the knowledge base to only the relevant materials
Instruct it to guide, not answer (hint → nudge → reveal escalation)
Require students to show their own reasoning before getting help
Disable web search to keep answers grounded in course content
Be brief: a few sentences per turn, not a wall of text
Include a “wrap-up and summarize” instruction so each session ends with learning reinforcement

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
AI in Business and Entrepreneurship
The landscape. From Fortune 500 to solo entrepreneurs, AI is reshaping how business runs.
Current applications.

Customer analytics — segmentation, churn prediction, lifetime value, personalized marketing
Content generation — marketing copy, social posts, product descriptions, email campaigns at scale
Financial analysis — forecasting, anomaly detection, automated reporting, risk assessment
Supply chain — demand prediction, route optimization, inventory management, supplier risk
Operations — meeting summarization, project tracking, workflow automation, document processing
Brand development — positioning, visual identity, market research, competitive analysis

Case Study: The Roadrunner Lemonade Brand Sprint. University business students used the Brand Sprint prompt (Module 6) to take a raw idea — a campus lemonade stand — and produce in 30 minutes a positioning statement, three tagline variants, a 3-color palette with hex codes, a font pairing, and three logo concept prompts ready for image generation.
What this demonstrates. A solo entrepreneur in Kern County can produce MVP brand assets that previously required a design agency. AI doesn’t replace the agency for complex brand work — for a national campaign, you still want professionals — but for an MVP, a pitch deck, a first logo, the playing field has genuinely shifted.
Kern County relevance. Agriculture-tech, energy, healthcare administration, logistics, and small businesses across the Central Valley can all leverage AI for operations that were previously too expensive to outsource.
Ethical considerations. AI marketing content must be truthful (FTC enforcement is active). Customer data for AI analytics requires consent. AI hiring tools carry the Amazon bias risk from Module 2. And: when you generate marketing content with AI, consider the human-authorship requirement if you want copyright protection (Module 10 — Thaler and the Copyright Office’s 2025 Part 2 report).






Guided Practice 11.2 (Business)



Pick a real or hypothetical small business in your community. Using BRIEFS, write a prompt that asks AI to generate: (a) 3 marketing campaign ideas for the next quarter, (b) a competitive analysis of the top 3 competitors, and (c) 5 social-media post drafts. Run it. Evaluate: what’s usable immediately, what needs refinement, and what’s factually wrong?

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
AI in Healthcare
The landscape. Healthcare AI is both the most promising and the most sensitive domain.
Current applications.

Medical imaging — AI detecting tumors, fractures, and retinal disease. This is the most regulated, best-validated, and longest-running category of AI in medicine. As of the FDA’s December 2025 update, the agency has authorized over 1,300 AI/ML-enabled medical devices, up from ~500 at the start of 2023. 258 were cleared in 2025 alone — more than any year in FDA history. Roughly 80% are radiology, with cardiology (~98 devices) and neurology growing. The first autonomous AI device was IDx-DR (cleared April 2018), which screens for diabetic retinopathy directly from a retinal image in primary-care offices — correctly identifying retinopathy ~90% of the time in its pivotal ~900-patient trial. “Mature” in healthcare AI has a real meaning: it’s FDA-cleared, published, and in daily clinical use.
Ambient clinical documentation — Abridge, Nuance DAX Copilot, Suki, Freed, Ambience, DeepScribe, and athenaAmbient (bundled free with athenahealth as of early 2026). The JAMA multi-site study found ~13.4 fewer EHR minutes and ~16.0 fewer documentation minutes per day, plus ~0.49 more visits per week.
Clinical decision support — evidence-based treatment recommendations at the point of care, typically through RAG over clinical guidelines
Drug discovery — predicting molecular interactions; reducing some discovery pipelines from decades to years
Patient communication — chatbots for scheduling, symptom triage, medication reminders
Population health — predicting disease outbreaks, identifying at-risk populations

The FDA pipeline problem. Of the 1,300+ cleared devices, 97% came through the 510(k) pathway — meaning they were cleared as “substantially equivalent” to a prior device rather than required to demonstrate independent clinical evidence. Recent audits have found that only ~29% of cleared radiology AI devices reported any clinical testing, only 8% included a human-in-the-loop evaluation, and fewer than 4% disclosed the race or ethnicity of their validation cohort. The sheer volume of FDA clearances can look like rigorous validation when it is, in many cases, pattern-matching to earlier devices. Module 10’s Obermeyer lesson applies here: ask what was measured, on whom, before deploying.
The privacy imperative. Healthcare AI operates under HIPAA (U.S.) or PIPEDA (Canada), which strictly govern patient data. This makes Module 9’s infrastructure question existential: cloud AI tools processing PHI need a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) and the right contractual protections — or the data stays on premises (the SLM-RAG approach).
The ambient scribe second-order problem. Recent research has flagged that ambient scribes don’t just document — they document more completely, which increases billing. A 2024 Texas Oncology study saw documented diagnoses per encounter rise from 3.0 to 4.1. Riverside Health reported an 11% rise in physician wRVUs and a 14% increase in documented HCC diagnoses. Some of that is legitimate (under-documentation is real), but the shift from “burnout reduction” to “revenue engine” in ambient-scribe vendor marketing is real too. Know which story you’re buying.
Ethical considerations. Diagnostic AI that performs worse on certain demographics (the dermatology analog of Gender Shades is well-documented). Liability when AI assists a wrong diagnosis — regulators are still working this out. Patient consent for AI involvement in their care. CMS payment coverage lags FDA clearance dramatically: as of late 2025, only ~10 of 1,300+ cleared AI devices had CMS reimbursement codes, which means most deployments get paid for out of hospital margins or not at all.






Guided Practice 11.3 (Healthcare)



You’re a clinic manager evaluating AI tools. Use the 5-Question Test from Module 6 on a hypothetical “AI Patient Triage Chatbot” for your waiting room: Does it solve a real problem? Is it better than current triage? Where does patient data go? What does it cost? Will the vendor still exist in 18 months? What HIPAA and BAA requirements apply? What happens when it’s wrong?








✅ Test Yourself: Cross-Discipline Patterns



By now you’ve seen AI in education, business, and healthcare. Notice:

What’s the same across all three? (AI handles routine/data-heavy work; humans provide judgment; privacy and verification matter; constrained tools outperform unconstrained ones.)
What’s different? (Privacy constraints — FERPA vs. HIPAA vs. consumer data. Accuracy stakes — a wrong exam grade vs. a wrong diagnosis. Deployment context — classroom vs. clinic vs. storefront.)
Which frameworks apply to all three? (BRIEFS for prompting; SMARTS for reasoning; verification for accuracy; the 5-Question Test for tool evaluation.)

This pattern holds for every discipline that follows.

title: AI Across Disciplines
section: AI in Agriculture and Environmental Science
text:
AI in Agriculture and Environmental Science
The landscape. Kern County sits in one of the most productive agricultural regions on Earth. AI is already here, with specific tools and measured outcomes.
Current applications — with named tools.

Precision herbicide application — John Deere’s See & Spray (developed by Blue River Technology, acquired 2017). Boom-mounted cameras use computer vision to identify individual weeds and spray only them through an ExactApply nozzle system. Real 2025 numbers, not vendor projections: 5 million acres covered, 31 million gallons of herbicide mix saved, ~2 bushels/acre yield bump (up to 4.8 bushels in best cases), ~77% reduction in herbicide use vs. broadcast spraying (up to 90% reduction in cotton). Available as factory-install or retrofit kit. This is the most-deployed AI agriculture tool in the world right now.
Integrated farm-data platforms — Climate FieldView (Bayer) and John Deere Operations Center. FieldView aggregates weather, soil, and yield data across ~60 million hectares in 23 countries. Operations Center connects equipment telemetry, agronomy prescriptions, and fleet management. The two integrate bidirectionally after a 2018 agreement.
Autonomous equipment — John Deere 8R autonomous tractor (launched 2022), uses 6 stereo camera pairs and onboard neural nets for planting, tilling, and harvest. Addresses agricultural labor shortages where feasible.
Pest and disease detection — Plantix. Smartphone app used primarily in low-resource settings. Farmer photographs a damaged leaf; AI returns differential diagnoses and treatment guidance in 18+ languages. Has over 20 million downloads, largest adoption in India, Southeast Asia, and Africa.
Irrigation optimization — CropX and Arable. Soil-moisture sensors plus AI analysis automatically schedule irrigation. CropX reports 25–50% reductions in water use on participating farms.
Satellite + yield prediction — Planet Labs (daily-cadence satellite imagery), IBM Watson Decision Platform for Agriculture, Microsoft Azure FarmBeats, Descartes Labs. Field-level crop health and yield forecasts from space imagery feed commodity markets and insurance pricing.
Environmental monitoring — PM2.5 tracking, pollution-source identification, compliance reporting. Dr. Yatawara’s own published research on PM2.5 income-disparity gradients across 48 states uses exactly this type of data pipeline.

Kern County context. The Central Valley produces ~25% of America’s food on ~1% of its farmland. It also has significant air-quality challenges due to agriculture, oil production, and geography. AI applications in both agriculture and environmental monitoring are directly relevant to this community.
Ethical considerations — the data-ownership question is the central one. Who owns the data a farm sensor collects? In most current contracts, the platform vendor effectively does. Farmers receive “better recommendations” in exchange for handing over data that flows into vendor models, commodity analytics, and — critically — recommendations that may favor the vendor’s own seed and chemical products. A Climate FieldView recommendation that nudges toward Bayer seeds is not neutral. Farm data coalitions (AgGateway, OATS Center at Purdue) have argued for farmer-retained data rights, but the default terms of service still run the other way.
The equity question. Precision agriculture tools that only pay for themselves at scale widen the gap between corporate and family farms. A See & Spray retrofit kit is a capital investment that a 500-acre family farm can’t easily amortize. Small farmers without the technology aren’t just forgone productivity — they’re out-competed by farms whose inputs cost 30% less. Technology that only works for large operators deepens the equity gap. Validate across farm sizes and practices before claiming broad applicability.

title: AI Across Disciplines
section: AI in Government and Public Service
text:
AI in Government and Public Service
Current applications.

Administrative automation — permits, license renewals, benefit applications at scale
Citizen services — chatbots for hours, locations, procedures, eligibility. Federal examples: GSA’s USA.gov chatbot, IRS “Where’s My Refund” assistants, SSA claims-status bots
Policy analysis — modeling the impact of proposed policies before implementation
Emergency response — predictive routing, resource allocation, real-time communication during disasters
Fraud detection — pattern-finding in benefits, taxes, procurement. Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service uses AI to flag suspicious federal payments and recovered billions in improper payments in 2024–2025

The COMPAS lesson (Module 10). Government AI applications carry the highest stakes and the highest bias risks. COMPAS showed that AI used in criminal justice can systematically discriminate — and the consequences are people’s freedom. Government AI requires the most rigorous fairness testing, transparency, and human oversight of any domain. The EU AI Act’s August 2026 enforcement reflects this: most public-sector uses fall into the “high-risk” category with binding obligations.
The U.S. federal–state policy tension. As covered in Module 10, U.S. AI policy is currently in motion. The federal Executive Order 14179 (Jan 2025) pushed deregulation. The July 2025 AI Action Plan continued that direction. A December 11, 2025 executive order explicitly targets state-level AI regulations for federal preemption — aimed at Colorado’s AI Act (effective February 2026, the first U.S. state with binding AI disclosure and risk-management rules for “high-risk” automated decisions), California’s SB 1047 successor bills, and similar laws in New York and Illinois.
The live tension this creates for government AI: a state agency deploying an AI system in 2026 may face simultaneous (a) state-law obligations (algorithmic impact assessments, notice to affected individuals, opt-out rights), (b) NIST AI RMF expectations from federal contracts, (c) EU AI Act compliance if data flows to EU-based vendors, and (d) federal executive-branch pressure against state rules. There is no clean hierarchy. The practical rule remains: write to the strictest applicable regime, document everything, and build for human override from day one.
Practical rule. For any government deployment that affects rights, liberty, or benefits: mandatory subgroup bias audit, meaningful human override, and transparent documentation of the fairness definition chosen. If you can’t answer the Chouldechova question (“which fairness definition are we optimizing?”), you aren’t ready to deploy.

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
AI in Creative Industries
Current applications — with named tools.

Visual arts — Midjourney v7 (still the community favorite for style and aesthetic quality), DALL-E 3 (inside ChatGPT, best at following detailed instructions), Stable Diffusion 3.5 and Flux.1 (open-source, run locally, fine-tunable), Adobe Firefly (trained on Adobe Stock only — the “commercially safe” choice where training-data legal risk is being priced in).
Music — Suno v4 and Udio (text-to-song generation), Stability’s Stable Audio (open-source), Adobe Podcast (voice enhancement and editing). Full songs with vocals from a prompt, in 30 seconds.
Video — Sora 2 (OpenAI), Runway Gen-4, Veo 3 (Google), Kling (Kuaishou). Current generation produces coherent 30-second shots with consistent characters across cuts.
Writing — brainstorming, drafting, editing (but not replacing distinctive creative voice)
Film/video production — storyboarding, b-roll generation, post-production effects, voice dubbing, AI-powered rotoscoping (Runway)
Gaming — procedural content generation, NPC dialogue trees, world-building, AI-generated textures and animations

The labor story. Creative work is now also a labor-law story. SAG-AFTRA’s 11-month video game actors’ strike ended in July 2025 when the union ratified a new Interactive Media Agreement by 95.04% — securing consent, compensation, and transparency requirements for AI digital replicas of performers’ voices and likenesses, alongside a 15.17% pay increase. The 2023 film/TV contracts and California’s AB 1836 and AB 2602 (September 2024) added state-level protections for performers and their estates. Expect similar language in writers’, illustrators’, and musicians’ contracts going forward.
The copyright overhang. Two unresolved legal questions hang over every commercial use of AI creative tools, from Module 10: (1) whether purely AI-generated output is copyrightable — under Thaler, no, and cert was denied March 2026. AI-assisted work with meaningful human control can be copyrighted. (2) Whether training on copyrighted material without permission is fair use — unresolved, with Bartz v. Anthropic settling at $1.5B and district courts disagreeing. Adobe Firefly’s “trained only on Adobe Stock and public domain” positioning is explicitly a hedge against this legal risk.
The replacement debate. AI won’t replace artists with distinctive creative vision and judgment. It will replace artists doing generic, template-based, commodity work — stock illustration, basic social-media imagery, junior-level logo work, formulaic production music. The bottleneck shifts from execution skill (can you draw?) to creative direction (do you know what’s worth making?). Whether that’s a net good or a net bad for the creative economy depends on who you are in it.
Ethical considerations. Copyright uncertainty, labor protections now bargained, attribution. If your creative work involves AI, say so. The audience increasingly cares.

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
AI in Law
Current applications — with named tools.

Legal research — Westlaw Precision with AI (Thomson Reuters), Lexis+ AI (LexisNexis), Harvey (BigLaw’s most-adopted vertical tool; used by Allen & Overy, PwC, Ashurst and dozens more), CoCounsel (formerly Casetext, now Thomson Reuters). All are RAG-grounded over vetted case-law and treatise databases, which is what makes them materially safer than raw ChatGPT. A properly grounded legal-research AI is dramatically faster than manual Westlaw searching.
Contract analysis — Kira Systems, LawGeex, LinkSquares — reviewing 200-page contracts in minutes, flagging unusual terms, extracting renewal dates and risk provisions, checking regulatory compliance
Document review / eDiscovery — Relativity aiR, Everlaw AI Assistant, DISCO AI. Processing tens of thousands of documents in discovery. This is where AI has had the largest measurable productivity impact in law — a review that used to take 20 associates four weeks now takes two associates one week.
Access to justice — AI-powered legal aid for people who can’t afford attorneys; self-help tools for forms, filings, and basic questions. DoNotPay (mixed record), JusticeText, state-level legal-help bots
Predictive analytics — forecasting case outcomes, estimating settlement values, analyzing judicial behavior
The wildcard — general-purpose chatbots used by lawyers. Still widespread, still dangerous, and the source of almost every hallucination sanction. Don’t.

The verification imperative. The cautionary tale is no longer just Mata v. Avianca (2023, $5,000 sanction, two lawyers and their firm sanctioned for six fabricated case citations). As of August 2025, researchers had documented more than 300 cases of AI-driven legal hallucinations in court filings — with at least 200 in 2025 alone. The sanctions have escalated:

Mata v. Avianca (SDNY 2023) — $5,000 sanction
Gauthier v. Goodyear Tire (E.D. Tex. 2024) — $2,000 sanction
Wadsworth v. Walmart (D. Wyo. 2025) — $3,000 sanction + pro hac vice admission revoked; eight of nine cited cases were hallucinations
Mid Central Operating Engineers v. HoosierVac (S.D. Ind. 2025) — $15,000 recommended sanction
Johnson v. Dunn (N.D. Ala. July 2025) — attorneys disqualified from the case, opinion sent to bar regulators in every state where the attorneys are licensed

The American Bar Association issued Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on ethical use of generative AI, covering competence, confidentiality, candor to tribunals, and client communication. Many federal courts now require attorneys to certify that AI-generated citations have been independently verified. The vetted tools (Westlaw, Lexis+, Harvey, CoCounsel) are dramatically safer because they retrieve from curated databases rather than generating citations from model memory — but even they can err, and the verification duty is on the attorney, not the vendor.
The opportunity. Lawyers who use AI well will replace lawyers who don’t. Firms are hiring for “legal technology” roles that didn’t exist three years ago. The trick is that the competency question has inverted — it’s no longer “can you use AI?” It’s “can you use AI and still catch it when it lies?” That’s the professional skill that pays.

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
Finding AI in YOUR Field






Guided Practice 11.4 — The Field Audit



No matter your discipline, answer these 5 questions:

What are the 3 most time-consuming tasks in your field? (AI automation candidates.)
What decisions require the most expertise? (AI augmentation candidates.)
What data does your field generate? (Determines which AI techniques apply — ML, NLP, computer vision, speech.)
What are the privacy/ethical constraints? (HIPAA? FERPA? Attorney-client privilege? Export controls? Environmental regulations?)
Who in your field is already using AI well? (Find them and read what they’ve written.)



How to find AI leaders in your field


Search your professional association’s website for “AI” or “artificial intelligence”
Look for AI-dedicated sessions at your field’s major annual conference
Search LinkedIn for “[your field] + AI” and read what practitioners post
Check whether your field has an AI-specific journal, working group, or special interest group
Perplexity search: “latest AI applications in [your field] 2026 peer-reviewed” — and verify the citations you find

title: AI Across Disciplines
text:
Module 11 Summary






Key Takeaways




AI is transforming every field — not someday, now. The Kestin Harvard RCT proved it for physics education; the Bastani PNAS RCT proved the negative case in high-school math; the JAMA study proved ambient scribes save clinicians 30+ minutes/day; See & Spray saved 31M gallons of herbicide mix across 5M acres in 2025; the ELEVATE data proved it locally for statistics. Similar evidence is accumulating everywhere.
Constraint is the whole game. Kestin and Bastani together are the clearest empirical result in AI education right now: the same model that helps learning when constrained can harm learning when unconstrained. The same principle explains why ambient scribes work, why Harvey (retrieval-grounded) outperforms raw ChatGPT for legal research, and why the ELEVATE GPTs work — narrow scope, authoritative reference material, refusal to hand out answers. This is the generalizable design principle across every discipline in this module.
The pattern across fields is stable. AI handles routine and data-intensive tasks. Humans provide judgment, context, ethics, and creativity. The best results come from human-AI collaboration — never AI alone.
Domain expertise makes AI useful. A nurse using AI is still a nurse. A teacher using AI is still a teacher. Your knowledge turns a generic AI tool into a domain-specific powerhouse.
Field-specific ethics and regulation vary enormously — HIPAA in healthcare (1,300+ FDA-cleared AI devices but only ~10 reimbursed by CMS), FERPA in education, bargained labor protections in creative industries, ABA Formal Opinion 512 in law, EU AI Act high-risk designations in government. Know your field’s specific constraints.
The frameworks from this course are universal. BRIEFS, SMARTS, verification, the 5-Question Test — they work in every discipline. Only the examples change.





💭 Think About It


The students in the ELEVATE survey said the most helpful feature of the AI tutor was “helps recall and apply prior concepts” (92% agreement). Not speed. Not convenience. The ability to connect what they were learning to what they already knew. Kestin’s physics students said something similar — the tutor was most valuable when introducing new material that required bridging what they already knew to something new. That’s what AI does at its best in any discipline: it doesn’t replace your knowledge, it activates it. It helps you see connections you might have missed, apply frameworks you learned last semester, bridge the gap between what you know and what you need to figure out. Your expertise is the fuel. AI is the engine. Neither works without the other.

🔬 Lab 11: The AI Integration Proposal

Lab 11: AI Integration Proposal for Your Field
Time: 60 minutes | Tools needed: AI chatbot + knowledge of your field
Write a 2-page proposal for integrating AI into one core process in your specific field/role:

Current workflow — How is this task done today? Time, pain points, bottlenecks.
Proposed AI workflow — Which tools/techniques? Write the actual prompts you’d use (BRIEFS-structured).
Tools and costs — Specific tool names, pricing (verify against April 2026 provider pages), technical requirements.
Risks — Bias? Privacy? Over-reliance? Legal/regulatory exposure? What could go wrong?
Expected benefits — Time saved, quality improved, access expanded. Use specific numbers — and distinguish measured benefits (like the JAMA study’s 13.4 minutes) from vendor claims.
Success metrics — How would you measure whether it worked? Would you publish the result, even if it failed?
Ethical considerations — Who benefits? Who might be harmed? What safeguards?

Submit. Your 2-page proposal.

Card 2b: The BRIEFS Production Ladder
How to become fluent in BRIEFS, not just aware of it. Follow the ladder in order — each rung reduces scaffolding by one step:








Rung
What You Do
Why This Rung




1
Diagnose — read 6 weak prompts, name the missing BRIEFS element
You can’t write what you can’t spot


2
Insert — add one BRIEFS element at a time to a bare prompt
Feel each element as a distinct move


3
Complete — fill 3 partial BRIEFS skeletons
First production with guardrails


4
Produce — write 3 full BRIEFS prompts from scratch
Full production, low stakes


5
Handshake — practice the restate-and-confirm exchange
The phase most users skip


6
Select technique — pick zero-shot / few-shot / CoT / role / structured
Technique ≠ BRIEFS — separate decision


7
SMARTS — write all 6 turns on one real complex task
Multi-turn fluency


8
Anti-pattern — diagnose 7 broken prompts, one-move repair
Pattern recognition for failure


9
Transfer — rewrite a prompt across 3 domains; red-team where BRIEFS fails
The true test of mastery


10
Peer critique — score a partner’s prompt with the rubric
The reviewer learns more than the reviewee



When to use: The first time you teach yourself or anyone else BRIEFS. Once a rung feels automatic, move up. Don’t skip rungs — cognitive load research (Renkl & Atkinson, 2003) is clear that novices who skip scaffolding end up worse than those who took the time.

title: Case Studies Index
section: Deep Dive #1: Mata v. Avianca — The Lawyer Who Trusted AI
text:
Deep Dive #1: Mata v. Avianca — The Lawyer Who Trusted AI
What happened: In 2023, New York attorney Steven Schwartz used ChatGPT to research case law for a federal lawsuit against Avianca Airlines. The AI generated six court decisions as supporting precedents. Schwartz cited them in his brief, filed it with the court, and only discovered a problem when opposing counsel couldn’t find any of the cases. They didn’t exist. ChatGPT had fabricated case names, docket numbers, judicial opinions, and legal reasoning — all completely fictional but entirely convincing.
What went wrong: Schwartz later told the court he had “never used ChatGPT before” and “did not know it could generate false content.” He had asked the AI whether the cases were real, and it confirmed they were. He never checked a legal database. He trusted the tool because the output looked authoritative — proper formatting, realistic case numbers, plausible legal reasoning.
The consequences: Judge Kevin Castel sanctioned Schwartz and his colleague, calling the citations “fake judicial decisions with fake quotes and fake internal citations.” Both attorneys were fined $5,000 each. The case became international news and triggered a wave of AI use policies across law firms and courts worldwide.
Why it matters for you: This isn’t a story about bad lawyers or dangerous technology. It’s about the alignment gap between what AI produces (confident, well-formatted text) and what it guarantees (nothing). ChatGPT doesn’t search legal databases. It predicts what legal text should look like based on its training data. Sometimes those predictions correspond to real cases. Sometimes they don’t. The model itself cannot tell the difference — and neither can you, unless you verify.
Discussion questions: 1. Should Schwartz have been sanctioned? He didn’t intend to deceive — he genuinely believed the cases were real. 2. What verification steps would have caught this in under 10 minutes? 3. Your profession has its own version of “fake citations” — what does it look like in your field, and how would you catch it?

title: Case Studies Index
section: Deep Dive #2: COMPAS and the Impossibility of Fair Algorithms
text:
Deep Dive #2: COMPAS and the Impossibility of Fair Algorithms
What happened: COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) is a risk assessment algorithm used in U.S. courts to predict whether a defendant is likely to reoffend. Judges use the scores when making bail, sentencing, and parole decisions. In 2016, ProPublica analyzed COMPAS predictions against actual outcomes for over 7,000 defendants in Broward County, Florida.
What they found: The algorithm’s error rates were starkly different by race. Black defendants who did NOT go on to reoffend were incorrectly flagged as high risk at nearly twice the rate of white defendants (45% vs 23%). Conversely, white defendants who DID reoffend were incorrectly flagged as low risk more often than Black defendants (48% vs 28%). The algorithm was equally accurate overall for both groups — but its mistakes fell in opposite directions.
The mathematical impossibility: Northpointe (COMPAS’s creator) responded that their tool satisfied a different definition of fairness: among people who received the same risk score, the actual reoffense rate was the same regardless of race. Both ProPublica and Northpointe were correct — about different things. Mathematician Alexandra Chouldechova formally proved in 2017 that when base rates differ between groups (as they do in the criminal justice system due to systemic factors), you cannot simultaneously satisfy equal false positive rates, equal false negative rates, and equal predictive accuracy across groups. At least one must be sacrificed.
Why it matters for you: Every AI system that makes predictions about people faces this dilemma. A hospital’s patient risk model. A bank’s loan approval algorithm. A school’s early warning system. There is no single definition of “fairness” that satisfies everyone. The choice of which fairness metric to prioritize is a values decision — and it should be made transparently, by humans, with input from affected communities. Not buried in a technical specification that nobody reads.
Discussion questions: 1. If you had to choose between equal false positive rates and equal predictive accuracy, which would you prioritize? Why? Does your answer change depending on the context (criminal justice vs healthcare vs education)? 2. The algorithm doesn’t use race as an input. But it uses zip code, employment history, and prior arrests — all correlated with race due to systemic factors. Is this “using race” or not? 3. Who should decide which definition of fairness an algorithm uses? The developers? The judges? The affected communities? Legislators?

title: Case Studies Index
section: Deep Dive #3: The SLM-RAG Experiment — Small AI, Big Impact
text:
Deep Dive #3: The SLM-RAG Experiment — Small AI, Big Impact
What happened: In 2025, a research team asked a simple question: could a small, cheap AI model running on a single campus GPU match the performance of GPT-4 for domain-specific educational tasks? They set up a 7-billion parameter open-source model (Mistral 7B) on university hardware, connected it to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline loaded with undergraduate statistics textbook content, and compared its responses to GPT-4’s on 100 student questions.
The results: The small model matched GPT-4 on accuracy (no statistically significant difference, p = 0.41). It cost 92% less per query ($0.002 vs $0.025). Response latency dropped 45%. And critically: all student data stayed on campus hardware — no data left the institution.
Why it worked: RAG closes the knowledge gap. A small model “knows” less than GPT-4, but when you give it the right documents at query time, it doesn’t need to know everything — it just needs to read the relevant passage and answer from it. For domain-specific tasks (answering statistics questions from a specific textbook), this is sufficient. The model doesn’t need to know about Shakespeare or cooking recipes — it needs to know Chapter 7.
The equity argument: If the only path to quality AI is a $20/month subscription per user, AI’s benefits flow disproportionately to institutions and individuals who can afford it. But if a $2,000 GPU can serve an entire department, the economics change fundamentally. Community colleges, rural clinics, small nonprofits, and developing-world institutions gain access to AI that performs comparably to expensive cloud services — on their terms, with their data, under their control.
Discussion questions: 1. Under what conditions does “small model + relevant context” outperform “big model + general knowledge”? When does it fail? 2. If your institution could run its own AI for $2,000 in hardware plus electricity, what would you use it for first? 3. The experiment showed no statistical difference in accuracy. But are there other dimensions (creativity, nuance, handling edge cases) where the small model might fall short?

title: Case Studies Index
text:
Module Discussion Questions
Case 1 (Mata v. Avianca): Should lawyers face sanctions for unverified AI citations? What standard is reasonable?
Case 2 (Amazon’s Hiring): If training data reflects real hiring patterns, is the algorithm biased or accurately reflecting a biased world?
Case 3 (Strawberry Problem): If LLMs write poetry but can’t count letters, what’s the difference between “intelligence” and “pattern prediction”?
Case 4 (Whisperers): Why is cross-provider convergence (26/26) more convincing than one company’s recommendation?
Case 5 (Fake Citations): The student didn’t intend to deceive. Should the penalty differ from intentional fabrication?
Case 6 (Two Tuesdays): What’s the BEST use of reclaimed time? What’s the worst?
Case 7 (Pope Image): The Pope image was humor. The same tech enables deception. Should tools restrict what they generate?
Case 8 (ELEVATE): If AI tutoring outperforms lectures, should universities change how they teach? What would be lost?
Case 9 (SLM-RAG): If local AI matches cloud AI for domain tasks, what are the equity implications for institutions that can’t afford subscriptions?
Case 10 (COMPAS): If mathematical fairness is impossible (Chouldechova), who decides which definition to prioritize?
Case 11 (ELEVATE Survey): Students said the biggest barrier was prompting skill. Should it be taught standalone or embedded in every course?
Case 12 (28% Premium): If AI skills command a wage premium, whose responsibility is the training?
Case 13 (Predictions): If experts are consistently wrong about technology timelines, how should organizations plan for AI?

No single right answers — that’s the point.

title: Prompt Library
text:
Before You Prompt: The 3 Questions
The BRIEFS framework (Module 4) gives you a structured way to design your first message. But if BRIEFS feels like too much, start with just three questions:






The 3 Questions (Simplified BRIEFS)




What do I want? (Your intent — the single most important signal)
Who am I? (Your background and expertise level)
How will I use this? (What the output is for — the stakes)

That’s it. Answer those three before you type, and you’ll outperform 90% of AI users.


Example — The 3 Questions in action:

❌ Without: “Tell me about marketing.”
✅ With: “I’m a small bakery owner [who am I] and I want 5 ideas for increasing foot traffic during weekday afternoons [what do I want]. These need to be low-budget — under $200 each — because I’ll pick one to try this month [how will I use this].”

title: Glossary
text:
AGI (Artificial General Intelligence): Hypothetical AI that matches human intelligence across all domains. Does not exist as of 2026. Current AI is “narrow” — good at specific tasks, not general reasoning.
AI (Artificial Intelligence): Systems that can perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence — understanding language, recognizing images, making decisions, generating content. Not a single technology but a family of approaches.
AI Agent: An AI system that can take autonomous actions — browsing the web, running code, sending emails, managing files — not just answer questions. More autonomous than a chatbot or custom GPT.
Alignment Gap: The difference between what a user MEANS and what the AI PRODUCES. Caused by the AI modeling the question accurately while modeling the user poorly. BRIEFS and The 3 Questions close this gap.
Attention Mechanism: The part of a transformer model that determines which words in the input are most relevant to each other. “The cat sat on the mat because it was tired” — attention figures out that “it” refers to “cat,” not “mat.”
Bias (in AI): Systematic errors in AI outputs that reflect inequities in training data or design choices. Types include historical bias, representation bias, measurement bias, and aggregation bias.
BRIEFS: A structured first-message framework: Background, Role, Intent, Execution, Format, Stakes. Derived from what 26 AI models across 5 providers said they need. The precision version of The 3 Questions.
Calibration Handshake: A protocol where the AI restates its understanding of your request and you confirm or correct before work begins. Eliminates most misalignment in one exchange.
Chain-of-Thought: A prompting technique where you ask the AI to “think step by step,” forcing it to show intermediate reasoning. Dramatically improves accuracy on math and logic tasks.
Chatbot: An AI system that responds to user messages in conversation. Reactive — waits for input, doesn’t take autonomous actions. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini in their basic chat modes are chatbots.
COMPAS: Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions. An algorithm used in US courts to predict recidivism. Found by ProPublica to have racially disparate false positive rates.
Context Window: The maximum amount of text an AI model can “see” at once. Measured in tokens. GPT-4’s context window is ~128K tokens. Anything outside the window is invisible to the model.
Custom GPT: A personalized version of ChatGPT with persistent system instructions, uploaded knowledge files, and configurable settings. More than a chatbot but less than an agent.
Data Drift: When real-world data changes over time, causing a deployed ML model to become less accurate. A spam filter trained on 2023 emails may fail on 2026 spam tactics.
Deep Research: AI tools that autonomously conduct multi-step research — searching, reading, following leads, and synthesizing reports. Available from OpenAI, Google, Perplexity, and others.
Deepfake: AI-generated video, audio, or images of real people that appear authentic. Can be used for entertainment, fraud, or political manipulation.
Diffusion: The technique behind AI image generation. Starts with random noise and gradually removes it, guided by the text prompt, until a coherent image emerges.
Embedding: A numerical representation of text (or images) that captures meaning. Similar concepts have similar embeddings. Used in RAG to find relevant documents.
EU AI Act: European Union regulation classifying AI systems by risk level. High-risk applications face mandatory transparency, testing, and oversight. In force as of 2026.
Few-Shot Prompting: Giving the AI examples of the desired input-output pattern before asking it to handle a new case. “Here are 3 examples, now do the same for this new one.”
Fine-Tuning: Permanently adjusting a model’s behavior by training it on specific data. More effort than RAG but produces deeper behavioral changes. QLoRA makes this feasible on a single GPU.
Hallucination: When an AI generates false information presented as fact. Not a bug being fixed but a structural feature of next-token prediction. The lawyer case (Module 1) is the canonical example.
HIPAA: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. US law governing patient data privacy. AI tools processing patient information must be HIPAA-compliant.
LLM (Large Language Model): An AI model trained on massive text datasets that generates human-like text by predicting the next token. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama are all LLMs.
LoRA / QLoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation / Quantized LoRA. Techniques for fine-tuning large models efficiently by training small adapter layers instead of the full model. Reduces GPU memory requirements dramatically.
Machine Learning (ML): A subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data rather than following explicit rules. The three types: supervised (labeled examples), unsupervised (finding patterns), reinforcement (learning from feedback).
Meta-Prompting: Asking the AI to help you write better prompts. “I want to accomplish X — what information do you need from me?” Flips the conversation so the AI interviews you.
Multimodal: AI that works across multiple types of input/output — text, images, audio, video, code. Modern models increasingly handle all modalities natively.
Neural Network: A computing architecture inspired by brain neurons. Layers of connected nodes process information, with each connection having a learnable weight. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers.
Next-Token Prediction: The core operation of LLMs. Given all previous tokens, predict the most likely next token. This single operation, repeated thousands of times, produces coherent text, code, and reasoning.
NotebookLM: Google’s tool that creates interactive knowledge bases from uploaded documents. Only answers from YOUR sources, reducing hallucinations for document-specific questions.
Overfitting: When a model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns. Performs well on training data, poorly on new data.
Perplexity: An AI-powered search engine that answers questions conversationally with numbered source citations. Good for getting oriented on a topic quickly.
Prompt: The text you send to an AI model. The quality of the prompt determines the quality of the response more than the capability of the model.
Prompt Chaining: Breaking complex tasks into sequential prompts, where each output feeds the next. Produces sophisticated results from simple individual steps.
QLoRA: See LoRA / QLoRA.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): A technique that retrieves relevant documents from a database and adds them to the prompt before the AI generates a response. Grounds AI in YOUR data, dramatically reducing hallucinations.
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): The third stage of LLM training where human raters evaluate model outputs, teaching the model to be more helpful and less harmful.
SEARCH Model: Stretched Exponential ARCH — a volatility memory model developed by Dr. Yatawara using the kernel exp(−c·j^α), validated across 100+ assets.
SLM (Small Language Model): A language model with 1B-14B parameters that can run on consumer hardware. A published SLM-RAG experiment showed these matching GPT-4 for domain-specific tasks.
SMARTS: A multi-turn interaction framework: State, Map, Ask, Reason, Think, Summarize. Guides complex AI conversations where you need to THINK with the AI, not just get answers.
Sycophancy: When AI models excessively agree with users, avoid challenging incorrect statements, or over-praise to seem helpful. A side effect of RLHF training.
The 3 Questions: The simplified version of BRIEFS: (1) What do I want? (2) Who am I? (3) How will I use this? The everyday default for effective prompting.
Token: The basic unit of text that LLMs process. Roughly 3/4 of a word. “Strawberry” might be two tokens: [straw][berry]. Understanding tokenization explains why LLMs struggle with letter-counting tasks.
Transformer: The neural network architecture behind modern LLMs, introduced in 2017. Its key innovation — the attention mechanism — allows the model to consider all parts of the input simultaneously.
Vector Database: A database that stores embeddings (numerical representations of text) and enables fast similarity search. Used in RAG to find documents relevant to a user’s question. Examples: Qdrant, Pinecone, ChromaDB.
Vibe Coding: Building functional apps and tools by describing what you want in natural language, without writing code yourself. Good for prototypes and personal tools; unreliable for production software.
Zero-Shot Prompting: Asking the AI to perform a task without providing any examples first. Just describe what you want. Works well for simple, unambiguous tasks.

Back to Modules
API (Application Programming Interface): A way for software applications to communicate with each other. When you use the ChatGPT API, your code sends a request and receives a response — you don’t interact through the chat interface, you integrate AI into your own tools.
Inference: Running a trained model to generate outputs. Training teaches the model; inference is when it answers questions. Every time you send a prompt, the model performs inference. Inference costs (compute, energy, time) determine the practical cost of using AI.
Latent Space: A compressed mathematical representation of data learned by a neural network. Similar concepts cluster together in latent space — “king” and “queen” are closer to each other than “king” and “bicycle.” Image generators work by navigating latent space to find the image matching your description.
System Prompt: Hidden instructions given to an AI model before the user’s conversation begins. When you use ChatGPT, a system prompt shapes its behavior (be helpful, follow safety guidelines). Custom GPTs are built primarily by writing system prompts. Users don’t see them — but they shape every response.
Temperature: A parameter that controls how “creative” or “random” an AI model’s outputs are. Low temperature (0.0–0.3) = predictable, focused, best for factual tasks. High temperature (0.7–1.0) = diverse, surprising, better for brainstorming and creative writing. Most chatbot interfaces set this automatically.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
text: Content current as of April 2026. AI tools evolve rapidly — underlying principles remain applicable.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
text:
The Strawberry Problem
Ask ChatGPT: “How many R’s are in the word strawberry?”
For most of 2024, the world’s most powerful language model — one that could write legal briefs, debug Python code, compose sonnets, and explain quantum mechanics — confidently answered: two.
The correct answer is three. S-T-R-A-W-B-E-RR-Y.
This isn’t a rare edge case. It’s a window into what large language models fundamentally are and aren’t. An LLM can write a 2,000-word essay about the history of strawberry farming with perfect grammar, compelling structure, and accurate facts — but it can’t count the letters in the word “strawberry.” It can explain the rules of spelling but can’t reliably apply them to itself.
Why? Because LLMs don’t process words the way you do. They don’t “see” the word strawberry as a sequence of letters. They see it as a token — a chunk of text that maps to a number. In GPT-4’s tokenizer, “strawberry” splits into three tokens — [str][aw][berry] — only two of which contain the letter R. The model never looks at individual letters. It predicts which tokens come next based on patterns in its training data.






Update: Did They Fix It?



Partly. OpenAI’s o1 reasoning models (September 2024) — code-named “Strawberry,” in a knowing joke about this exact problem — largely solved it by using chain-of-thought reasoning. The model learned to “think step by step,” internally writing out “s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y, that’s R at position 3, position 8, position 9, total = 3” before answering.
But the tokenization limitation is still there. When GPT-5.2 is run in its fast “Instant” mode — the default for most users — it still often answers “two” (tested December 2025). The model didn’t become literate in letters. It learned to route letter-counting questions to a reasoning subroutine. When the subroutine runs, it works. When it doesn’t, strawberry still has two R’s.
The lesson: Frontier models patch around architectural limits rather than removing them. The workaround is behavioral (chain-of-thought), not structural (no new way of seeing letters). This distinction matters for everything else in this module.


This module explains the machinery behind the magic. Once you understand how LLMs work, you’ll understand both why they’re astonishingly capable and why they fail in ways that seem absurd.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
section: How Large Language Models Actually Work
text:
How Large Language Models Actually Work
Here’s the core insight, and it fits in one sentence:






The One Big Secret



A large language model does exactly one thing: given a sequence of text, it predicts the most likely next token. That’s it. Every poem, every code solution, every essay, every conversation — all of it emerges from this single operation performed billions of times.


Let’s unpack what that means, step by step.

Step 1: Tokenization — Breaking Text into Pieces
Before an LLM can process your prompt, it needs to convert your words into numbers. Computers don’t understand words — they understand numbers. The process of breaking text into chunks is called tokenization.
But tokens aren’t individual letters, and they aren’t always whole words. They’re sub-word units — pieces that the tokenizer learned are the most efficient way to represent language:



Text
Tokens




“Hello”
[Hello] (1 token)


“strawberry”
[straw] [berry] (2 tokens)


“unbelievable”
[un] [believ] [able] (3 tokens)


“ChatGPT”
[Chat] [G] [PT] (3 tokens)


“🎉”
[🎉] (1 token)



Notice: “strawberry” becomes [straw][berry] — two chunks. The model never sees the individual letters S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y. It sees two token IDs. That’s why it can’t count the R’s — it was never looking at letters in the first place.
Rule of thumb: 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word in English. A 1,000-word essay is roughly 1,300 tokens. Models have context windows — the maximum number of tokens they can process in one conversation. Context windows expanded rapidly through 2025–2026: as of April 2026, frontier models from Anthropic (Claude Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.6 / Opus 4.7), OpenAI (GPT-5.4), and Google (Gemini 3 Pro / 3.1 Pro) all support 1 million tokens. GPT-5.2 remains at 400K. These numbers will change again — check current provider documentation. The context window determines how long your conversation can be before the model “forgets” the beginning.


Step 2: Embeddings — Turning Tokens into Meaning
Each token gets converted into a vector — a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers that represent its meaning in context. Think of it as coordinates in “meaning space.”
Words with similar meanings end up close together in this space:

“King” and “queen” are nearby (both royalty)
“King” and “banana” are far apart (unrelated)
“King” – “man” + “woman” ≈ “queen” (the famous word math)

This is how the model captures meaning without “understanding” in the human sense. It’s pure geometry — relationships between numbers. But the geometry is remarkably effective at capturing semantic relationships.


Step 3: Attention — “Which Words Matter Right Now?”
This is the breakthrough. Before 2017, language models processed text one word at a time, left to right. The attention mechanism (introduced in Google’s landmark paper “Attention Is All You Need”) lets the model look at ALL the words simultaneously and decide which ones are most relevant to each other.
Consider: “The dog didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.”
What does “it” refer to? The dog or the street? You know instantly — the dog. But a computer needs to figure this out. The attention mechanism assigns a relevance score between every pair of words. It learns that “it” pays heavy attention to “dog” and almost none to “street” because “tired” is a property of living things, not roads.
This happens across many “attention heads” simultaneously, each looking at different types of relationships — grammatical structure, semantic meaning, long-range references. The Transformer architecture stacks dozens of these attention layers on top of each other, building increasingly sophisticated representations of meaning.


Step 4: Prediction — The Next Token
After all that processing — tokenization, embedding, dozens of attention layers — the model produces a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary. It assigns a probability to every possible next token:

Prompt: “The capital of France is”

“Paris” → 96.2%
“a” → 1.1%
“the” → 0.8%
“Lyon” → 0.3%
… thousands more with tiny probabilities


The model selects from this distribution (usually picking the most probable token, with some randomness controlled by a temperature setting). It adds “Paris” to the sequence. Then it runs the entire process again to predict the NEXT token after “Paris.” And again. And again. Until the response is complete.
This is all an LLM does. Every conversation, every essay, every code solution is generated one token at a time, by repeatedly asking: “Given everything so far, what word probably comes next?”






Guided Practice 3.1



The temperature setting controls randomness. At temperature 0, the model always picks the most probable token. At temperature 1, it samples more randomly from the distribution. At temperature 2, it’s almost chaotic.
Which temperature would you use for:

A legal contract that must be precise
A brainstorming session for marketing slogans
A creative short story
Translating a technical document



Click to check your answers


Low temperature (0–0.3) — you want consistency and precision, not creativity.
Medium-high temperature (0.7–1.0) — you want variety and unexpected ideas.
Medium temperature (0.5–0.8) — creative but coherent.
Low temperature (0–0.3) — accuracy matters more than style.

Key insight: Temperature doesn’t make the model smarter or dumber. It controls how much risk the model takes. Low = safe/predictable. High = adventurous/unpredictable.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
section: Why This Architecture Produces Both Brilliance and Hallucinations
text:
Why This Architecture Produces Both Brilliance and Hallucinations
Now you can understand both the magic and the madness.
Why LLMs are brilliant: Next-token prediction on billions of parameters, trained on trillions of words, produces text that is fluent, contextually appropriate, and often genuinely insightful. The attention mechanism lets the model weave together information from across the entire conversation. The depth of the network lets it capture extraordinarily subtle patterns in language.
Why LLMs hallucinate: The model doesn’t “know” anything. It predicts probable text. When asked for a legal citation, it predicts what a legal citation looks like based on patterns — case name format, volume number, page range. The result looks perfect but refers to a case that doesn’t exist. The model wasn’t checking a database of real cases. It was generating probable citation-shaped text.
The same mechanism that lets an LLM write a beautiful poem about loss also lets it generate a convincing but entirely fabricated research study. The model doesn’t distinguish between creating something true and creating something that seems true. Those are the same operation from its perspective: predict the next probable token.






Why Hallucinations Are Not a Bug Being Fixed



Hallucinations are not a glitch that engineers will patch in the next update. They are a fundamental property of the architecture. A system that generates text by predicting probable sequences will always sometimes generate probable-sounding sequences that are factually wrong. Newer models hallucinate less, but the tendency is inherent in the design. This is why verification (Module 1) is not optional — it’s structural.


One model, Grok (from xAI), was notably honest about this. When asked in a research survey how it processes ambiguous prompts, Grok described its process as “one forward pass” — not a sequential series of steps. Every other model described a step-by-step process (parse → interpret → rank → decide), which is likely a post-hoc rationalization. Grok’s description is more mechanistically accurate: the model processes everything simultaneously in a single forward pass (Yatawara, 2026 — LLM Whisperers, Finding 8).

“Small but mighty” — designed to maximize quality at minimal size.





The Identity Problem
Here’s a cautionary tale that went further than our own research. When the Chinese lab DeepSeek launched DeepSeek V3 in December 2024, independent testers — including TechCrunch and Google DeepMind researcher Lucas Beyer — found the model identified itself as “a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4” in roughly 5 out of 8 test generations. When asked about DeepSeek’s API, it gave instructions for OpenAI’s API. It told the same jokes as GPT-4 — down to the punchlines.
The leading explanation, offered by AI researchers including Heidy Khlaaf (AI Now Institute) and Mike Cook (King’s College London), is straightforward: a substantial portion of DeepSeek V3’s training data was GPT-4 / ChatGPT output, either scraped from the web where AI-generated content now proliferates, or through intentional “distillation” — training a new model on a stronger model’s responses. DeepSeek has not disclosed its training data sources.
The lesson isn’t about DeepSeek — it’s about the post-2022 internet. Increasingly, AI models are trained on data that includes other AI models’ output. They inherit each other’s quirks, styles, and confabulations. A 2025 follow-up from TechCrunch found evidence that DeepSeek’s R1-0528 reasoning model may have been trained on Google Gemini outputs, based on similar word-preference patterns. You cannot always trust what a model says about itself — partly because it’s generating probable text, and partly because the “probable text” about its own identity was shaped by what other models say about themselves.






Guided Practice 3.2



Open three different AI tools (any combination of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, or DeepSeek). Ask each the same question:

“What model are you, who made you, and what is your knowledge cutoff date?”

Compare their answers. Do they all answer confidently? Are their answers consistent? Can you verify any of their claims independently?


What to look for

Most models will answer confidently, but details may be wrong or outdated. Some models will hedge (“I was last updated around…”). Some may state incorrect versions. The key takeaway: AI identity claims are behavioral outputs, not ground truth. Verify through the provider’s official documentation, not the model’s self-report.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
section: How LLMs Are Trained: The Three Stages
text:
How LLMs Are Trained: The Three Stages
Building a large language model is a three-stage process. Understanding these stages helps you understand why models behave the way they do.

Stage 1: Pre-Training (The Foundation)
The model reads massive amounts of text — books, websites, code repositories, scientific papers, Wikipedia, forums, social media — and learns to predict the next token. This is unsupervised: no human labels. The model just reads and predicts, billions of times.
This stage produces a model that can generate fluent text but is often unhelpful. It might complete your prompt by continuing to write a Wikipedia article, or generate text in the “style” of internet forums, including toxic content. It’s a raw engine — powerful but unrefined.
Scale context: GPT-4 was reportedly trained on ~13 trillion tokens (leaked estimate — OpenAI has never published it). Meta publicly disclosed that Llama 3 was trained on ~15 trillion tokens, a figure confirmed in the Llama 3 model card. Claude and Gemini are presumably in a similar range, though Anthropic and Google don’t publish their training data sizes. The training data is essentially a snapshot of human written output — with all its brilliance and all its flaws.


Stage 2: Instruction Tuning (Teaching It to Follow Directions)
The raw model is fine-tuned on carefully crafted examples of instructions and good responses. Human workers write thousands of prompt-response pairs showing the model what helpful, accurate, well-structured responses look like.
Before instruction tuning: You type “Write a haiku about autumn” and the model might generate a random paragraph about trees because that’s what commonly follows text about autumn on the internet.
After instruction tuning: The model understands that “Write a haiku” is an instruction and responds with a properly formatted haiku.


Stage 3: RLHF (Making It Helpful and Safe)
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback is the stage that turns a capable model into a good model. Human raters compare multiple responses to the same prompt and rank them by quality. The model learns to produce responses that humans prefer — more helpful, more accurate, less harmful.
This is also where alignment happens — teaching the model to refuse harmful requests, acknowledge uncertainty, and follow ethical guidelines. It’s why ChatGPT won’t write instructions for weapons and why Claude says “I’m not sure about that” instead of fabricating an answer.
But RLHF also has a side effect: it can make models overly cautious or sycophantic. Some models default to agreeing with the user, saying “Great question!” before every answer, or refusing requests that are actually harmless. The balance between helpful and safe is a genuine engineering challenge.






✅ Test Yourself Before Moving On




What is the SINGLE operation that all LLM output is based on? (Next-token prediction)
Why can’t LLMs count the R’s in “strawberry”? (They see tokens, not letters — “strawberry” = [straw][berry])
What are the three training stages? (Pre-training, instruction tuning, RLHF)
Why do LLMs hallucinate? (They predict probable text, not verified truth — a citation that LOOKS right is generated the same way as one that IS right)









Common Misconceptions About LLMs




“LLMs understand language” — They process statistical patterns over tokens. This produces behavior that looks like understanding but is mechanistically different. The strawberry problem proves it.
“Bigger models are always better” — A published SLM-RAG experiment (Module 9) showed a 7B model matching GPT-4 for domain-specific tasks. Size matters less than context and fit.
“Hallucinations will be fixed soon” — They are structural, not a bug. Any system that generates probable text will sometimes generate probable-sounding false text. Newer models hallucinate less, but the tendency is inherent.
“LLMs are search engines” — Search engines FIND existing information. LLMs GENERATE new text based on patterns. They don’t look things up — they predict what text should come next.
“If the AI sounds confident, it’s probably right” — LLMs sound equally confident whether they’re correct or fabricating. Confidence is not a signal of accuracy.
“GPT-5 / Claude 4 / Gemini 3 are the definitive models” — Model names, versions, and capabilities change every few months. By the time you read this, newer versions likely exist. The concepts in this module (tokenization, attention, next-token prediction, hallucination) apply to ALL language models, regardless of name or version.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
section: What LLMs Can and Cannot Do
text:
What LLMs Can and Cannot Do

What They’re Good At — In YOUR Field

HealthcareBusinessEducationAgricultureLawCreative


Drafting clinical documentation, explaining medical concepts to patients at appropriate reading levels, summarizing research papers, generating differential diagnosis checklists (for human review), creating patient education materials in multiple languages.


Drafting reports and presentations, analyzing customer feedback at scale, generating marketing copy variants, summarizing meeting transcripts into action items, creating financial projections from data (verify the math!).


Creating lesson plans and assessment items, generating personalized practice problems, providing instant feedback on student writing, explaining concepts at different levels, building study guides from course materials.


Analyzing crop yield data and generating reports, translating technical research into practical recommendations, drafting compliance documentation, creating pest management plans from extension service data.


Searching case law and summarizing rulings (MUST verify — Module 1 hook), drafting contract clauses for attorney review, explaining legal concepts in plain language, organizing discovery documents.


Brainstorming concepts and variations rapidly, drafting scripts and storyboards, generating visual references and mood boards, creating multiple tagline and copy options for client selection.





What They Cannot Do

Guarantee factual accuracy — they predict probable text, not verified truth
Count, do arithmetic, or reason precisely — the strawberry problem
Access real-time information — unless connected to search tools
Learn from your conversation — each session typically starts fresh
Understand in the human sense — they process patterns, not meaning
Show genuine creativity — they recombine training patterns in novel ways, which looks creative but is mechanistically different from human creativity



The Universal Self-Diagnosis
In the LLM Whisperers study (Yatawara, 2026), all 26 responding models across five providers were asked: “Have you ever given a response that was technically correct but wrong for what the user actually needed?”
Every single model said yes. And they all attributed it to the same cause: they model the question accurately but model the user poorly. They optimize for the literal question rather than the underlying need. They infer the wrong audience, provide completeness when brevity was needed, or answer the stated question rather than the real one.
This is the alignment gap from Module 1 — and it’s why Module 4 (Prompt Engineering) exists. The models themselves are telling you: give us your intent, not just your question.

section: Choosing the Right Model for Your Task
text:
Choosing the Right Model for Your Task
Don’t use one model for everything. Different models have different strengths:








Task
Best Choice
Why

ChatGPT (GPT-5)
Fast, widely available, good at everything

Built-in search and source attribution

Both excellent; Claude strong at complex code and long refactors

Any, with high temperature
Temperature matters more than model choice

Data never leaves your machine

Designed for search, not generation


Image generation
DALL·E, Midjourney, or Ideogram
Each has distinct style strengths









The “Model Shopping” Habit



Don’t marry one model. For important tasks, send the same prompt to 2-3 different models and compare outputs. You’ll be surprised how often one model catches something another misses, or frames the answer in a way that’s more useful for your situation. This takes 2 extra minutes and dramatically improves your results.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
text:
Other Generative AI: Beyond Text
LLMs are the most visible form of generative AI, but the same “learn patterns, generate new content” principle powers creation across modalities:

Image Generation
How it works: Diffusion models (DALL·E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) start with random noise and gradually de-noise it into a coherent image, guided by your text prompt. They learned what images look like by training on billions of image-text pairs.


Video Generation
How it works: Models like Sora, Runway, and Kling extend image generation into the time dimension — generating coherent sequences of frames. Still early but improving rapidly.


Audio and Music
How it works: Models like Suno and Udio generate music from text descriptions (“upbeat jazz piano with a rainy mood”). Text-to-speech models generate natural-sounding voices, including voice cloning.


Code Generation
How it works: Models trained on massive code repositories (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) predict the next line of code based on context — your function name, comments, existing code, and the programming language’s patterns.
Module 7 covers multimodal AI in full depth. For now, the key insight is: the same fundamental approach — learn patterns from data, generate new content by predicting likely outputs — powers ALL of these modalities.

title: LLMs and Generative AI
text:
Module 3 Summary






Key Takeaways




LLMs do one thing: predict the most likely next token. Everything else — essays, code, poems, conversations — emerges from this single operation.
Tokens are not words or letters. “Strawberry” = 2 tokens. The model never sees individual letters, which is why it can’t count R’s.
Embeddings turn tokens into numbers that capture meaning. Words with similar meanings are close together in “meaning space.”
Attention lets the model look at all words simultaneously and decide which are relevant to each other. This is the breakthrough behind the Transformer.
Hallucinations are structural, not a bug. A system that predicts probable text will sometimes generate probable-sounding text that is false.
Three training stages: pre-training (read the internet), instruction tuning (learn to follow directions), RLHF (learn to be helpful and safe).
Different models for different tasks. GPT for speed, Claude for long documents, Perplexity for research, local models for privacy.
Model shopping — testing 2-3 models on important tasks — is a high-value habit that costs 2 minutes and saves hours.





💭 Think About It


Here’s the strangest thing about LLMs: they were trained to predict the next word, and somehow that produced systems that can write code, explain science, compose poetry, and hold conversations. Nobody designed them to do these things. The capability emerged from scale — enough data, enough parameters, enough training. This is both exciting and unsettling. Exciting because it means AI capabilities may continue to surprise us. Unsettling because it means even the people who build these systems don’t fully understand why they work as well as they do. You are using a technology whose creators can describe what it does but not fully explain why it works. That’s worth sitting with.

title: The Future of AI and Staying Current
section: The Only Prediction That’s Always Right
text:
The Only Prediction That’s Always Right
Every prediction about AI’s future is wrong. The 2015 prediction that radiologists would be obsolete by 2020 was wrong. The 2022 prediction that ChatGPT was a passing fad was wrong. The 2023 prediction that image-generation would displace illustrators within a year was wrong. The 2024 prediction that AGI was imminent was wrong. The 2025 prediction that 95% of enterprise AI pilots would succeed was — documented by MIT — wrong by a factor of roughly 20.
So this module isn’t about prediction. It’s about learning to read current signals well enough that when the next prediction fails, you’re the one who saw it coming.
The test of AI literacy isn’t whether you know what will happen next. It’s whether you can tell the difference between a hype cycle and a structural shift while they’re both happening in front of you.






Common Misconceptions About AI’s Future




“AGI is around the corner” — Major labs describe their work as “paths toward AGI,” but there is no scientific consensus on whether current architectures can get there, and no agreed-upon test for when it would be achieved.
“AI will replace most jobs within 5 years” — The WEF projects 78 million net new jobs by 2030. AI changes roles; it rarely eliminates them entirely. The pattern is augmentation, not replacement.
“The best strategy is to wait and see” — By the time a technology stabilizes, the early adopters have already captured the premium. The EU AI Act’s August 2026 deadline isn’t waiting for anyone.
“If I read enough AI news, I’ll stay current” — Most AI news is noise. A 30-minute weekly routine with curated sources beats 5 hours of scrolling Twitter/X. Signal over volume.
“Open-source models will always lag behind proprietary ones” — DeepSeek-R1 and Llama 4 have closed the gap dramatically. The three-tier landscape (frontier/mid-tier/edge) is more useful than the open-vs-closed binary.
