title: The Art and Science of Prompting
text:
Module 4 Summary






Key Takeaways




Prompting is communication, not typing. The quality of AI output depends more on the quality of your input than on the model’s capability.
BRIEFS (Background, Role, Intent, Execution, Format, Stakes) designs your first message based on what 26 LLMs across 5 providers independently said they need.
SMARTS (State, Map, Ask, Reason, Think, Summarize) guides multi-turn conversations for complex tasks, keeping you in control of the reasoning.
Together: BRIEFS opens the conversation → Calibration Handshake confirms alignment → SMARTS guides the reasoning → Verified output.
Core techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, role-based, structured output) are your everyday toolkit.
Advanced techniques (prompt chaining, constraint setting, meta-prompting, persona stacking) handle complex scenarios.
Don’t over-engineer. Simple questions don’t need six-component frameworks. Use BRIEFS and SMARTS when the stakes or complexity warrant it.
The calibration handshake (model restates → user confirms) eliminates most misalignment in one extra exchange — or zero, if your first message is well-structured.
The practice ladder matters more than the frameworks themselves. You can read about BRIEFS in ten minutes. Becoming fluent in it is the work of Exercises 4.A through 4.J. The research is clear: reading about a framework and doing scaffolded practice produce very different skill levels (Zhang et al., 2025, found that students with strong theoretical knowledge still wrote short, informal prompts without structured scaffolding).





💭 Think About It


The models told us what they need: intent first, context second, constraints third. BRIEFS gives them that. SMARTS gives you a way to think WITH them, not just AT them. Together, they turn AI from a search engine into a thinking partner. But here’s the deeper lesson: the same skills that make you good at prompting AI — clarity, specificity, structured thinking, knowing your own intent — also make you a better communicator with humans. The frameworks aren’t just for machines. They’re for anyone who has ever sent a vague email and gotten a useless reply.








📇 Print Your Cheat Sheets



The BRIEFS and SMARTS frameworks are summarized on printable reference cards in the Framework Cards appendix. Print them. Pin them next to your screen. The best framework is the one you actually use.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text: Content current as of April 2026. Model names and prices change every few months; the infrastructure principles — where your data goes, what closes the knowledge gap, when to prompt vs. retrieve vs. fine-tune — are what’s durable.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
The $0.002 Experiment
In 2025, a research team at a public university asked a simple question: could a small, cheap AI running on a single campus GPU match the accuracy of GPT-4?
The answer surprised even the researchers.
They took two small language models — Mistral-7B and DeepSeek-7B, each with 7 billion parameters (compare GPT-4’s estimated 1.8 trillion) — fine-tuned them on university course materials using a technique called QLoRA, and paired them with a local vector database that could retrieve relevant textbook passages on demand. The system is called SLM-RAG (Small Language Model with Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
Across 186 graded prompts from two undergraduate statistics courses:



Model
Median Score (0–5)
Mean Latency
Cost per 1K Tokens




SLM-RAG (Mistral-7B)
4.3
6.8 seconds
$0.002


SLM-RAG (DeepSeek-7B)
4.2
7.1 seconds
$0.002


GPT-4
4.4
12.4 seconds
$0.025



The difference in accuracy was not statistically significant (p = 0.41). The SLM-RAG system matched GPT-4 while cutting cost by 92% and latency by 45%. All traffic stayed on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU on campus. No student data ever left the building.
This experiment proved something that the industry’s marketing mostly obscures: for domain-specific work where you can provide relevant context, you do not need a frontier model. A small, well-configured model running on your own hardware can match the giants — at a cost and privacy profile that changes what’s possible for schools, clinics, and small organizations (Yatawara et al., 2025, Campus-Hosted Small Language Models with Retrieval-Augmented Generation, AI Journal, MDPI).
This module teaches you the infrastructure landscape as it actually stands in April 2026 — what runs where, what costs what, and how to make the right choice for your situation.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
section: Cloud vs Local: Where AI Runs (and Where Your Data Goes)
text:
Cloud vs Local: Where AI Runs (and Where Your Data Goes)
Every AI tool you use runs on one of two kinds of infrastructure. The distinction matters far more than most people realize, because where the computation happens determines where your data goes.

Cloud AI (APIs and chat platforms)
When you use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity, your prompt is sent to remote servers owned by the AI company. The model runs there, and the response comes back. Most people never think about this.
Advantages. No hardware. Always the newest model. Trivial to use.
Disadvantages. Your data travels to — and is at least briefly processed on — someone else’s servers. Ongoing subscription or per-token costs. You depend on the provider’s pricing, policies, and continued existence. No internet, no AI.


Local AI (on your own hardware)
With tools like Ollama or LM Studio, you download and run AI models on your own machine. The weights live on your SSD, the computation happens on your GPU or CPU, and your data never leaves the box.
Advantages. Complete privacy. Zero marginal cost after hardware. Works offline. No rate limits.
Disadvantages. Hardware required — though less than you’d think (see below). Local models are usually a half-step behind the frontier on pure reasoning benchmarks. You handle updates. Initial setup is a Saturday project.


Hybrid: the pattern organizations actually use
Almost every serious organization ends up with a hybrid stack:

Cloud for general-purpose, low-sensitivity work — drafting, brainstorming, summarizing public documents
Local or on-premises for anything touching regulated data — student records (FERPA), patient data (HIPAA), client files, proprietary IP, financial detail

The SLM-RAG experiment is this philosophy: when student data matters, bring the AI to the data instead of sending the data to the AI.






Common Misconceptions About AI Infrastructure




“Local AI is always worse than cloud AI.” For domain-specific work with RAG, a 7B local model matched GPT-4 at p = 0.41. Size isn’t everything. Context is.
“Cloud AI is private enough.” Free tiers may use your conversations for training. Enterprise tiers contractually don’t, but data still transits external servers. For HIPAA/FERPA, local is often the only genuinely compliant option.
“You need a $5,000 GPU to run local AI.” Phi-4-mini (3.8B), Gemma 3 4B, and Llama 3.2 3B all run well on an 8 GB laptop. An M-series MacBook runs 8B models at 40+ tokens/second. The entry bar is low.
“Fine-tuning is always worth it.” For most tasks, RAG is cheaper, faster, and good enough. Fine-tune only when you need the model to adopt a behavior pattern, not reference specific content.
“Open-source means second-tier.” Llama 4, DeepSeek R1/V3, Qwen 3, and GLM-4.7 post competitive numbers against proprietary frontier models on major benchmarks as of Q1 2026. Several are released under permissive licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0). The open-source stack is world-class.





Which infrastructure for YOUR situation?

HealthcareEducationSmall BusinessGovernment


Recommended. Hybrid. HIPAA-compliant cloud for administrative and educational content; local or on-premises for anything touching PHI. RAG over clinical guidelines for decision support. Ambient AI scribes (Abridge, Nuance DAX Copilot, Suki, Freed) run through vendor BAAs and are now common — a recent JAMA multi-site study reported they cut clinician EHR time by ~13 minutes per day and documentation time by ~16 minutes.
Key constraint. HIPAA is non-negotiable, and a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is the minimum bar for any vendor. Ambient scribes also raise a second-order question: if the AI documents more diagnoses, billing goes up — make sure the clinical motivation, not the coding motivation, is driving adoption.


Recommended. Cloud AI (enterprise tiers with FERPA language in the contract) for teaching support and content creation. Institutional or local hosting for anything involving student records. Custom GPTs (ChatGPT Edu) or Claude Projects for student-facing tutors that stay inside the course corpus.
Key constraint. FERPA governs student data — and free-tier cloud tools do not satisfy it. CSU’s ChatGPT Edu deployment is the template most public universities are converging on.


Recommended. Start with free cloud tiers. Upgrade to paid ($20/user) when you hit message limits. Move to Team plans at ~5–20 users. Consider local only when (a) you handle sensitive client data or (b) your token bill exceeds the amortized cost of a $2,000 GPU.
Key constraint. Budget — but don’t over-optimize prematurely. The first $20/month buys 95% of the value. The hard cost decision comes at the $200–$2,000/month level.


Recommended. On-premises or government-cloud (FedRAMP High / IL-5) for any data involving citizens. Local RAG over policy documents and procedures. Avoid generic SaaS chatbots for anything beyond public-facing FAQ.
Key constraint. Data sovereignty, public accountability, and — as the COMPAS case in Module 10 showed — fairness testing before any deployment that affects a person’s rights, liberty, or benefits.

Practical levers that most teams miss. The list prices above are a starting point. Two mechanisms can cut real API spend by 80–95%:

Prompt caching. Repeated context (system prompts, long documents, a whole codebase) is cached and billed at ~10% of the input rate on cache hits. For RAG and agent workloads, this is the single biggest cost lever.
Batch processing. Asynchronous batch APIs ship results within 24 hours at a ~50% discount across providers. If your task can wait, you pay half.

The SLM-RAG sweet spot. For a university department or small clinic handling ~200 queries/day on domain-specific content, a $2,000 GPU running a local model with RAG costs roughly $50–$80/month (electricity plus amortized hardware over 5 years) vs $500–$1,500/month for equivalent flagship API usage. Break-even sits at 3–4 months. That math is what made the original SLM-RAG experiment viable — and what makes it replicable by almost any public institution.

section: Small Language Models: Why Smaller Can Be Better
text:
Small Language Models: Why Smaller Can Be Better
The AI industry’s loudest marketing message is “bigger is better.” The numbers tell a more interesting story. For domain-specific tasks with appropriate context, small models match or beat their giant counterparts — and do so at 50× less compute.
The key technique is quantization. A 7B parameter model at full 16-bit precision needs ~14 GB of VRAM. Quantized to 4 bits (Q4_K_M) — the current community default — it needs ~5 GB with negligible quality loss. That’s the reason the same model that required an $8,000 server GPU two years ago now runs on a MacBook Air.

VRAM rule of thumb (Q4_K_M quantization)
A quick planning heuristic you can actually use:

~0.6 GB of VRAM per billion parameters at Q4_K_M
8 GB VRAM → comfortable for 7–8B models (Llama 3.3 8B, Qwen 3 8B, Phi-4-mini)
12 GB VRAM (RTX 3060/4060) → 12–14B models (Phi-4, Gemma 3 12B, Qwen 3 14B)
24 GB VRAM (RTX 4090 / A5000) → 22–32B models (Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 3 32B, Mistral Small)
48 GB+ VRAM → 70B models at Q4 (Llama 3.3 70B) or 2×24 GB cards
Apple Silicon unified memory counts as VRAM — an M-series Mac with 32 GB runs 12–14B models comfortably



When SLMs beat big models

Domain-specific Q&A where RAG can supply the context
Privacy-sensitive settings where data cannot leave the building
High-volume simple tasks (classification, extraction, routing) where $0.002 vs $0.025 per 1K tokens compounds into real money
Latency-sensitive apps — smaller models respond faster
Edge deployment — on-device on phones, laptops, or field equipment



When you still want the frontier

Multi-step agentic reasoning where the model must plan, act, check, and revise
Broad world knowledge where no RAG corpus is available
Novel problems that require the strongest generalist available
Tight production deadlines where “mostly works” beats “works once we’ve tuned it”

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG is the single most important applied-AI technique to understand in 2026. It solves the one problem every LLM has: it doesn’t know your data.

The problem
A trained LLM has read billions of web pages, books, and articles. It has not read your organization’s policy manual, your course textbook, this quarter’s sales reports, or the patient intake forms for a specific clinic. Ask it a question about any of those and it does one of two things: (1) it admits ignorance, or (2) it hallucinates a fluent-sounding answer based on patterns from similar-looking documents it did read. Option 2 is the dangerous one — and the one behind most of the LLM failures in Module 1.


The solution
RAG inserts a retrieval step between the user’s question and the model’s answer:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. CHUNK  — split your documents into small passages   │
│            (typically 300–1,000 characters each)       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. EMBED  — convert each chunk into a vector           │
│            (a list of numbers encoding meaning)        │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. STORE  — save the vectors in a vector DB            │
│            (Qdrant, Pinecone, ChromaDB, FAISS, pgvector) │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. RETRIEVE — when a question comes in, find the top-K │
│              most semantically similar chunks          │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5. AUGMENT — inject those chunks into the prompt:      │
│              "Based on these passages from our manual…"│
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 6. GENERATE — the LLM answers using YOUR text as       │
│              context, dramatically reducing hallucination │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Analogy. RAG is like handing an expert consultant your company’s manual before the meeting. They’re still the expert — but now their advice is grounded in your specific situation, not the generic one from their training.
Why this closes the knowledge gap. Modern LLMs are excellent at reading text and synthesizing it; they’re worse at recalling specific text from their training. RAG converts a recall problem into a reading problem — which is the one the model is good at. That is why a 7B model plus relevant context competes with a 1.8T model without it: small model + right context ≈ big model without context.


RAG in the SLM-RAG experiment
In SLM-RAG, course PDFs were chunked into ~500-character passages, embedded with the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embedding model, and stored in a local Qdrant vector database. When a student asked a question, the top-4 most similar passages were retrieved and prepended to the prompt with explicit “Based on these passages…” instructions. That single architectural choice — not a bigger model, not more training data — is what closed the gap with GPT-4.


What actually makes RAG work in 2026
The six-step pipeline above is the shape of RAG. The engineering — what separates a demo that looks good on three questions from a system that holds up in production — happens in three places. These are the decisions that determine whether your RAG system is actually useful.
1. The embedding model is the single most important choice. Vector search retrieves whatever the embedder says is “similar.” If the embedder doesn’t capture domain-specific meaning, nothing downstream saves you. Current defaults:

text-embedding-3-small (OpenAI) — 1536 dims, cheap, strong general baseline, configurable dimensions
BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 — 384 dims, free, open-source, excellent for English. What SLM-RAG used.
BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 / BAAI/bge-m3 — larger, better, still free; bge-m3 supports 100+ languages
jina-embeddings-v3 — strong multilingual performance
Domain-adapted — if you have labeled query/document pairs from real use, fine-tuning a bi-encoder on your corpus beats any off-the-shelf model for your task

For any RAG system that matters, evaluate at least two embedders on a held-out set of ~50 query–passage pairs from your domain before committing.
2. Hybrid retrieval beats dense alone. Pure vector search has a well-documented failure mode: it retrieves things that are semantically close but miss specific terms. Ask about “phi regulatory compliance” and dense search may return passages about HIPAA generally while skipping the one document that literally says “phi disclosure requirements.” The production-grade pattern:
Query
  ├──→ Sparse (BM25): top-50 by keyword/lexical match
  ├──→ Dense (embeddings): top-50 by semantic similarity
  │
  └──→ Merge with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
         │
         └──→ Rerank top-50 with cross-encoder → top-5 → LLM
BM25 is the 1990s keyword-search algorithm. It finds exact term matches, handles entity names, product codes, and technical jargon that dense embeddings often fuzz over. RRF is a one-line fusion algorithm: each document gets a score of sum(1 / (k + rank)) across the two lists, with k typically 60. Documents that rank well in both lists win. LangChain’s EnsembleRetriever, LlamaIndex’s hybrid retriever, and every serious vector DB (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector, Elasticsearch) support hybrid out of the box.
3. Reranking is where precision comes from. The retriever’s job is recall — casting a wide net. The reranker’s job is precision — carefully reordering the net’s contents. A cross-encoder reranker (Cohere Rerank, BAAI/bge-reranker-v2, Jina Reranker) takes the query and each candidate together as a concatenated input and produces a relevance score. Unlike bi-encoder embeddings, it sees the interaction between query and document tokens, which is substantially more accurate. Cost: 50–200 ms to rerank 50 candidates. Payoff: typically 15–30% improvement in top-5 precision on real RAG benchmarks.
Standard production pattern: hybrid retrieve top-50 → rerank with cross-encoder → pass top-5 to the LLM. If your RAG system doesn’t follow this pattern, it’s almost certainly leaving quality on the table.


GraphRAG: when vector search isn’t enough
Classic RAG retrieves passages based on similarity to the query. That’s excellent for “find me the fact” questions. It fails on “global” questions: “What themes appear across this corpus?”, “Summarize the main arguments in my 200 annual reports,” “Which authors disagree with each other?” No single passage contains the answer — the answer emerges from the structure of the corpus.
GraphRAG (Microsoft’s 2024 open-source release) addresses this by pre-building a knowledge graph during ingestion. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from each document, builds a graph, then clusters the graph into hierarchical communities. At query time, the system traverses the graph instead of just retrieving nearest-neighbor chunks. On thematic and summary-level questions, GraphRAG consistently outperforms classic RAG on benchmarks — often substantially. The cost: graph construction is expensive (you run an LLM over the whole corpus once, upfront), and you need a graph database and schema.
Practical decision rule. Start with hybrid + rerank. If your users are asking questions like “what are the main findings across these papers” rather than “what does section 4.2 say about X”, GraphRAG is worth the engineering lift. Otherwise, hybrid + rerank covers 95% of real use cases.


Long context windows: does RAG still matter?
A real 2025–2026 question. Gemini 2.5 Pro offers 2M tokens of context; Claude Opus 4.7 is at 200K–1M depending on tier; Llama 4 Scout ships with a 10M-token context window. You can fit a whole textbook in the prompt. So why bother with retrieval?
Three reasons RAG still matters even in the long-context era:

Cost. A 500K-token prompt at flagship rates costs $1–3 per query. RAG retrieves the 2,000 tokens that actually matter and bills you for those. Over a million queries that’s the difference between a $2M and a $20K bill.
Latency. Processing 500K tokens takes 5–30 seconds depending on model. RAG retrieves in <100 ms and generates the answer in 2–5 seconds.
“Lost in the middle.” Well-documented effect: LLMs attend less reliably to information in the middle of long contexts than at the beginning or end. A 200-page PDF dumped into the prompt gets worse retrieval than a surgically selected 4-passage excerpt.

The pragmatic synthesis: long context changes the constraint, not the principle. For large corpora (anything more than a single book), RAG wins on cost, speed, and accuracy. For a single long document the user is actively working with, long context is cleaner. Real systems use both: RAG over the large corpus, long context for the working document.






✅ Test Yourself: RAG Basics




What problem does RAG solve? (LLMs don’t know your specific data; RAG retrieves and injects it as context.)
List the 6 steps of the pipeline. (Chunk → Embed → Store → Retrieve → Augment → Generate.)
Why does RAG reduce hallucinations? (The model answers from text that is present in the prompt instead of reconstructing from training memory.)
What’s the difference between retrieval and reranking? (Retrieval = recall, cast a wide net for top-50 candidates; reranking = precision, carefully reorder to put the 5 most relevant at the top using a cross-encoder that sees query–document interactions.)
When is RAG the wrong choice? (When you need a behavior pattern or style — that calls for fine-tuning — or when the task requires no domain grounding at all. For “global” questions over a corpus, consider GraphRAG instead.)

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
section: Fine-Tuning: Teaching the Model Your Voice
text:
Fine-Tuning: Teaching the Model Your Voice
Where RAG provides context at query time, fine-tuning permanently nudges the model’s weights so its default behavior changes.

Prompt vs. RAG vs. fine-tune — when each wins









Approach
What it does
Best for
Effort




Prompting
Instructions + examples in the conversation
One-offs, general questions, prototyping, “is this even worth automating?”
Minutes


RAG
Retrieve YOUR docs, add them as context
Domain-specific Q&A, grounding in proprietary content, reducing hallucinations
Hours to a few days


Fine-tuning
Permanently adjust model weights on your examples
Adopting a specific style, vocabulary, tone, or output schema
Days; GPU required



The decision rule: if the answer is in a document, use RAG. If the way you want the model to answer is what’s special — your house style, a specific rubric, a structured output schema — fine-tune. If you don’t know which, start with RAG. RAG is reversible in an hour; fine-tuning is a weekend you can’t get back.


QLoRA: why fine-tuning is now cheap
Traditional fine-tuning of a 7B model required multiple server GPUs and hundreds of GB of memory. QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation) changed that:

Load the base model in 4-bit quantized form (14 GB → ~5 GB for a 7B model)
Freeze the base weights entirely
Attach small LoRA adapters — tiny trainable matrices that learn the delta between the base behavior and the behavior you want
Train for a few epochs on your Q&A pairs

For SLM-RAG, QLoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and DeepSeek-7B ran in hours — not days — on a single A6000. The result was a model that used the course’s vocabulary, followed the course’s problem-solving approach, and referenced concepts in the order the course taught them.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
The Open-Source AI Ecosystem
A vibrant ecosystem of free, open-source tools makes all of this accessible to individuals and small organizations.

Hugging Face — the GitHub of AI
Hugging Face hosts hundreds of thousands of models, datasets, and evaluation benchmarks, almost all freely downloadable. If you need a model for text generation, embeddings, speech, translation, vision, or almost any task, Hugging Face has it. The transformers and datasets libraries are the lingua franca of applied ML.


Ollama — run models locally with one command
Ollama makes local inference embarrassingly easy:
# Install (macOS/Linux/Windows)
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# Pull and run a model
ollama run llama3.3:8b

# Or try a reasoning model
ollama run deepseek-r1:7b
No cloud. No API keys. No subscription. Your prompts never touch the internet. Ollama also exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on localhost:11434, which means any app built for OpenAI (or Claude, via proxies) can point at a local model with a one-line config change.


LM Studio / Jan — GUI alternatives
If the command line isn’t your thing, LM Studio and Jan.ai provide polished desktop GUIs for downloading, configuring, and chatting with local models. LM Studio in particular is how most non-technical people first experience local AI.


LangChain / LlamaIndex — build real applications
Once you’ve moved past chat, these frameworks are how you connect a model to tools, databases, documents, and workflows. LlamaIndex is specifically optimized for RAG; LangChain is more general. Both support local models, cloud APIs, and most vector databases out of the box. They are the right level of abstraction for building a RAG system, a multi-step agent, or any workflow that chains an LLM with other systems.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
The Infrastructure Decision Framework






Choosing the Right Approach



Ask these questions in order, and stop at the first “yes”:

Is the data sensitive or regulated? (HIPAA/FERPA/PII/client-confidential?) → Consider local or on-premises.
Do I need domain-specific accuracy over my own documents? → Add RAG.
Do I need the model to adopt a specific voice, style, or output schema? → Consider fine-tuning.
Is per-token cost a binding constraint? → Consider SLMs for the hot path; reserve flagship models for the genuinely hard 5% of requests.
Do I need cutting-edge capability I can’t get locally? → Use the best cloud model available — with caching and batching.
Am I still exploring? → Start with a free cloud tier. Move to local/custom only once you know what actually works.

Most people should start with cloud AI, add RAG when they hit the “it doesn’t know our stuff” wall, and only fine-tune when prompting and RAG visibly can’t close the gap.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
Guided Practices






Guided Practice 9.1 — Cost Calculator



You’re advising a small nonprofit that processes 200 document queries per day. Compare the options:

Option A. ChatGPT Team at $25/user/month × 3 staff users.
Option B. Claude API — estimate 500 input tokens + 200 output tokens per query, Haiku 4.5 at $1/M input, $5/M output.
Option C. Local Llama 3.3 8B on a $2,000 desktop (Ollama, electricity only).

For each: compute monthly cost, identify the main advantage, and identify the main risk. Which do you recommend and why?


Hints

Option A. 3 × $25 = $75/month. Simple, no setup. Risk: staff may paste sensitive data into Team tier without reading the data policy.
Option B. 200 queries × 30 days = 6,000 queries/month. Input: 3M tokens × $1/M = $3. Output: 1.2M × $5/M = $6. ≈ $9/month. Cheaper, but requires a developer to wrap it in a usable interface. Cache-heavy RAG workloads could drop this to pennies.
Option C. ≈ $30/month electricity + amortized hardware (~$33/month over 5 years) = ≈ $63/month. Data stays local. Risk: requires someone competent to set it up and update models quarterly.
Recommendation depends on technical capacity. If the nonprofit has no developer: A. If it has one who can spend a day wrapping the API: B (by far the best cost-per-query). If it handles sensitive client data: C.









Guided Practice 9.2 — RAG vs Fine-Tuning Decision



For each scenario, decide whether RAG, fine-tuning, both, or neither is appropriate. Justify in one sentence.

A hospital wants an AI that answers patient questions using its post-surgery care protocols.
A marketing agency wants an AI that writes copy in their distinctive brand voice across all clients.
A student wants help studying for a chemistry exam.
A law firm wants an AI that can reference their 10,000-page internal policy manual.
A restaurant wants a chatbot that takes reservations.
A publisher wants an AI that can both match their house style and cite their own back catalog accurately.



Answers


RAG. Ground responses in the actual protocols; fine-tuning adds risk and no clear benefit for a medical content lookup.
Fine-tuning. Brand voice is a behavior pattern, not a retrievable document — and the pattern must apply to new topics, so RAG alone can’t carry it.
Neither. Use a good prompt with SMARTS. A general-purpose model already knows high-school chemistry.
RAG. Classic use case. 10K pages vastly exceeds any context window, but vector search handles it in milliseconds.
Neither. This is a structured booking workflow, not a language task. Use a proper booking system with an LLM wrapper only if you want one.
Both. Fine-tune on past published pieces for voice, then add RAG over the back catalog for accurate citations. This is the only scenario in the list where combining is the right answer.

title: AI Infrastructure — Under the Hood
text:
Module 9 Summary






Key Takeaways




Cloud AI is convenient but sends your data to external servers. Local AI keeps everything on your machine but requires hardware and setup. Most real organizations run a hybrid — cloud for general, local for regulated.
Small language models (3B–14B parameters at Q4_K_M quantization) handle the vast majority of production tasks, especially when paired with RAG. SLM-RAG proved it: a 7B local model matched GPT-4 accuracy at 92% lower cost and half the latency.
RAG — retrieve your documents, inject them as context, generate — is the single most effective technique for grounding AI in your data and suppressing hallucinations. If you learn one infrastructure pattern in 2026, make it this one.
Fine-tuning permanently adjusts model weights. QLoRA makes it affordable on a single GPU. Use it when you need the model to adopt a specific behavior pattern, not when you just need it to look things up.
Decision order. Prompting (fast, free) → RAG (domain grounding) → Fine-tuning (behavioral change) → Custom infrastructure (full control). Don’t jump to step 3 when step 2 will do.
Ollama runs models locally with one command. Hugging Face hosts hundreds of thousands of free models. LangChain/LlamaIndex connects them to your data and workflows. The open-source stack is world-class in 2026.
The equity argument. If only a $200/month subscription buys you good AI, AI’s benefits flow to whoever can afford it. If a single campus GPU matches the frontier for your actual work — every school, every clinic, every small business can participate on its own terms.





💭 Think About It


The SLM-RAG experiment wasn’t just a technical achievement — it was a statement about equity. If the only way to access good AI is a $200/month cloud subscription routed through someone else’s servers, then AI’s benefits flow to institutions and individuals who can afford it, and the data flows somewhere else. But if a single GPU on a campus server can match a frontier model for domain-specific work, then every school, every clinic, every small business can have AI that works for them — on their terms, with their data, at a cost they can sustain. The infrastructure choice isn’t merely technical. It’s political. It determines who gets to participate in the AI revolution and who gets left behind.

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: The Algorithm That Learned to Be Sexist
text:
The Algorithm That Learned to Be Sexist
In 2018, Reuters broke a story that stunned the tech world. Amazon had built a machine learning system to automate hiring — scan resumes, score candidates, surface the best ones. The model trained on ten years of Amazon’s hiring data to learn what a “good” resume looked like.
It worked beautifully. The scores were consistent. The system was fast. There was just one problem: the model had taught itself to penalize women.
Because Amazon’s tech workforce had been predominantly male for a decade, the model learned that “male” was a feature of successful candidates. It downgraded resumes that contained the word “women’s” — as in “women’s chess club” or “captain of the women’s soccer team.” It penalized graduates of two all-women’s colleges. It had learned, with mathematical precision, to replicate a decade of human bias.
Amazon scrapped the tool. But the lesson endures: machine learning doesn’t discover truth. It discovers patterns in data. If the data contains bias, the model learns bias — and serves it back to you with the authority of mathematics.
This module teaches you how machine learning actually works — not the equations, but the ideas.

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: The Big Idea: Learning from Data Instead of Following Rules
text:
The Big Idea: Learning from Data Instead of Following Rules






The One-Sentence Summary



Traditional programming: Humans write rules → computer follows them. Machine learning: Humans provide data → computer discovers the rules.


Imagine you want to teach someone to recognize spam emails.
The traditional approach: You write a list of rules. If the subject line contains “FREE MONEY,” it’s spam. If there are more than three exclamation marks, it’s spam. You write hundreds of rules, maintain the list forever. Spammers adapt, you write more rules.
The machine learning approach: You collect 100,000 emails — 50,000 spam, 50,000 not spam — and show them to the algorithm. You say: “Figure out what makes spam different from real email.” The algorithm examines every email, looking for patterns that distinguish the two categories. It discovers its own rules.
The second approach is how your email’s spam filter actually works. Nobody writes spam rules by hand anymore.






Common Misconceptions About Machine Learning




“ML is magic” — It’s math. Specifically, it’s optimization: adjusting numbers to minimize prediction errors. No magic, no consciousness, no understanding.
“More data always = better” — More representative data helps. More biased data just produces a more confidently biased model.
“ML is objective” — ML finds patterns in data. If the data reflects human decisions (hiring, lending, policing), the model inherits human biases — and scales them.
“The algorithm is neutral” — Choosing what to predict, what data to collect, and how to measure success are all human decisions that shape the outcome before the algorithm runs.
“ML will figure it out” — ML needs human oversight at every stage: data selection, feature engineering, model evaluation, deployment monitoring, and ethical review.




ML in YOUR Field — Real Examples

HealthcareBusinessEducationAgriculture



Supervised: Predicting hospital readmission risk from patient records (labeled: readmitted / not readmitted)
Unsupervised: Discovering patient subgroups with similar symptom patterns for personalized treatment
Reinforcement: Optimizing drug dosing schedules by learning from patient response data over time




Supervised: Predicting customer churn from purchase history (labeled: churned / retained)
Unsupervised: Segmenting customers by behavior to target marketing campaigns
Reinforcement: Dynamic pricing that adjusts in real-time based on demand signals




Supervised: Predicting which students are at risk of failing based on engagement data (labeled: passed / failed)
Unsupervised: Discovering common misconception patterns across thousands of student responses
Reinforcement: Adaptive learning systems that adjust difficulty based on student performance




Supervised: Classifying crop diseases from photos (labeled: healthy / diseased / specific disease type)
Unsupervised: Identifying zones within a field that have similar soil characteristics for variable-rate treatment
Reinforcement: Optimizing irrigation scheduling by learning from soil moisture sensors and weather data

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: The Three Flavors of Machine Learning
text:
The Three Flavors of Machine Learning

1. Supervised Learning: “Here’s the Answer Key”
You give the algorithm labeled examples — data with the correct answer — and it learns to predict answers for new data.
Real-world examples: Email spam detection (labeled “spam” or “not spam”), medical diagnosis (X-rays labeled “tumor” or “no tumor”), language translation (sentence pairs in two languages).


2. Unsupervised Learning: “Find the Patterns”
No labels. You give the algorithm raw data and say: “Find the structure.” It discovers groupings humans might not see.
Real-world examples: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection (finding cyberattacks), topic modeling across thousands of documents.


3. Reinforcement Learning: “Trial, Error, Reward”
The algorithm learns by doing — taking actions, receiving rewards or penalties, and adjusting strategy.
Real-world examples: AlphaGo beating the world Go champion, self-driving cars, TikTok’s algorithm learning what keeps you scrolling.






Guided Practice 2.1



Identify the ML type for each scenario:

A hospital predicts readmission risk using labeled patient records.
A retailer discovers product groupings from purchase data.
A chatbot improves via customer satisfaction ratings.
A bank detects fraudulent transactions.



Click to check your answers


Supervised — labels exist (readmitted vs not).
Unsupervised — no predefined categories.
Reinforcement — actions + rewards.
Could be unsupervised (anomaly detection) or supervised (labeled fraud examples). Most systems use a hybrid.

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: How a Model Learns: The Training Pipeline
text:
How a Model Learns: The Training Pipeline
Here’s the full process from raw data to deployed model:
RAW DATA → Clean & Label → Split (Train/Validate/Test)
                                    ↓
                            TRAINING LOOP:
                    Predict → Compare → Adjust → Repeat
                         (millions of iterations)
                                    ↓
                    Validate → Tune → Test on unseen data
                                    ↓
                    DEPLOY → Monitor for drift → Retrain

Step 1: Collect Data
Everything starts with data. This is where most problems begin. If data is biased, the model learns bias. Amazon’s hiring tool learned from biased data and produced biased outputs.


Step 2: Prepare and Split the Data
Data is cleaned and split into three sets:

Training set (~70-80%): What the model learns from
Validation set (~10-15%): Checks learning during training
Test set (~10-15%): Final evaluation on unseen data

Why split? Because memorization is not learning. A student who memorizes last year’s answer key fails when the professor writes new questions.


Step 3: Train the Model
The model processes training data in an optimization loop: predict → compare → adjust → repeat. Millions of times.


Step 4: Validate and Tune
If the model performs well on training data but poorly on validation data, it’s overfitting: memorizing rather than learning.
If it performs poorly on both, it’s underfitting: it hasn’t learned enough.






The Goldilocks Problem




Overfitting: Performs perfectly on training data, fails on new data. Learned the noise, not the signal.
Underfitting: Performs poorly on everything. Hasn’t captured the patterns.
Just right: Performs well on both known and unknown data. Learned the patterns, not the specific examples.

Concrete example: You’re building a model to predict house prices. It trains on 10,000 homes in one city. An overfit model memorizes that “houses on Elm Street sell for $400K” — it learned specific addresses, not the pattern (square footage + bedrooms + neighborhood quality → price). When tested on homes in a different city, it’s useless. An underfit model just predicts “every house costs $300K.” The right model learns that bigger homes in better neighborhoods cost more — a pattern that transfers to ANY city.




Step 5: Test and Evaluate
Final evaluation on data the model has never seen. The closest simulation of real-world performance.


Step 6: Deploy and Monitor
The model goes live — but real-world data changes over time (data drift). A model that worked in January might fail in June. A spam filter trained in 2023 may miss 2026’s spam tactics. Ongoing monitoring is essential.






✅ Test Yourself: The Training Process




Why is data split into three sets? (Training = learn, Validation = check during training, Test = final evaluation on unseen data)
What’s overfitting? (Memorizing training data rather than learning general patterns — performs well on training data, poorly on new data)
What’s the #1 law of machine learning? (Garbage in, garbage out — the model is only as good as its data)
A house price model that only works in the city it was trained on is an example of: (Overfitting — it memorized specific data instead of learning transferable patterns)

title: How Machine Learning Works
text:
Neural Networks: A Simple Explanation

The Building Block: A Single Neuron
A neuron takes in numbers, multiplies each by a weight (how important that input is), adds them up, and passes the result through a function that decides whether to “fire.” One neuron is useless. Millions connected in layers learn extraordinarily complex patterns.
A concrete forward pass: Imagine a single neuron deciding if an email is spam. It receives three inputs: (1) number of exclamation marks = 5, (2) contains “FREE” = 1 (yes), (3) from known sender = 0 (no). Each input has a learned weight: exclamation marks × 0.3 = 1.5, contains FREE × 0.8 = 0.8, known sender × (-1.0) = 0.0. Sum = 2.3. If the threshold is 1.5, the neuron fires: spam. The weights were learned during training — adjusted millions of times until the neuron got good at catching spam without flagging real emails.


Layers: Input → Hidden → Output

Input layer: Receives raw data (pixels, words, numbers)
Hidden layers: Transform data, extracting increasingly abstract features. Early layers detect simple patterns (edges in images, common words in text). Deeper layers combine simple patterns into complex ones (edges → shapes → faces)
Output layer: Produces the result (“87% cat, 13% dog”)



Deep Learning = Many Hidden Layers
“Deep learning” just means many layers — sometimes dozens or hundreds. More layers = more complex patterns. Frontier LLMs are estimated to have dozens to over 100 layers, though most commercial model architectures (including GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini) are not publicly disclosed — these figures come from leaked estimates and inference, not official sources.
The analogy: A factory assembly line. Raw materials enter one end. Each station performs a transformation. No single station produces the finished product. But after dozens of stations, raw materials become a car. In a neural network, raw pixels enter the input layer. Each hidden layer transforms them. No single layer “understands” the image. But after many layers, the network correctly identifies a cat.






Guided Practice 2.2



A “hot dog or not” image classifier:

What would the training data look like?
What might the hidden layers detect at different depths?
What could go wrong if training data only included American-style hot dogs?



Click to check your answers


Thousands of photos labeled “hot dog” and “not hot dog.”
Early layers: edges and colors. Middle layers: shapes (cylindrical bun, elongated sausage). Deep layers: the full “hot dog” concept.
The model might fail on bratwurst, corn dogs, or Asian-style hot dogs. It learned “American hot dog” patterns, not the universal concept. This is exactly how bias enters ML.

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: The Data Pipeline: Where Everything Begins
text:
The Data Pipeline: Where Everything Begins
COLLECT → CLEAN → LABEL → TRAIN → EVALUATE → DEPLOY → MONITOR

Where Bias Enters the Pipeline








Stage
How Bias Enters
Example




Collection
Data doesn’t represent the full population
Medical AI trained mostly on white patients


Cleaning
Removing “outliers” that are underrepresented groups
Dropping non-English name applications


Labeling
Human labelers bring their own biases
Professional women labeled “receptionist”


Training
Model optimizes for the majority pattern
Amazon: “male” = “successful”


Evaluation
Test set has the same biases as training set
Model looks great — same blind spots


Deployment
Applied to populations it wasn’t trained on
US facial recognition deployed in Africa









The #1 Law of Machine Learning



Garbage in, garbage out. A model is only as good as its data. If the data reflects historical biases, the model reproduces them — often more efficiently and at greater scale than humans.








Guided Practice 2.3 — The Bias Spotter



A company builds an ML model to predict which job applicants will be “successful employees” based on 5 years of performance review data. Identify the bias risk at each stage:

Data: What’s likely in 5 years of performance reviews? (Think: who does the reviewing?)
Labels: How is “successful” defined? (Revenue generated? Manager ratings? Tenure?)
Features: Which input variables might be proxies for protected characteristics?
Evaluation: If the test set has the same biases as the training set, will you even detect the problem?
Deployment: What happens when the model is applied to applicants from backgrounds underrepresented in the training data?



Key risks


Data: Performance reviews carry well-documented biases — studies show women and minorities receive more subjective criticism and less credit for collaborative work.
Labels: If “successful” means “high manager rating,” the model learns what managers reward — which may reflect bias, not performance. If it means “stayed 3+ years,” it penalizes people who were underpaid and left for better opportunities.
Features: Zip code, university name, extracurricular activities, and even name formatting can be proxies for race, socioeconomic status, and national origin.
Evaluation: Yes — this is the insidious part. If your test set has the same biases, the model looks great on paper while systematically discriminating.
Deployment: The model will score these applicants as “low probability of success” because it has few examples of people like them succeeding — creating a self-fulfilling prophecy.

This is exactly what happened at Amazon (Module 2 hook). The model worked perfectly on biased data.

title: How Machine Learning Works
section: Evaluating AI Outputs: Five Questions to Always Ask
text:
Evaluating AI Outputs: Five Questions to Always Ask

What data was it trained on? (Who collected it? What’s missing?)
What was it optimized for? (Accuracy? Engagement? Profit?)
Who validated it? (Diverse populations? Diverse teams?)
What are its known failure modes?
Who benefits and who’s harmed?

title: How Machine Learning Works
text:
Module 2 Summary






Key Takeaways




Machine learning is learning from data, not following rules.
Three types: Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement.
The training process splits data and iterates until the model generalizes well.
Neural networks are layers of simple operations. Deep learning = many layers.
Overfitting is memorization, not learning. The Goldilocks problem.
Bias enters at every stage of the data pipeline.
“Garbage in, garbage out” — the data shapes the model.
Always ask: What data? What optimization? Who validated? Who benefits?





💭 Think About It


Machine learning doesn’t discover truth — it discovers patterns in data. And data is collected by humans, labeled by humans, and reflects human decisions about what to include and what to leave out. When an AI system discriminates, the tempting response is to blame the algorithm. But the algorithm did exactly what it was designed to do: find patterns in the data it was given. The real question isn’t “why is the AI biased?” The real question is “why is the data biased?” — and that’s a human question, not a technical one.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
section: The Lawyers Who Cited Six Cases That Didn’t Exist
text:
The Lawyers Who Cited Six Cases That Didn’t Exist
In June 2023, a New York federal judge sanctioned two attorneys and their law firm $5,000 for submitting a legal brief containing six fabricated court decisions. The attorneys — Steven Schwartz and Peter LoDuca of Levidow, Levidow & Oberman — were representing a client, Roberto Mata, in a personal-injury suit against the airline Avianca. Schwartz had used ChatGPT to find case law supporting his argument. The chatbot returned six opinions that looked real: Varghese v. China Southern Airlines, Martinez v. Delta Airlines, Shaboon v. EgyptAir, and three others — complete with plausible citations, quoted holdings, and internal references to other cases.
When opposing counsel couldn’t locate the cases and the court ordered Schwartz to produce copies, he asked ChatGPT again. The chatbot doubled down: “Varghese… is a real case” and “can be found in reputable legal databases such as LexisNexis and Westlaw” (Mata v. Avianca, 678 F. Supp. 3d 443, S.D.N.Y. 2023).
None of them existed.
The case became the most cited example of AI hallucination in professional practice — but it was not a one-off. Damien Charlotin, a French legal scholar, maintains a public database of court rulings that address AI-fabricated content in legal filings; as of April 2026, it tracks roughly 1,300 such rulings worldwide. A Stanford CodeX analysis of 114 U.S. cases through October 2025 found that 90% involved solo practitioners or small firms, and of the cases that identified the AI tool, half named some version of ChatGPT.
This story illustrates both the danger and the opportunity of AI for research. The danger: AI will confidently fabricate sources — and even fabricate the verification that those sources exist. The opportunity: when used correctly — with the right tools, the right workflow, and the right verification habits — AI can make you a dramatically more effective researcher than you’ve ever been.
This module teaches you the right way.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
The New Research Landscape
Research used to mean one thing: go to a search engine, type keywords, wade through results, read articles, take notes, synthesize. It was slow, thorough, and entirely manual.
AI has fractured this into three distinct approaches, each with different strengths:









Approach
How It Works
Best For
Watch Out For




Traditional search (Google, library databases)
Returns links. You read and synthesize.
Known-item search, academic databases, primary sources
Slow but reliable — you verify as you go


AI-powered search (Perplexity, Google AI Overviews)
Returns synthesized answers WITH citations
Quick factual questions, getting oriented on a topic
May cite real sources but misrepresent what they say


AI research agents (Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research)
Autonomously conducts multi-step research over minutes
Complex questions requiring synthesis across many sources
Can go deep but may follow wrong paths. Always verify conclusions.



The key insight: these are complementary, not competitive. The best researchers in 2026 use all three — AI to accelerate discovery, traditional search to verify and go deep, and their own judgment to synthesize.






What’s the Actual Hallucination Rate?



Hard numbers from peer-reviewed research:








Tool type
Hallucination rate on legal queries
Source




General-purpose LLMs (e.g., GPT-4, PaLM 2)
58% - 82%
Dahl et al. (2024), J. Legal Analysis


LexisNexis Lexis+ AI (RAG-grounded)
~17%
Magesh et al. (2025), J. Empirical Legal Stud.


Westlaw AI-Assisted Research (RAG-grounded)
~33%
Magesh et al. (2025)



Even the best RAG-grounded tools hallucinated on roughly 1 in 6 queries. Retrieval-augmented generation helps, but it does not solve hallucination. If you’re citing AI output where accuracy matters, verify every claim, every citation, every time.








Common Misconceptions About AI Research




“AI citations are always real” — 23 out of 47 were fake in our opening story. AI generates plausible-sounding citations as easily as real ones.
“If it cites a real paper, the claim is accurate” — AI can cite a real source but misrepresent what it says. The citation trap.
“NotebookLM replaces reading the original” — It supplements reading, not replaces it. Always check AI summaries against the source.
“Deep Research is always better than manual search” — Deep Research is great for breadth but can follow wrong paths. For a specific known source, manual search wins.
“AI research is cheating” — Using AI to FIND and ORGANIZE information is AI-assisted research. Having AI WRITE your analysis is a different thing. SMARTS keeps you on the right side.




What AI Research Looks Like in YOUR Field

HealthcareBusinessEducationAgriculture



“What’s the latest evidence on [treatment] for [condition]?” — Perplexity with Academic focus
Uploading 15 clinical guidelines into NotebookLM to compare recommendations across organizations
Deep Research on drug interaction profiles for a specific patient population
Critical: Medical research AI MUST be verified against peer-reviewed sources and clinical databases (PubMed, UpToDate)




“What are the market trends in [industry] for Q1 2026?” — Deep Research for competitive analysis
Uploading quarterly reports into NotebookLM to extract patterns across periods
Using AI to analyze customer feedback themes from 500+ survey responses
Critical: Financial claims from AI must be verified against SEC filings, analyst reports, or primary data




“What does the research say about [teaching method]?” — Perplexity with Academic focus
Uploading curriculum standards into NotebookLM to map learning objectives
Deep Research on AI literacy frameworks for a curriculum proposal
Critical: Educational research claims should be verified in ERIC, Google Scholar, or discipline-specific databases




“What are the recommended treatments for [crop disease] in [region]?” — Perplexity
Uploading extension service bulletins into NotebookLM for quick reference during the growing season
Deep Research on precision agriculture technologies for a grant proposal
Critical: Agricultural recommendations must be verified against local extension office guidance and soil/climate data

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
AI-Powered Search Tools

Perplexity
Perplexity is a search engine that answers questions conversationally and shows you exactly which sources informed each claim. Think of it as “Google that actually reads the pages for you.”
What it does well:

Returns concise answers with numbered source citations
Lets you ask follow-up questions (conversational search)
Shows you the actual sources so you can verify
Excellent for getting oriented on a new topic quickly
“Focus” modes let you search academic papers, YouTube, Reddit, or the full web

What to watch for:

It can misrepresent what a source actually says (cites a real article but summarizes it incorrectly)
Citation ≠ verification — just because it links a source doesn’t mean the claim matches the source
For academic work, always click through to the original source and confirm

Best use case: “I need to understand [topic] quickly and I want to know where the information is coming from.”


Google AI Overviews
Google now displays AI-generated summary boxes at the top of search results for many queries. These synthesize information from multiple web pages into a paragraph answer.
What it does well:

Fast — the answer appears before you click anything
Integrated with Google’s massive search index
Shows source links below the summary

What to watch for:

Early versions made embarrassing errors (suggesting people add glue to pizza to keep cheese from sliding off — sourced from a joke Reddit post)
Summaries can be misleading when the topic is nuanced or contested
You can’t ask follow-up questions — it’s a one-shot summary

Best use case: Quick factual lookup where you’ll verify the answer anyway.






The Citation Trap



AI-powered search tools cite real sources. This creates a dangerous illusion of reliability. The citation makes you trust the claim — but the AI may have misinterpreted, oversimplified, or outright misrepresented what the source actually says. Always click the source. Read the relevant section. Confirm the claim matches. Citations are starting points for verification, not proof of accuracy.








✅ Test Yourself: AI Search Tools




What’s the key difference between Perplexity and a regular Google search? (Perplexity synthesizes answers with numbered citations; Google returns links you read yourself)
What is the “citation trap”? (AI cites real sources but may misrepresent what they say — citation ≠ verification)
When would you use traditional Google over AI search? (When you need a specific known document, a specific database, or the most authoritative primary source)

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
Deep Research Agents
Deep Research is a newer category of AI tool that goes beyond answering a single question. These agents autonomously conduct multi-step research — searching, reading, synthesizing, following threads, and producing comprehensive reports.

How Deep Research Works

You give the agent a research question or topic
The agent creates a research plan (which sub-questions to investigate)
It searches the web, reads multiple sources, and extracts key findings
It follows leads — if one source mentions a related study, it searches for that too
It synthesizes everything into a structured report with citations
The whole process takes 5-30 minutes depending on complexity



Available Deep Research Tools








Tool
Provider
Strengths




Deep Research
OpenAI (ChatGPT Pro)
Thorough, produces long-form reports with citations


Deep Research
Google (Gemini Advanced)
Leverages Google’s search index, good at finding recent sources


Research mode
Perplexity Pro
Faster than others, good at following citation chains


Claude with search
Anthropic
Strong at synthesis and nuanced analysis of what it finds





When to Use Deep Research vs Regular Search







Use Deep Research When…
Use Regular Search When…




The question requires synthesis across many sources
You need one specific fact


You want a comprehensive overview of a topic
You need a specific document you already know exists


You need to compare multiple perspectives
You need to search a specific database (academic, legal, medical)


You’re starting research on an unfamiliar topic
You need the most authoritative primary source









Guided Practice 5.1



Pick a topic you’re curious about but don’t know well. Use three different approaches to research it:

A regular Google search (5 minutes of reading results)
Perplexity (ask the same question)
A Deep Research agent if available (or a detailed ChatGPT/Claude conversation with search enabled)

Compare: Which approach gave you the most useful overview? Which gave you the most trustworthy information? Which was fastest? Which would you use for different stages of a research project?


What most people find

Regular Google gives you the most control but takes the most time. Perplexity gives a fast, well-cited overview that’s great for getting oriented. Deep Research gives the most comprehensive synthesis but may include errors you’d miss without verification. The winning strategy: start with Perplexity to get oriented, use Deep Research for comprehensive synthesis, then verify key claims with traditional search and primary sources.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
NotebookLM: Your Documents, Made Interactive
Google’s NotebookLM is one of the most underappreciated AI tools available. It lets you upload documents (PDFs, Google Docs, web pages, YouTube videos) and creates an interactive knowledge base that you can ask questions about.

What Makes NotebookLM Special
Unlike ChatGPT or Claude, which draw on their general training data, NotebookLM only answers from your uploaded sources. If the answer isn’t in your documents, it tells you — rather than hallucinating. This makes it dramatically more reliable for document-specific questions.


Use Cases

Studying: Upload lecture notes, textbook chapters, and study guides. Ask questions. Get answers grounded in YOUR course materials.
Meeting prep: Upload the agenda, last meeting’s minutes, and relevant reports. Ask “What were the action items from last meeting?” or “What’s the background on agenda item 3?”
Literature review: Upload 10-20 research papers. Ask “What do these papers agree on?” or “What methodological approaches are used across these studies?”
Policy analysis: Upload policy documents, regulations, and guidelines. Ask specific questions about what’s allowed, required, or prohibited.
Learning a new field: Upload foundational papers and textbooks. Ask the AI to explain concepts using only those sources.



Audio Overviews
NotebookLM can generate audio summaries of your documents — a podcast-style conversation between two AI voices discussing the key ideas in your uploaded material. This is genuinely useful for:

Reviewing material while commuting or exercising
Getting a high-level overview before diving into detailed reading
Identifying which sections of a long document are most relevant







NotebookLM vs General AI Chatbots



The key difference: grounding. ChatGPT answers from its training data (the entire internet). NotebookLM answers from YOUR documents. This means NotebookLM is less likely to hallucinate — but it can only answer questions covered by the documents you uploaded. Use ChatGPT/Claude for broad questions. Use NotebookLM for document-specific questions where accuracy matters more than breadth.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
AI for Data Analysis
One of the most practical AI applications for working professionals: analyzing data without being a data scientist.

What AI Can Do With Your Data

Summarize a spreadsheet: “What are the key trends in this sales data?”
Create visualizations: “Make a bar chart comparing Q1 vs Q2 revenue by region”
Run calculations: “Calculate the year-over-year growth rate for each product category”
Find patterns: “Are there any correlations between customer age and purchase frequency?”
Clean messy data: “Standardize the date formats and remove duplicate rows”
Generate SQL queries: “Write a query to find all customers who haven’t purchased in 90 days”



Tools for AI Data Analysis








Tool
How It Works
Best For




ChatGPT Advanced Data Analysis
Upload files, ask questions in natural language
Quick analysis of CSVs and spreadsheets


Claude
Upload files, strong at explaining methodology
Analysis that requires careful reasoning


Google Sheets + Gemini
AI built into the spreadsheet
Analysis within your existing workflow


Microsoft Copilot in Excel
AI built into Excel
Enterprise users already in Microsoft ecosystem





The Critical Skill: Knowing When to Trust the Analysis
AI data analysis has a subtle danger: it can produce a chart that looks professional, a statistic that looks precise, and a conclusion that looks authoritative — while being completely wrong about what the data means.
Common failure modes:

Confusing correlation with causation — “Sales increase when temperature increases” doesn’t mean heat causes purchases (both increase in summer)
Ignoring missing data — analyzing only the rows that have values, producing misleading averages
Wrong statistical test — running a t-test when the data isn’t normally distributed
Cherry-picking results — presenting the one analysis that supports a conclusion while ignoring contradictory patterns

The rule: Use AI to DO the analysis (compute, visualize, summarize). Use YOUR brain to INTERPRET the analysis (what does it mean, what’s missing, what conclusions are justified).






Guided Practice 5.2



Find a publicly available dataset (e.g., from data.gov, Kaggle, or your own work). Upload it to ChatGPT or Claude and ask:

“Summarize this dataset. How many rows, how many columns, what are the key variables?”
“What are the 3 most interesting patterns or trends in this data?”
“Create a visualization that shows the most important finding.”
“What questions can this data NOT answer?”

Pay attention to question 4 — does the AI acknowledge the limitations of the data, or does it gloss over them?


What to look for

Most AI tools handle questions 1-3 well — they can compute, summarize, and visualize. Question 4 is the test of critical thinking. Good models will acknowledge limitations (sample size, missing variables, time period constraints). Weaker responses will claim the data “shows” conclusions that require additional evidence. If the AI doesn’t mention limitations, you need to identify them yourself.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
The Research Verification Workflow
Here’s the process that separates AI-enhanced research from AI-dependent research:

The 4-Step Verification Loop
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. DISCOVER — Use AI to find information     │
│     Perplexity, Deep Research, ChatGPT/Claude │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  2. VERIFY — Check key claims against         │
│     original sources. Click the citation.     │
│     Does it actually say what AI claimed?     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  3. DEEPEN — Use traditional search for       │
│     the most important findings. Find         │
│     primary sources. Read the original.       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  4. SYNTHESIZE — Use YOUR judgment to         │
│     combine findings. What does it mean?      │
│     What's missing? What's uncertain?         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘


The Citation Verification Checklist
For every AI-generated citation you plan to use:

Does the paper/article actually exist? (Search the title in Google Scholar or the publisher’s website)
Is the author real? Do they work in this field?
Is the journal/publication real and reputable?
Does the paper actually say what the AI claims it says?
Is the year correct?
Are the specific statistics or quotes accurate?

This takes 60-90 seconds per citation. It’s the difference between the student with 47 citations and 24 real ones versus a student with 47 citations and 47 verified ones.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
section: The Line Between AI-Assisted and AI-Generated
text:
The Line Between AI-Assisted and AI-Generated
This distinction matters — academically, professionally, and ethically:








Category
What It Means
Example




AI-assisted research
You use AI to find, organize, and analyze — but the thinking, synthesis, and writing are yours
Using Perplexity to find sources, then reading them yourself and writing your own analysis


AI-generated content
AI produces the output — you edit, verify, or submit as-is
Asking ChatGPT to “write a literature review on X” and submitting the output


AI-enhanced workflow
AI handles mechanical tasks while you handle intellectual ones
AI cleans your data and makes charts; you interpret the results and draw conclusions



Most academic and professional contexts accept AI-assisted research and AI-enhanced workflows. AI-generated content is more controversial and often prohibited or restricted. Know your institution’s policy (Module 10 covers this in depth).
The SMARTS framework (Module 4) naturally produces AI-assisted rather than AI-generated work — because SMARTS keeps YOU in the reasoning loop. You think, the AI supports. That’s the difference.

title: AI for Research and Analysis
text:
Module 5 Summary






Key Takeaways




Three research approaches: Traditional search (reliable, slow), AI-powered search (fast, needs verification), Deep Research agents (comprehensive, needs oversight). Use all three.
Perplexity gives fast, cited answers. Google AI Overviews give quick summaries. Both require you to click through and verify what the sources actually say.
Deep Research agents autonomously investigate complex questions. They’re powerful but can follow wrong paths. Always verify conclusions.
NotebookLM creates grounded knowledge bases from YOUR documents — more reliable than general chatbots for document-specific questions.
AI data analysis is powerful for computing, visualizing, and summarizing. But INTERPRETING what the data means is still YOUR job.
The 4-step verification loop: Discover (AI) → Verify (check sources) → Deepen (primary sources) → Synthesize (your judgment).
Every citation must be verified. 60-90 seconds per citation. No exceptions.
AI-assisted ≠ AI-generated. Use AI to find and organize. Use your brain to think and write. SMARTS keeps you on the right side of this line.





💭 Think About It


AI can read faster than you. It can search more broadly, summarize more quickly, and find connections across more sources. But it can’t think about what it reads. It can tell you what 50 papers say. It can’t tell you which ones matter, which ones are methodologically sound, and which conclusions are justified by the evidence. The research skill of the future isn’t finding information — it’s evaluating information that AI found for you. That requires domain knowledge, critical thinking, and judgment. Those are human skills. They just became the most valuable skills in the room.
